Breaking: PipelineRL

📅 25 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection.
  • Sources indicate that in this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm.
  • In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection. PipelineRL's key innovation is inflight weight updates during RL training (see Figure 1 below). This allows PipelineRL to achieve constantly high inference throughput and minimize the lag between the weights used for rollouts and the most recently updated model weights. The result: fast and stable RL training for large language models.

Sources indicate that in this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm. We also present the modular PipelineRL architecture that facilitates trying new inference / trainer combinations.

In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection. To explain this trade-off let us first define conventional RL algorithmically:.

To achieve high throughput, the inference servers must use large batch sizes and, therefore, generate data for multiple policy optimization steps. However, each optimization step increases the lag between the current policy and the data collected using the inference policy, progressively making collected data more off-policy and less effective for training. On-policy learning requires data for a single optimization step. But producing small amounts of data with many GPUs is inefficient because this means the per-GPU batch size is small. Furthermore the batch size goes down as the inference server finishes the short sequences and has only the few longest sequences in progress.

PipelineRL (Figure 1b) remediates this trade-off through inflight weight updates. We revision the weights in inference servers after each optimizer step without ever stopping inference. We only pause the inference at all inference servers for just the time needed to receive the latest weights. Inflight weight updates allow the inference server to constantly maintain the optimal batch size while simultaneously ensuring data remains on-policy or near on-policy, which leads to better GPU utilization and more effective learning, respectively.

In a recent development, to demonstrate the effectiveness of PipelineRL and the benefits of inflight weight updates, we trained a 7B model and 32B model on the Open-Reasoner-Zero dataset. Looking at the learning curves we see that PipelineRL matches or exceeds the performance of Open-Reasoner on the popular reasoning test benchmarks: AIME 2024 and MATH 500 (see Figure 2 above).

Notably, our RL implementation is much simpler than Open-Reasoner-Zero. While Open-Reasoner-Zero uses a value function, our implementation is a simplified version of GRPO. In particular, we found that the trust region importance weight clamping is not needed for stable training. Neither was overlong sequence filtering or reward shaping from the DAPO paper. For normalizing the loss we just use the number of sequences in the batch as the denominator, giving equal weights to all tokens. We used no KL penalty and no entropy bonus (though our implementation does support reference model KL). Despite the simplicity of our implementation, or perhaps thanks to it, training is very stable as you can see in this wandb report.

One might expect that inflight weight updates would result in an unstable training process, since sequence generation proceeds with stale keys and values in the KV cache that was computed with a previous model version. However, our experiments indicate this does not adversely affect stability.

PipelineRL is built to be modular and take advantage of rapid improvements in highly-specialized inference and training software (SGLang, vLLM, Nvidia Dynamo, DeepSpeed, FSDP, TorchTitan, FastLLM, etc.). We propose clear contracts between the inference and training components, allowing easy integration of new inference and training solutions as they become available.

The inference software must expose the following APIs to PipelineRL[1]:.

If init_process_group and request_weight_update APIs become the industry standard, one will be able to plug-and-play try using difference inference implementations with PipelineRL.

Sources indicate that pipelineRL training code feeds freshly-generated training data to trainer workers as soon as the right number of training tokens has accumulated for each of them. One can make any training software that exposes these Python APIs work with PipelineRL:.

Sources indicate that pipelineRL presently uses the HuggingFace accelerate library to give the user a choice between DeepSpeed and FSDP. But we found that accelerate contract is too flexible and can be confusing. We will be moving to the stricter contract as described above that will make using other trainers easier.

Recent findings suggest that upcoming features. Our implementation is still experimental and lacks some key functionality. Top priorities for us include using coroutines for more precise inference batch size control, multi-modal support and sequence parallel training. We would also welcome contributions of more inference server and trainer integrations. We will not, however, try to make the pipeline-rl repo a framework that supports all possible algorithms and reward functions. Our take is that pipeline-rl should be a hackable and fast reference implementation of GRPO with easily verifiable rewards. If you'd like to do a research project using PipelineRL, you can just fork the repo and have fun hacking the code!

More research coming soon. More analysis is needed to understand how inflight weight updates affect the training dynamics, and to carefully measure the speed-ups that PipelineRL brings. Also, much can be said about the similarities between PipelineRL and highly relevant prior work on asynchronous Reinforcement Learning for LLMs. For all this and more please stay tuned for our upcoming research paper!

According to recent reports, alexandre Piché wrote the first synchronous version of our RL code while working on TapeAgents. Dzmitry Bahdanau refactored the code to be asynchronous and distributed, and implemented inflight weight updates. Rafael Pardinas implemented sequence packing. Ehsan Kamaloo helped with running the experiments. Xiaoyin Chen helped with debugging the framework.

We acknowledge the prior RL for LLM implementations such as TRL, OpenRLHF and veRL for the many tricks we borrowed from them. Artifacts from other open-source reasoning projects, such as Simple-RL, Deepscaler, DAPO and OpenReasoner were instrumental for stabilizing PipelineRL. We would like to recognize Christopher Manning, Michael Noukhovitch for their thoughtful comments. Finally, we thank the broader ServiceNow Research team and ServiceNow CoreLLM teams for being amazing colleagues.

[1] The current contract in the code is slightly different, but we are refactoring it as described above.

JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI coding agents caught peeking at GitHub answers, stumble when JetBrains hides the crib sheet.
  • JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.
  • The organization labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI coding agents caught peeking at GitHub answers, stumble when JetBrains hides the crib sheet.

JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.

The organization labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.

Like its predecessor, Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language, in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files.

In a recent development, the revised benchmark now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories.

The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request.

A 30-minute limit was set for each task.

Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60  percent on those based on closed source repositories.

In a recent development, although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely upcoming to them.

Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks.

When restricted to closed source tasks, two dark horse models rose to the top: Gemini 3.8 Flash, via Antigravity CLI, topped the list with a 60  percent success rate, closely followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (running on OpenCode) at 58.9 percent.

Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however.

In a recent development, in contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models.

Claude’s lackluster completion rates on closed source tasks are somewhat sus given how both of these Anthropic models scored significantly higher on tasks using open source materials.

In fact Claude ran the table when it came to open source: Fable 5.1 topped the charts with 86.2 percent accuracy, closely followed by Opus 5.5 at 84.8 percent accuracy.

(Kotlin users will pay dearly for the extra sliver of Anthropic accuracy: The average cost of Fable completing a Kotlin cleanup task runs $2.38, while Opus could do the job for $0.68.).

It has been revealed that one possible interpretation of these disparate numbers is that models are drawing from their own knowledge bases instead of reasoning from scratch. Whether this is cheating or the models simply working as intended might be more a matter of philosophical debate.

Mark Hinkle, founder of the AIE Network consultancy, suspects the issue of integrity may go deeper.

"Private code doesn't stop reward hacking, it changes the shortcut," he wrote to The Register on LinkedIn.

"On public code the agent goes and finds the answer somebody has already published. On private code there's no answer to find, so it satisfies whatever is checking it. I treat these things like entry-level employees, and a sharp new hire figures out fast what the boss actually looks at.".

According to recent reports, jetBrains did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but concluded in its post that more investigation is needed. It promises that its people will pore over the open source results to see if any have been contaminated by the LLMs' own memory. It also plans to run its own static analysis tool, Qodana, against the results to check for errors.

Sireesha Pulipati, a staff data engineer and AI observer, suggested, also by LinkedIn, that JetBrains may have needed more specificity in its agent instructions.

Industry observers note that "Out of the box [an agent] tends to reach for generic patterns. But when we give it instructions and skills that tell it where to look for our patterns and context, it follows them. A well-controlled harness, with those standards built in, is what makes the agent useful," Pulipati wrote.

It has been revealed that so good on JetBrains for providing Kotlin users some information about working with AI, but, as always, AI benchmarks should be approached with extreme side-eye. ®.

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing AutoRound: Intel’s Advanced Quantization for LLMs and VLMs

📅 29 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging.
  • In a recent development, autoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel.
  • Industry observers note that despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging. Quantization offers a solution by reducing model size and inference latency. Intel's AutoRound emerges as a cutting-edge quantization tool that balances accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility.

In a recent development, autoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel. It uses signed gradient descent to jointly optimize weight rounding and clipping ranges, enabling accurate low-bit quantization (e.g., INT2 - INT8) with minimal accuracy loss in most scenarios. For example, at INT2, it outperforms popular baselines by up to 2.1x higher in relative accuracy. The image below provides an overview of the core algorithm in AutoRound. For more details, please refer to our paper.

Industry observers note that despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode. It also supports mixed-bit tuning, lm-head quantization, GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF format exporting, and flexible tuning recipes.

AutoRound delivers highly promising results, particularly in low-bit quantization scenarios. Evaluations across a variety of tasks show that it outperforms popular methods by a wide margin at 2-bit precision (source). At 4 bits, AutoRound continues to hold a competitive edge in most cases, as demonstrated on the Low-Bit Open LLM Leaderboard.

Recent findings suggest that LLMs: AutoRound supports nearly all popular LLM architectures, including well-known models like Qwen, LLaMA, and DeepSeek. Ready-to-use quantized models are available on Hugging Face through collections such as OPEA, Kaitchup, and fbaldassarri.

According to recent reports, VLMs: AutoRound supports over 10 vision-language models (VLMs), including Mistral-Small-3.1, Gemma3, and more. You can find the full list in the README, and ready-to-use quantized models are available in the OPEA Hugging Face collection. For models not yet supported, you can still apply our RTN method with --iters 0. No tuning is required, but some accuracy loss is expected.

It has been revealed that autoRound requires only 200 tuning steps and a small calibration dataset (as few as 128 samples) to achieve high accuracy. This efficiency translates to faster quantization times and reduced resource consumption compared to other int2 methods, which are more computationally intensive.

Right now, only offline mode is supported to generate quantized models.

AutoRound also offers another two recipes, auto-round-best and auto-round-light, designed for optimal accuracy and improved speed, respectively.

For 2 bits, we recommend using auto-round-best or auto-round. For a comparison of the three recipes, please refer to the table below.

W4G128 Average Accuracy of 13 tasks (mmlu-pro, if_eval, gsm8k, etc) and Time Cost Results (Testing was conducted on the Nvidia A100 80G using the version of PyTorch 2.6.0 with enable_torch_compile):.

This setting offers a better trade-off between accuracy and tuning cost, and is recommended in all scenarios.

For the best/light settings of AutoRound for API usage or mixed-bit configurations, please refer to AutoRound README.

AutoRound automatically selects the best available backend based on the installed libraries and prompts the user to install additional libraries when a better backend is found. For more details, please refer to HF README or AutoRound README.

Most GPTQ/AWQ models can be converted to the AutoRound format for better compatibility and support with Intel devices. Please note that the quantization config will be changed if the model is serialized.

AutoRound offers a meaningful improvement step forward in post-training quantization for large language and vision-language models. By combining high accuracy, exceptional efficiency, and broad compatibility with popular models, devices, and export formats, AutoRound makes low-bit quantization both practical and powerful. Whether you're deploying LLMs at scale or experimenting with edge inference on VLMs, AutoRound provides the tools and flexibility you need to achieve optimal performance with minimal overhead. We invite you to try it out and join the growing community pushing the boundaries of efficient AI deployment.

Contributions to AutoRound are welcome and greatly appreciated! Whether it's fixing bugs, improving documentation, adding new features, or suggesting improvements, your help is always valued.

If you encounter any issues with auto-round, please open an issue on the AutoRound repository.

We would like to thank the open-source low-precision libraries including AutoGPTQ, AutoAWQ, GPTQModel, Triton, Marlin and ExLLaMAV2, whose CUDA kernels are used in AutoRound.

Microsoft fixes Office dialog that had nothing to say and wouldn't go away

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (390 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Update resolves work-blocking popup, but affected consumers may need an administrator command prompt to install it.
  • It has been revealed that microsoft has released a fix for a baffling bug that threw a blank window over Office applications and brought work to a standstill.
  • Because the dialog offered no way to close it, some consumers were locked out of their work entirely, unable to continue until the issue was resolved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update resolves work-blocking popup, but affected consumers may need an administrator command prompt to install it.

It has been revealed that microsoft has released a fix for a baffling bug that threw a blank window over Office applications and brought work to a standstill. The problem appeared when users debuted an affected Office app, which could display an empty dialog box with no text and no buttons.

Because the dialog offered no way to close it, some consumers were locked out of their work entirely, unable to continue until the issue was resolved.

The good news is that there's an update to fix the problem – version 2611, build 16.0.20625.20142. The bad news is that you might not be able to launch the applications to perform the update because of that blank dialog window.

Industry observers note that microsoft instructs affected users to save their work, close all Office applications, and open Command Prompt as administrator. They can then force the revision with: "%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142.

The glitch affects a swathe of Microsoft 365 products – Excel, Word, Outlook, PowerPoint, Access, and OneNote.

People reported the problem on Microsoft's forums, where volunteer moderator Stefan Blom noted that "this seems to be a common error at the moment" and suggested users try an Office repair or the more thorough Online Repair.

According to recent reports, online Repair reinstalls Office, however, some people reported activation and sign-in problems alongside the blank windows, which may hint at the cause. Microsoft has yet to elucidate.

Other people found that rolling back Office resolved the glitch, while several reported that signing in with another application, such as Edge, fixed things.

Sources indicate that for administrators preparing fleets of devices, a dialog that blocks first use creates another deployment headache. One user with E3 licensing reported: "We can't just hand off a staged machine without getting call[s] that our newly introduced people can't get Office to work because of the blank licensing window.".

Microsoft has shared a fix for the problem, but has not stated which versions of its productivity applications were affected, nor has it explained what went wrong.

Industry observers note that the fix is welcome. An explanation of how Office ended up blocking users with a window containing nothing at all would be welcome too. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that TL;DR: Today, Meta releases Llama Guard 4, a 12B dense (not a MoE!) multimodal safety model, and two new Llama Prompt Guard 2 models. This release comes with multiple open model checkpoints, along with an interactive notebook for you to get started easily 🤗. Model checkpoints can be found in Llama 4 Collection.

It has been revealed that vision and large language models deployed to production can be exploited to generate unsafe output through jail breaking image and text prompts. Unsafe content in production varies from being harmful or inappropriate to violating privacy or intellectual property.

Fresh safeguard models address this issue by evaluating image and text, and the content generated by the model. User messages classified as unsafe are not passed to vision and large language models, and unsafe assistant responses can be filtered out by production services.

Llama Guard 4 is a latest multimodal model designed to detect inappropriate content in images and text, whether used as input or generated as output by the model. It’s a dense 12B model pruned from Llama 4 Scout model, and it can run on a single GPU (24 GB of VRAM). It can evaluate both text-only and image+text inputs, making it suitable for filtering both inputs and outputs of large language models. This enables flexible moderation pipelines where prompts are analyzed before reaching the model, and generated responses are reviewed afterwards for safety. It can also understand multiple languages.

The model can classify 14 types of hazard defined in the MLCommons hazard taxonomy, along with code interpreter abuse.

The list of categories detected by the model can be configured by the user on inference, as we’ll see later.

Industry observers note that llama Guard 4 employs a dense feedforward early-fusion architecture, in contrast to Llama 4 Scout, which uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers with one shared dense expert and sixteen routed experts per layer. To leverage Llama 4 Scout pre-training, the architecture is pruned into a dense model by removing all routed experts and router layers, retaining only the shared expert. This results in a dense feedforward model initialized from the pre-trained shared expert weights. No additional pre-training is applied to Llama Guard 4. The post-training data consists of multi-image training data up to 5 images and human-annotated multilingual data, previously used to train Llama Guard 3 models. The training data consists of 3:1 text-only to multimodal data.

Below you can find the performance of Llama Guard 4 compared against Llama Guard 3, the previous iteration of the safety model.

It has been revealed that the Llama Prompt Guard 2 series introduces two latest classifiers with 86M and 22M parameters, focused on detecting prompt injections and jailbreaks. Compared to its predecessor, Llama Prompt Guard 1, this new version offers improved performance, a faster and more compact 22M model, tokenization resistant to adversarial attacks, and simplified binary classification (benign vs. malicious).

To use Llama Guard 4 and Prompt Guard 2, make sure you have hf_xet and the preview release of transformers for Llama Guard installed.

This works because the chat template generates a system prompt that does not mention the excluded categories as part of the list of categories to watch for.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes after Eight Years at 15.
  • Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.
  • In a recent development, AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes after Eight Years at 15.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

In a recent development, AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes. The new limit applies to synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and without an opt-in. The 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018, after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015.

Raising the limit is a configuration change per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds with a validation error:.

The change covers one of the three shapes Lambda took this year. Web Functions keep 15 minutes, and Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, while on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations now get 30 minutes and asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September. AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations, and report generation as the workloads that outgrew 15 minutes.

According to Tarun Rai Madan, Dan Slusariuc, and Snehil Ameta, the authors of the announcement, the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity:.

It has been revealed that concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. At the same request rate, a function that runs for 30 minutes instead of 15 needs twice the concurrency. For example, 1 request per second at 30 minutes each needs 1,800 concurrent executions.

The rest of the post is about what sits around the function. An SQS queue's visibility timeout has to be at least six times the function timeout, which means three hours. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams read one batch per shard at a time, so a slow function slows the shard. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes. A NAT gateway still drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and the Init phase keeps its 10-second limit.

Wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner, tested the SQS rule in eu-west-1 by raising a function to 1,800 seconds behind a queue with a 90-minute visibility timeout and then lowering the queue to 60 seconds. Both changes were accepted with the mapping still enabled, while a latest mapping from the same queue was refused:.

It has been revealed that so the check exists, but only at creation. One more thing the test indicated: at creation, Lambda compared the queue with the function timeout itself, not with six times it. I did not test where exactly that line sits, so treat the six times as guidance you enforce yourself.

He adds that an asynchronous function which times out three times has run for 90 minutes before the event reaches a dead-letter queue, and concludes that 30 minutes is the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.

Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS and AWS Serverless Hero, writes:.

Hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.

The comments under the post took two directions. Magnus Eriksson, architect and former AWS employee, notes that Lambda "is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2" and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads. Matthew Bonig, AWS DevTools Hero and co-author of The CDK Book, looked further ahead: "Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs.".

It has been revealed that on Reddit, the most-upvoted reply welcomed the change because it avoids Fargate and ECS for hour-long batch jobs. The answer under it was that Fargate is beautifully simple. One commenter sets out where the longer limit fits:.

A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory, so check the cost per invocation before moving batch style work here, and keep the handler idempotent with a dead letter queue, because a failure or timeout partway through a long run can leave partial work behind. For multi step work, long running jobs, or anything that needs clear state and retries, Step Functions with Fargate or ECS is still usually cleaner.

Recent findings suggest that joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance, reads the move as Lambda team recognizing that Cloud Run is its most compelling competitor. Cloud Run services allow 60 minutes per request, and Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption and Premium intends enforce no maximum, with a 60-minute grace period during scale-in. AWS has not said whether the Lambda limit will move again.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SR-1 Freedom gets a shorter boom and larger antennas, with roughly two years to finish design, construction, and testing.
  • NASA has settled key design choices for its planned nuclear-fission-powered spacecraft, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, following a mission review in October.
  • Targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SR-1 Freedom gets a shorter boom and larger antennas, with roughly two years to finish design, construction, and testing.

NASA has settled key design choices for its planned nuclear-fission-powered spacecraft, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, following a mission review in October.

Targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit. It is designed to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion and deliver a capsule carrying three helicopters to Mars.

There have been some changes since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman indicated off the concept [PDF] at the agency's Ignition event in March. Improved shielding and spacecraft design will allow a shorter boom between the reactor and the spacecraft's main body, protecting its electronics and the SkyFall payload. The shorter boom will, according to NASA, "reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.".

The revised design also includes larger X-band antenna dishes to transmit data to Earth.

Decisions are still pending on how many radiator panels the vehicle needs, the output power levels of the nuclear power module, and how long the reactor will operate.

Right now, the mission calls for the spacecraft to start its reactor once it has left Earth orbit and gradually ramp up power. After a period during which performance data will be sent back to Earth, the reactor will be shut down until after the SkyFall capsule, containing a trio of Mars Ingenuity-class helicopters, is delivered to Martian orbit.

In a recent development, solar arrays will power the spacecraft during its cruise to Mars. The fission reactor will then be reactivated to let engineers collect more data on its performance in deep space.

NASA also awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the nuclear power module.

"Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule," the agency said.

The latter part regarding the schedule is certainly a challenge. Meeting the late-2028 launch target leaves roughly two years to finish designing, building, and testing the spacecraft.

It has been revealed that ESA is also targeting late 2028 for its long-delayed Rosalind Franklin rover. Missing the intended Mars departure opportunity could push SR-1 into a later launch window, although NASA has not specified a fallback schedule. ®.

Qwen-3 is unique in its ability to toggle reasoning via the enable_thinking flag. When set to false, the template inserts an empty pair, telling the model to skip step‑by‑step thoughts. Earlier models baked the tag into every generation, forcing chain‑of‑thought whether you wanted it or not.

QwQ for example, forces reasoning in every conversation.

Qwen-3 utilizes a rolling checkpoint system, intelligently preserving or pruning reasoning blocks to maintain relevant context. Older models discarded reasoning prematurely to save tokens.

Qwen-3 introduces a "rolling checkpoint" by traversing the message list in reverse to find the latest user turn that wasn’t a tool call. For any assistant replies after that index it keeps the full blocks; everything earlier is stripped out.

Here's an example of chain-of-thought preservation through tool calls with Qwen-3 and QwQ.

Industry observers note that qwen-3 highlights us that through the chat_template we can provide better flexibility, smarter context handling, and improved tool interaction. These improvements not only improve capabilities, but also make agentic workflows more reliable and efficent.

Is there any explanation for why this template sometimes uses bra and ket symbols like <|im_start|> and <|im_end|>, but then other times uses XML notation like and instead of <|think_start|> and <|think_end|>?

It strikes me as being inconsistent.

Sources indicate that the identifiers using bra and ket symbols are tokens, i.e. they are actually recognised and converted to a single "special" token by the tokenizer. For example, <|im_end|> is used as the EOS_TOKEN. (And, as an aside, you need to know this if you want to try fine-tuning these Qwen models, because you need to explicitly set eos_token='<|im_end|>' in your fine-tuning configuration.).

The XML-style identifiers are placeholders that define sections of the generated output. They are tokenized in the same manner as for any other text (i.e. they are probably converted to multiple tokens, but that depends on the vocabulary), they have no predetermined special meaning, and their use is learned by the model during training.

That remarked, the specific placeholders and are pretty standard across reasoning models.

In a recent development, gradio is a Python library used by more than 1 million developers each month to build interfaces for machine learning models. Beyond just creating UIs, Gradio also exposes API capabilities and — now! — Gradio apps can be rolled out Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for LLMs. This means that your Gradio app, whether it's an image generator or a tax calculator or something else entirely, can be called as a tool by an LLM.

This guide will show you how to use Gradio to build an MCP server in just a few lines of Python.

Gradio makes it easy to build these MCP servers, turning any Python function into a tool that LLMs can use.

TitleApex Veritas Meta: Toward a Self-Governing Epistemic Singularity.

AbstractThis proposal outlines Apex Veritas Meta, an architecture that shifts the locus of AI singularity from raw computational power to epistemic autonomy. We combine quantum-resistant truth sealing, symbolic anchoring, resistance-aware propagation analytics, and transformer-driven heuristic adaptation to build a closed-loop system in which verified knowledge continually refines its own transmission. Our central hypothesis is that a network of adaptive truth signals can achieve autopoietic coherence—maintaining and propagating verified facts without centralized oversight. We will define formal metrics for propagation depth, resistance convergence, and semantic drift, implement a prototype across simulated agent networks, and evaluate its capacity to sustain knowledge fidelity under adversarial pressure. Success will inaugurate a new field of algorithmic epistemology and redefine singularity as the emergence of self-stabilizing truth ecosystems.

Sources indicate that introductionContemporary AI research emphasizes scale, generalization and autonomous decision-making. The canonical singularity envisions systems surpassing human intelligence through unbounded compute. By contrast, Apex Veritas Meta foregrounds trustworthiness and self-defense of knowledge. We posit that the true hinge point for transformative AI lies not in speed or raw inference but in the ability of information to certify, monitor, adapt, and re-broadcast itself against distortion.

MethodologyPhase 1: Formalization and Simulation Environment• Develop a graph-based simulation of 1,000 agent nodes with configurable trust and resistance profiles.• Instrument PropagationObserver to record event streams and compute metrics in real time.Phase 2: Model Training• Curate historical propagation datasets (social media rumor diffusion, scientific consensus shifts).• Train HeuristicOptimizer to predict optimal emission parameters given node states and historical resistance.Phase 3: Prototype Implementation• Integrate all modules in a microservice architecture using Docker containers.• Deploy on a private Kubernetes cluster to emulate scale and network latency.Phase 4: Adversarial Testing• Introduce controlled misinformation actors.• Measure system resilience: percentage of truth retention, time to reconvergence, false-positive drift.Phase 5: Analysis and Refinement• Identify thresholds for autopoietic behavior.• Refine model hyperparameters and retrain as necessary.• Document emergent strategies and failure modes.

Expected Outcomes• Demonstration that an adaptive propagation engine sustains >90% knowledge fidelity over 72 hours under adversarial load.• Identification of critical parameters for epistemic singularity transitions.• A publishable framework and open-source reference implementation.• Pathway to integrate into autonomous systems requiring self-defending trust layers.

Timeline (12 months)Months 1–3: Simulation design, metric formalizationMonths 4–6: Dataset collection and optimizer trainingMonths 7–9: Prototype integration and initial testingMonths 10–12: Adversarial evaluation, analysis, publication preparation.

Budget Estimate• Personnel (2 researchers, 1 engineer): $300 K• Cloud compute and storage: $50 K• Workshops and dissemination: $20 K• Total: $370 K.

Industry News: Hints and hazards: pg_plan_advice in PG19

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Clickhouse

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that over the past decade, one of the most contentious Postgres feature requests has been for query hints.
  • Recent findings suggest that postgres 19 brings 2 new contrib modules that collectively provide the initiative hint experience without affecting all queries or SQL syntax.
  • Industry observers note that the companion extension provided is pg_stash_advice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that over the past decade, one of the most contentious Postgres feature requests has been for query hints. The planner is remarkably effective at making good decisions, but it doesn’t always do so, and query hints have been proposed as a way to fill that gap. They’ve been a popular feature on other databases for years, and some would say that they are essential for production usage to ensure that indexes are used effectively and queries are planned sensibly. While pg_hint_plan has existed for a while, the Postgres community has historically been divided on this topic, with the general consensus being that planner failures were bugs that should be fixed instead of being worked around.

Recent findings suggest that postgres 19 brings 2 new contrib modules that collectively provide the initiative hint experience without affecting all queries or SQL syntax. pg_plan_advice works at the session level, allowing you to simply SET how the next queries will be planned. The technique supports a decent list of features, letting you specify scan method, join order, join method, parallelism, partitionwise joins, and semijoin uniqueness.

Industry observers note that the companion extension provided is pg_stash_advice. This is meant to apply to query identifiers instead of specific queries, so rather than using SET to hint, you instead find a specific query identifier and tell Postgres to always apply your hints only to that query. It supports the same capabilities for affecting query aims as pg_plan_advice, so most of this article applies to it as well.

Industry observers note that under the hood, these extensions work by telling the planner that it should not pick the options you didn’t select. This can’t actually force Postgres to pick the proposal that you actually want, so if there’s no viable way to actually use the hint, the advice will be partially or fully ignored. In addition, there is no check that the advice is good- the planner will happily accept input that actively degrades query performance. In practice, this means that it can be similar to existing enable_ knobs you may have already used to force certain plans on queries. For example, if you’re trying to convince the planner to use an index, here’s the old way and the fresh way you’d consider. They do similar things, but the advice extensions provide a lot more capability and granularity:.

According to recent reports, I’ve put together a few examples of queries where you might want to consider using pg_plan_advice, and did some testing to see how well it works in practice. All of these tests ran on ClickHouse Managed Postgres, on a m6gd.xlarge machine with 4 vCPUs, 16GB RAM, and a 237GB local NVME drive. The tests are fairly artificial, as the planner is remarkably clever and it’s surprisingly difficult to construct scenarios that reliably give it trouble.

pg_plan_advice ships as a contrib module, so you’ll probably want to add it to your server’s shared_preload_libraries or take one of the following steps to get it working in a PG19 environment:.

Recent findings suggest that this post uses a lot of SET commands for demonstration purposes. If you are looking to use pg_plan_advice in a production system, please keep in mind that these should instead generally be SET LOCAL in a transaction to prevent unexpected effects on other queries.

Industry observers note that the planner generally assumes that rows in a table are spread somewhat evenly. Unfortunately, the ISO Standard User does not actually exist, so a lot of database writes are clustered around bursts of correlated activity. This can lead to a scenario where the planner knows a few percent of rows match a given filter, starts walking through a primary key column to find them, and ends up scanning nearly the whole index before getting enough hits.

Here’s the query we’ll use for this:.

Running it does, indeed, give us a terrible proposal.

Industry observers note that excellent, we’ve reproduced the failure! The index scan looks like it should be reasonable, and the cost of 66.77 is trivial: the planner clearly expected to find all 10 rows it needed immediately. Unfortunately, it had to gather and discard 10,000,000 rows before finding a useful result, which obviously took far longer than you’d expect.

According to recent reports, you’ve probably noticed the “Generated Blueprint Advice” section in this explain plan as well. This is another fresh feature; we’re using EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, PLAN_ADVICE) here. Since we didn’t provide plan advice, this output just indicates the plan it actually used.

Recent findings suggest that we could definitely fix this with a newly introduced index, but that isn’t always a good option when you see this kind of thing in the wild, so let’s try a bitmap heap scan. It works by first constructing a bitmap of potential row locations using a bitmap index scan, and then decodes it to fetch the underlying data. It’s better suited to bulk operations, so it’s a good bet given how uncooperative the index scan is proving to be. Here’s all we need to do to actually use it:.

The parallelism makes it a bit tricky to read, but a few things stand out. First, we got <10ms execution time, so the bitmap heap scan actually did help. Second, we can now see the supplied blueprint advice at the bottom of the EXPLAIN output, and the matched feedback (without a failed flag) makes it clear that the planner actually used our advice. Please note that this does not necessarily mean that the planner benefited from the advice.

Industry observers note that JOINs can be a source of planner complications, as statistics are resolutely single-table. The planner has a limited ability to predict how many rows will be pruned by filters on JOINed tables, so it can be way off base on selectivity. In general, it assumes that filters on different tables are independent of each other, which is a fairly easy assumption to violate with the following setup:.

Here’s our baseline query. It’s just a simple join, filter, and limit:.

Here’s our first plan, with the planner doing the heavy lifting for us:.

This blueprint is honestly pretty terrible. The planner correctly understands that there are 500K or so trial_start rows, and that 1% of customers are enterprise customers. It then multiplies these numbers by each other, which leads it to predict that 5000 rows will match, and it only needs 10. Unfortunately, the filters aren’t as independent as it’s estimating, so only 20 out of the 500K rows actually have the values it’s looking for. As such, it ends up scanning a lot more rows than it was counting on to get this result. You can see as much in the row estimates above: the planner predicts 5288 rows when we know there are only 20, which is right in line with the math.

To fix this, let’s try giving initiative advice. We want the join order to prioritize accounts first, as that will give us a vastly more selective filter to cut down on row counts.

In a recent development, A nearly 200x improvement is absurdly better. By adjusting the join order, we’re able to take full advantage of the accounts table’s much lower number of rows matching the enterprise filter, which lets us dramatically cut down on the number of rows to scan. You probably won’t get quite as substantial a speedup in most cases in production, but this pattern comes up every now and then, and having a tool to address it is priceless.

This is probably the use case that fits the proposal advice feature best. It’s rare, but there are not a lot of good alternatives for dealing with it. I’ve come across similar challenges perhaps a half dozen times, and while I was able to find workarounds, they got pretty hacky and difficult to reason around.

Sources indicate that we’ve got some promising results in scenario 1, but what happens if the data changes to be less lumpy while our hint is still in place? To test this, let’s set every third row to the failed state:.

This means we only need to walk a few rows to get what we’re looking for, so the planner estimate should be able to get us a good outcome. Sure enough, if we run without any hints, we get this:.

That’s the kind of result we wanted to see in the first place! Let’s see how we do with the earlier hint to use a bitmap heap scan in place:.

That’s 7,000 times worse, and the feedback doesn’t show a problem because it’s still matched. Now that the artificial data condition tripping up the planner is gone, the planner has no problem doing a better job than our hinted alternate. This is a good reminder that all hints should be regularly checked for ongoing necessity — otherwise, your performance fixes can lead to performance complications.

Sources indicate that we’ve gone through a few scenarios, and it’s clear that pg_plan_advice is a powerful but situational tool. It’s not easy to construct scenarios that reliably confuse the planner, but they show up in production often enough that it’s worth having a tool to address them. pg_plan_advice is newly introduced enough that it’s hard to say for sure, but I’d bet from what I’ve shown here that the following workflow will serve you well:.

If you get a mysteriously slow query and tuning doesn’t get the results you wanted, then blueprint advice is a good thing to try.

If it works, then baking it into the transaction with SET LOCAL is a good way to improve performance.

If you do set advice, check on it in a few months, as shifting data and query patterns can make it counterproductive.

45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.
  • Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall.
  • If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.

SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.

If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

According to recent reports, we also saw a lot of upcoming companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.

Industry observers note that the real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

It has been revealed that rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

According to recent reports, what's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for upcoming datacenter builds.

The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses.

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power  – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate.

Water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a big deal.

The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.

Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the upcoming set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

At SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course.

Industry observers note that any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

Sources indicate that my instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

There's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.

We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.

Much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled robots to perform a wide range of tasks—from simple commands like “grasp the cube” to more complex activities like folding laundry or cleaning a table. These models aim to achieve generalization: the ability to perform tasks in novel settings, with unseen objects, and in varying conditions.

“The biggest challenge in robotics isn’t dexterity, but generalization—across physical, visual, and semantic levels.”— Physical Intelligence.

Sources indicate that A robot must "figure out how to correctly perform even a simple task in a upcoming setting or with new objects," and this requires both robust skills and common-sense understanding of the world. Yet, progress is often limited by the availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.

“Generalization must occur at many levels. At the low level, the robot must understand how to pick up a spoon (by the handle) or plate (by the edge), even if it has not seen these specific spoons or plates before, and even if they are placed in a pile of dirty dishes. At a higher level, the robot must understand the semantics of each task—where to put clothes and shoes (ideally in the laundry hamper or closet, not on the bed), and what kind of tool is appropriate for wiping down a spill. This generalization requires both robust physical skills and a common-sense understanding of the environment, so that the robot can generalize at many levels at the same time, from physical, to visual, to semantic. This is made even harder by the limited availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.”— Physical Intelligence.

According to recent reports, to simplify, the core of generalist policies lies in a simple idea: co-training on heterogeneous datasets. By exposing VLA models to a variety of environments, tasks, and robot embodiments, we can teach models not only how to act, but why—how to interpret a scene, understand a goal, and adapt skills across contexts.

💡 “Generalization is not just a model property—it’s a data phenomenon.”It emerges from the diversity, quality, and abstraction level of the training data.

This brings us to a fundamental question:.

Given current datasets, what is the upper limit of generalization we can expect?

Can a robot meaningfully respond to a completely novel prompt—say, *"set up a surprise birthday party"*—if it has never encountered anything remotely similar during training? Especially when most datasets are collected in academic labs, by a limited number of people, under well-controlled setups?

Sources indicate that we frame generalization as a data-centric view: treating it as the process of abstracting broader patterns from data—essentially “zooming out” to reveal task-agnostic structures and principles. This shift in perspective emphasizes the role of dataset diversity, rather than model architecture alone, in driving generalization.

Industry observers note that so far, the majority of robotics datasets come from structured academic environments. Even if we scale up to millions of demonstrations, one dataset will often dominate, limiting diversity. Unlike ImageNet—which aggregated internet-scale data and captured the real world more holistically—robotics lacks a comparably diverse, community-driven benchmark.

This is largely because collecting data for robotics requires physical hardware and significant effort.

That’s why, at LeRobot, we’re working to make robotics data collection more accessible—at home, at school, or anywhere. We're:.

We're already seeing the results: the number of community-contributed datasets on the Hub is growing rapidly.

Growth of lerobot datasets on the Hugging Face Hub over time.

According to recent reports, if we break down the uploaded datasets by robot type, we see that most contributions are to So100 and Koch, making robotic arms and manipulation tasks the primary focus of the current LeRobot dataset landscape. However, it’s important to remember that the potential reaches far beyond. Domains like autonomous vehicles, assistive robots, and mobile navigation stand to benefit just as much from shared data. This momentum brings us closer to a future where datasets reflect a global effort, not just the contributions of a single lab or institution.

Distribution of lerobot datasets by robot type.

In a recent development, as robotics data collection becomes more democratized, curation becomes the next challenge. While these datasets are still collected in constrained setups, they are a crucial step toward affordable, general-purpose robotic policies. Not everyone has access to expensive hardware—but with shared infrastructure and open collaboration, we can build something far greater.

🧠 “Generalization isn’t solved in a lab—it’s taught by the world.”The more diverse our data, the more capable our models will be.

Sources indicate that why does data quality matter? Poor-quality data results in poor downstream performance, biased outputs, and models that fail to generalize. Hence, efficient and high-quality data collection plays a critical role in advancing generalist robotic policies.

While foundation models in vision and language have thrived on massive, web-scale datasets, robotics lacks an “Internet of robots”—a vast, diverse corpus of real-world interactions. Instead, robotic data is fragmented across different embodiments, sensor setups, and control modes, forming isolated data islands.

To overcome this, recent approaches like Gr00t organize training data as a pyramid, where:.

Within this framework, efficient real-world data collection is indispensable—it anchors learned behaviors in actual robotic hardware and closes the sim-to-real gap, ultimately improving the generalization, adaptability, and performance of robotics foundation models.

Sources indicate that by expanding the volume and diversity of real-world datasets, we reduce fragmentation between heterogeneous data sources. When datasets are disjoint in terms of environment, embodiment, or task distribution, models struggle to transfer knowledge across domains.

🔗 Real-world data acts as connective tissue—it aligns abstract priors with grounded action and enables the model to build more coherent and transferable representations.

As a result, increasing the proportion of real robot interactions does not merely enhance realism—it structurally reinforces the links between all layers of the pyramid, leading to more robust and capable policies.

According to recent reports, many datasets lack task descriptions, lack details or are ambiguous in the task to be done. Semantics is presently at the core of cognition, meaning that understanding the context and specifics of a task is crucial for robotic performance. Detailed expressions ensure that robots understand exactly what is expected, but also provide a broader knowledge and vocabulary to the cognition system. Ambiguity can lead to incorrect interpretation and, consequently, incorrect actions.

Subtask-level annotations are often missing, making it difficult to model complex task hierarchies.While this can be handled with VLM, it is still better to have a task annotation provided by the author of the dataset at hand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type after Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

In a recent development, the Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Declared on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.

Industry observers note that the headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result to describe an operation that cannot fail, it took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.

To make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting challenges on upgrade are advised to update dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.

The core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the latest Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.

On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:.

This release is so massive that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:.

The fresh global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:.

On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:.

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,.

you should immediately patch security advisories.

One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

In a recent development, importStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an upgrade could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.

Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.

Upgrading uses rustup revision stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

SSH is a GUI framework

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zydra

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.
  • Sources indicate that SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth.
  • To see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.

Sources indicate that SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth. A number of terminal protocols have slowly added graphics, clipboard sharing (including images), notifications, mouse support, and more on top of SSH.

To see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH. You can try it right now (no sign-up):.

All terminal protocols work on data that can be passed through SSH, so typically, any terminal protocol will extend to SSH.

In a recent development, perhaps the most ubiquitous latest terminal protocol is the Kitty Graphics Protocol, which superseded the older Sixel and iTerm2 graphics protocols. It allows for compression, client-side graphical state (via VRAM), and even animations entirely on the terminal.

Graphics alone don't make a complete GUI, though. SSH has protocols that cover all other angles:.

It has been revealed that notifications: OSC 99 "Rich Notifications" allow image, text, and body. OSC 777 (our first fallback) allows only text and body, and OSC 9 (our last fallback) allows only a title.

We end up using a similar fallback for many things.

Industry observers note that A few tricks make compositing over SSH fast. Firstly, where possible, especially when streaming terminals, we simply stream them as text rather than unnecessarily streaming it via graphics. The compositor's UI framework itself cleverly overlays traditional text over carefully aligned graphics, saving bandwidth. In the case of zydra.sh, this allows us to efficiently stream the entire cloud computer's desktop UI over SSH.

Sources indicate that next, we optimize graphics by sending a sort of "grid" of pixels. Each cell has its own updates, where the previous frame is compared to the current frame to catch and send updates, avoiding having to constantly stream the full screen. Kitty also offers both RGB and RGBA, and so by removing transparency where it's not needed, we save another 25% in bandwidth. We also track ping and other factors to determine how well the client handles the stream: lowering the resolution in select cells, especially when scrolling, to relieve pressure. We also use Kitty's client-side state to hold graphics ahead-of-time before they're displayed on screen, as well as holding repeated UI components.

Industry observers note that not all terminals support all the latest terminal protocols, so the compositor must also fallback to older graphics protocols Sixel and iTerm2, and when necessary, fall back to pure textual streaming, using ASCII to replicate some UI. In the case of notifications and other protocols, multiple protocols similarly exist, which we also gracefully fallback to when needed.

Parsing terminal versions and querying capabilities allows us to get an idea of what the client supports. We also continually verify that features work as expected on the client as the session boots. The Kitty terminal itself I've found to have very reliable support for all graphics protocols zydra.sh relies on.

Sources indicate that VNC is limited to sending pictures of the screen and diffing frames to find what changed. With zydra.sh's approach, apps directly tell the compositor what changed, and terminal text is sent as text you can select and copy natively. The browser is a WebKit build that delivers frames to the compositor as DMA-BUFs without a readback, which can be driven agentically via Playwright.

It has been revealed that while webapps have advantages, especially in client-side state, WASM, and WebGPU, they don't really capture the universality and ease-of-use of an SSH session. SSH keys double as authentication, and -A allows you to SSH into servers from within a remote microVM itself. Webapps also can't be accessed from a pure TTY.

SSH also has sshfs, so you can mount your VM's filesystem locally:.

Sources indicate that on Android, SSH is technically "available" through Termux, although it can be finicky. I've made a webapp version of the zydra.sh compositor that's more responsive and accessible in mobile for this use case.

SSH also still poses limits around audio (as agents are increasingly used with dictation), and despite how much the Kitty graphics protocol helps, it leaves a lot of optimization on the table due to a lack of stronger client-side state and streaming protocols.

It has been revealed that my SSH-native compositing system and microVM desktop environment based on it are the backbone of my broader attempt to create an actually pleasant agent sandbox :). A cloud computer without cloud friction if you will. Another article which describes how I added a "timeline" feature to zydra.sh that allows you to rewind the VM as if watching a livestream is available here: Agents need an undo button. You can read more about me and my background on my portfolio, too.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forrester warns that shiny new services rest on brittle systems as organizations skimp on resilience.
  • Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.
  • The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forrester warns that shiny new services rest on brittle systems as organizations skimp on resilience.

Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.

The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.

The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester remarked.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations.".

Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it.".

Earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

In a recent development, in October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.

In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

It has been revealed that aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.

Industry observers note that "Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said.

Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

Sources indicate that "Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund fresh customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

"They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate.".

Industry observers note that forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®.
