📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure).

Laura Savino discusses the psychological friction of AI adoption for senior engineers & architects. She explains how shifting from static expertise to learning in public lowers anxiety, accelerates tooling fluency, and prevents burnout. Leaders will discover actionable strategies to support their teams, debunk tech zealotry, and foster an adaptive engineering culture that thrives during upheaval.

Laura Savino a software engineer at Adobe Photoshop. She brings her background in education and humanities to technical topics, creating talks that spark ongoing conversations.

In a recent development, software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Laura Savino: Several friends and colleagues have come to me to tell me recently that they are pregnant with their first child, and have taken comfort from a really odd bit of perspective that I've given them, because I have two lovely kids, two very much wanted and uneventful pregnancies. I hated being pregnant. Every so often, I look around a crowd of people, and I'm like, everyone here is the result of a pregnancy, and it creeps me out. It's beautiful. It's a miracle of life. It is also not my jam. The thing that made me willing to do it at all and that gave me great comfort along the way was actually the myth of the frog. This frog is swimming around in water that starts at a comfortable temperature, but is slowly heated through to a boil, and if you do it gradually enough, the frog won't really notice that its environment is no longer like anything it's ever experienced before, and the frog is eventually cooked.

Recent findings suggest that this odd myth gave me a lifeline of hope, because if that frog can adapt to extreme, unprecedented conditions, so can I. Because the difficult parts usually come on gradually, day by day. If having a child started with the eighth-month pregnancy discomfort, very few of us would do it. It would be banned as inhumane torture if we could instantly make people eight months pregnant.

Sources indicate that some of you are like, "It's 9:00 in the morning. We're at a software conference. Can we please not talk about spontaneous advanced gestation? It is a repulsive idea." When we see a person eight months pregnant who got there gradually, the way we all luckily do, we just think, how nice. It's not repulsive at all, it's beautiful. It's usually obvious that they're just handling it like champions. It turns out the frog thing is thoroughly debunked. At a certain point, ectotherms change locations to keep themselves safe. The myth works to reassure me and my pregnant friends because of the way I frame it. It's not that the thing gets worse and worse slowly, and you don't notice and eventually are cooked. It's that you yourself change. You adapt. Yes, your context becomes more and more difficult, but if you're committed to sticking it out, you flex some increasingly creative coping strategies and skills, you become able to handle it. You worry about eighth month after you've figured out the seventh month and the sixth month, you'll be fine.

It has been revealed that let's tangent from there. I have these two amazing kids, one is 8. We've had Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse on repeat in our house this past month. There's this one scene that captures me. A newly bitten Spider-Man is trying to learn to thwip, that's the technical term, and he's doing it while being chased by an evil giant robo-scientist through the trees, so Spider-Man is like dodging trees, and he yells, "Whoa, whoa, I can't do this yet." His trainer quips, "Everyone knows that the best way to learn is under intense, life-threatening pressure." Another anecdote. My friend TJ. TJ is an all-around delightful person, but their rarest trait and the highest compliment that I can reach for is that they are a functional programming language aficionado and are not an asshole about it. These days we're all a little or a lot more on board with the functional aspects of Rust and Kotlin and Swift, and strongly preferring pure functions is just mainstream now.

Side Effect punk is dead. Remember Haskell, the language? Remember when there was a whole functional programming dogma with true believers, with the hyper-conviction of the newly converted, and there were memes about monads. If your brain could follow certain logical compressions, you were with it. You were good. You were likely to survive, and everybody else was getting left in the imperative rubble. When I learned TJ appreciated Haskell, I was like, but you're so chill about it. They were like, it's a really interesting tool. This was the first time that I'd met a functional programming enthusiast that I could relate to.

I am Laura Savino. I'm a developer on Photoshop, somewhat on the iOS UI, but also on the C++ library that supports real Photoshop PSD file editing on your phone. Before I became a software engineer, I thought I was going to be a language teacher. I was for a minute. I took master's-level courses in things like how to teach American English pronunciation, how to design a test that tests what you want it to evaluate, which is hard. I taught English in France and French in Seattle, and English again at that time in South Korea, and eventually learned to code. Fast-forward several years, and here I am on the QCon London stage. Today's talk, I hope, will start to shift your identity from someone who's good at doing a specific thing to someone who's good at learning near anything. I'm taking it as an anthology of vignettes with research for structural support. In rough order of appearance, so you have a sense of time passing. There will be cabinet-making, teen vampires, December-born horses, a Zen priest, football kits, awkward dance floors, and a puppy. I will provide a slide with references at the end, so you can settle in.

Industry observers note that I started with three stories, one about a frog, one about Spider-Man, and one about these monad pushers, and this is not exactly an un-telegraphed reveal that these stories map shockingly neatly onto the onslaught of AI. The first one, the frog metaphor that comforted me so much in my pregnancy, part of what makes the AI transition so disorienting is that we're being asked, many of us, to take it on. Like, now, now, now, the water is plasma, and you frogs will get in there, and you will like it. If you're not already orchestrating, you're so far behind, you might as well take up goat herding, because the goats are more your speed. For Spider-Man, a substantial reason the AI transition is so daunting is that many people's livelihoods are directly tied to how well we adapt. It's fine. The robot arm's chasing us, they're motivating. We all just ducked in here for a minute to throw them off our trails.

Lastly, about my chill friend, it's tough out there because of all the zealots. I think most of them are not actually assholes. I genuinely believe they're mostly just excited, and they cannot imagine a reasonable person in possession of all the facts who's not exactly as excited as they are. They respond by either assuming you're an unreasonable person or giving you more facts, and I'm not sure which is worse. The ultimate well-meaning zealot is the Chris Traeger character on Parks and Rec played by Rob Lowe. This character is intense, precise, and painfully optimistic. There's this one scene where he says he's logged 65,000 miles running in his lifetime, and his goal is to run to the moon. Some AI enthusiasts are giving a little Chris Traeger running to the moon. We recognize they're telling us about something healthy and good, and they may even have our best interests at heart, but no part of me wishes I had my running shoes on so I could join him to the moon. How do we bring people with us?

Sources indicate that I experienced a massive at-the-time transition in Cocoa, in the Apple development community that did this well. See, it was possible for a long time to go into Apple development with a great deal of hubris. You were an Apple developer. You knew all the tricks and tips. You'd hand-molded a lock and knit release cycles. Back of the cabinet here means, sure, no one's going to see this part of the code, but we're still going to make it just so because we take pride in our work. For a minute there, you could be confident that your deep UI kit and Objective-C knowledge meant that big companies would pay you and a team of three or four devs and a crack designer, absolute truckloads of cash to write them an app because everyone needed apps and no one knew how to write them except us. It was a really good time to be an Apple developer.

Then Apple dropped Swift, brand new language. You're welcome, everyone. Soon all our new APIs will be in this brand-new language that you have to use. We were willing to give up our semicolons. No one likes those, but they ripped away our square brackets too. This was one of those watershed community moments. One perspective I really liked at the time was, we're knocked back to being beginners again, and we like it. We're on even footing. We're learning together. Isn't this exciting? The change electrified us in good and bad ways. On the good side, I distinctly remember watching people who'd shipped indie software on CDs, people who were intimately familiar with why NSString is prefixed that way because they used to code in NEXTSTEP. These developers dived headfirst into the new language. I was sitting around with The Omni Group folks, like OmniFocus, OmniGraffle, these are Apple ecosystem legends, with our laptops out in the hotel lobbies of San Francisco, just trying to figure out, what can I do with this new language? On the less good side.

Swift was announced in June, and on my production app, we had an intern who waited several weeks till late July, before Xcode, our IDE was even out of beta, the intern added Swift to the project just for fun. The tool chain support was abysmal. I couldn't exactly embrace the beginner's mind when I was trying to ship a feature and couldn't even type because my IDE kept lagging out with this message. It was frustrating and not at all production ready because the tool chain was literally in beta. On the whole, with the benefit of rose-colored nostalgia, it was good. Most super senior principal developers, these pinnacles of technical excellence, were having to relearn how to get the eighth element out of a string, like just rookie stuff. The behaviors that got rewarded were the ones where people learned in public. The people who learned the most were the ones who asked the most questions, who'd notice when they didn't understand something and say, this is something I don't understand.

It has been revealed that how interesting? They'd post forum questions and ask each other how things worked. They would post early code samples where they did not look like geniuses who knew all the answers, but just enthusiastic rookies who wanted to learn. You know how much people love correcting people on the internet, so anyone who posted something inaccurate got told about it real quick. How do you be ok with that, though? How do you psychologically handle going from the expert hot commodity to a total noob and keep up decent spirits while you do it?

My friends, has anyone considered the old standby straight-up denial? I don't think any of us are in first-order denial about AI where we refuse to accept that it exists or is changing things, but for myself, I am absolutely deep in second-order denial where you acknowledge the basic facts of the thing, but you deny the implications of those facts. Sure, the technology is here, but I am not ready to face its implications. I usually try to add a lot of details when I'm giving a talk, but here, I am going to kindly draw a veil and let the camera discreetly pan away because you do not need me to share my particular doomsday flavors. Besides, it weakens the denial. Denial can also stem from a fear that you or those you love lack the skills or resources to handle the consequences of a change. That's real.

Apparently, denial can have protective effects, though. This one study, "The role of denial in recovery from coronary heart disease," found that people who were in deep denial actually had better short-term outcomes than the ones who were actually facing reality. If you had deeper denial, you'd spend less time in intensive care and have fewer heart-related symptoms while you were in hospital. This rings true for me. Even if I've decided a thing is crucial to me, even when it's well-aligned with my values, if I face the full implications of how hard it's going to be, I will probably not do it. I might say, I don't have to exercise at the gym. I'm just going to put my shoes on and show up and we'll just see what happens. Denial can work to get us to start down a hard road and give us hope long enough to adapt to this ever-changing water.

Sources indicate that protective denial, it's incredibly common. We're also all going to die someday, but memento mori has somehow fallen out of fashion. If you want to sit in second-order denial with me for a little longer, that's ok. For a little longer, because the heart patients with serious denial had worse outcomes long-term. They didn't follow their medical advice, because why would they? They were fine. They got re-hospitalized more. Denial is not sustainable. If a little self-misdirection is what it takes to follow your values to stay in the room and not make a down payment on a yacht, go ahead, indulge. Let me suggest another indulgence, brain candy. When I was trying to improve my Spanish, I read the Twilight books, and I'm guessing most of you haven't read them or won't admit to having read them, because they're cloying vampire, werewolf, romance novels written for pre-teens. My Spanish became tan brillante como el pelo de Eduardo a la luz del sol, because brain candy, in the domain you're trying to learn, is just like the little carrot thrown down the path to convince the recalcitrant, what, I'm supposed to be good at this part of you, to at least look over and start to think about how to maybe head down this otherwise daunting path.

In a recent development, sometimes you truly need to lower the stakes mentally just so you can push through. Get out of that intense, life-threatening pressure. Solve an actual problem that only you have. Make some tool, make some toy, make a flatulence app with your 8-year-old, something real, but where no one will evaluate you on the outcome because evaluation changes us. We don't learn so we can achieve the task we care about, we learn to pass the test assigned to us. This is bad even if you're an excellent test taker.

According to recent reports, I took a break from my French major one summer to spend eight weeks in an intensive Japanese language study in northern Japan, where they promised to teach us the equivalent of two university semesters of Japanese. I was very good at French at that point. I had just breezed through a pair of graduate seminars and my placement test in the Japanese program put me in the very lowest level class. I'd only taken two basic Japanese classes by this point, but I just still felt like, "Hello, don't you know who I am? I'm good at languages. Why am I in the beginner's class with these people who can barely put a sentence together?" Granted, I couldn't say, do you know who I am, in Japanese, which is maybe a sign that their class placement was somewhat valid, but I had a demonstrated skill in a fundamentally different but still related area.

In a recent development, some of us are feeling this way about computing right now. I'm good at computers. I am a senior professional programmer. I once learned Python in an afternoon. If this latest computing skill is hard for me, either is something is wrong with the system or something is wrong with me. Don't you know who I am? For me in Japan, my identity was so caught up in being good at languages that I worked hard to avoid ever making a mistake, not just on coursework, but asking the bus driver for a transfer ticket. I wanted my Japanese to be perfect. I actually learned the most about learning that summer on a weekend excursion, just me and a classmate, where we stayed at a family-run Buddhist temple out in the countryside. I won't go into the expectation thrashing experience of preparing myself for a solemn weekend of meditation and instead watching sumo wrestling on TV with a priest and his family, but the larger foundation-shattering surprise was the way my classmate spoke to our Japanese hosts and that she would just say things.

She'd trip over words. She'd mess up her verb endings. My grammar wasn't great, but I could recognize a bunch of mistakes even if I couldn't correct them. I was so deep in this prove to everyone that I'm good at this mentality that if I didn't know how to say something properly, I'd keep quiet so I didn't embarrass myself. Amy, though, just talked. They're like laughing, conversing. The priest gets another beer. What stuck with me long after I forgot all the extra kanji I learned that summer, is that interacting imperfectly builds fluency. You get early feedback before unwanted behaviors are calcified. Find your version of a Zen retreat where you can just play with the tools with no expectations of evaluation. You'll develop facility and fluency that much faster.

It has been revealed that another way to fail when something's not a test. Many years ago, as I was just learning to code, like mapping out how to do red-black trees on a whiteboard level, I went out with some friends and some friends of friends to rent a karaoke room. One of these friends of friends turned out to be an engineering manager at Microsoft, which is a hazard of where I live in Seattle. I remember the fear and dread and shame that I felt when I was unable to successfully navigate the karaoke interface via any of the in-room remote controls. See, I saw this as my chance to prove my technical prowess and maybe get hired on at Microsoft. Why would the engineering manager consider my resume if I couldn't even modify the output settings of a retro karaoke system? I don't remember what any of us saying, but I do remember holding that remote in my hand and thinking that I was never going to get a job in tech.

Now we're all looking back at 15 years ago me and inwardly shouting, everybody knows these systems are hard. Just try, don't give up, it's fine. We have so much compassion. What is your tool today that you're like, I still don't have this thing working. What are they all going to think of me? I better hide it and fake it and just play it cool. If you have that mental block, lower the stakes, make a tool, make a toy, something unspeakably inane that is tailored to exactly your interests. It can lower the activation energy required to take that next step towards learning.

Another way I make daunting things feel more approachable is thinking of them as a practice round. Picture this, every Sunday morning, I'm at a former aircraft hangar that's been turned into an indoor kids' sports hell hole arena. There are five football fields, a dozen simultaneous kid classes, there's adult workout classes, there's birthday rooms, plus an enormous bouncy house situation. I promise you whatever you're picturing, there are more bouncy houses. There's screaming and there's tears and there's kids running and begging for snacks, and I'm paying to be here. I went to great effort to dig the 4-year-old's soccer uniform out of his dirty laundry hamper and convince him to leave the house and convince him to leave the car. My reward for that is sitting on an uncomfortable bench drinking truly some of the worst coffee in Seattle. I want to paint for you this picture of aggressively, brightly colored despair, because what you need to appreciate is that it was a big deal for me to change perspectives.

In a recent development, because I realize that if you see this not as a whole collection of circumstances designed to maximize my suffering, but hundreds of families who each separately fought through the chaos that is having a child on a chilly, damp weekend morning and got them to leave the house. If we could see in a little heads-up display what people overcame to get through that door, we would be walking around high-fiving and pouring each other pints. Nobody mentions all these hurdles. They just act like, yes, kids are wearing their kits here on time, relatively few boogers, as if they didn't execute a dozen fancy maneuvers to get there. If I don't tell someone that I struggled to get my kid there dressed, I won't hear their advice. Yes, my kid sleeps in her football kit. Sunday mornings have become my time to bask in the glory that not only have all of us made it through a gauntlet, but we've also successfully identified flaws in our own getting-out-of-the-house systems.

Sources indicate that we're basically red teaming our own lives. How did you do at getting out of the house without yelling and tears? C-minus. How will you do at learning from what went wrong? Are you committed to bringing better snacks next time? The point isn't how well you executed the thing today, but how well you've internalized and applied the changes for next time. Put the snacks in the car right now, and today counts as a success.

Sources indicate that when I was deciding whether to take this job I had at Photoshop, I called up a friend for advice, because I had two offers for very different jobs, one that I was sure I would be good at, that they would be lucky to have me, and the other was a stretch. It was on Photoshop, where I'd have to brush up on modern C++ and L1 caches and deal with real legacy code. My friend stated that if I had the appetite to learn the newly introduced thing, the hard thing, that I should do it now. Because at some point, he said, you're like, I don't want to learn a whole new paradigm again. I've been there. I've done that. I'm good. This advice was perfect when I was choosing my destiny, and learning modern C++ was supposed to be my last big career challenge. Now, very few of us have a choice about whether to invest a ton of energy in learning this new thing.

It has been revealed that I have to somehow generate energy for learning or hit burnout real hard. I feel like maybe external energy building works for salespeople. Like I could just shout, are you ready? Let's get pumped. Everyone would be like, yes, let's go. We're engineers who got to where we are by taking skepticism to an art form. How many people have looked at some shiny latest tech, mentioned, no, and then just watched it crumble off into the sunset? No amount of like, rah, rah, do it, is going to convince us in all of the do it, learn, go. It's like being told by a scowling Simon Cowell to do a heartfelt interpretive dance. You're not at your best. How do we, the hopeful skeptics who do believe in a better future, in spite of it all, how do we generate energy to learn? Let's actually start by not spiraling, perhaps, by not leaking happiness.

Recent findings suggest that one way I patch the leak is comparing current me to past me, because I'm obviously better than I was 10 years ago, aren't you? Think of you 10 years ago, and the glimmers of what you most value now that we're just starting to show. We were all goobers then compared to us now. Yet, we are all deeply discounting how much wiser we will be in the next 10 years, because we've got it figured out now. This is an actual studied phenomenon with a whole name, the end of history illusion. More specifically, we see the present as the moment where we have finally become the person we'll be for the rest of our lives.

In a recent development, more published sources. Just this year, Dr. Maya Shankar published a really timely book called "The Other Side of Change." I feel like she gets us as software people today, because she was well on the path to becoming a professional violinist when she had a career-ending injury, at which point she went into the field of psychology. She eventually became the behavioral sciences advisor to the UN. She did all right. I am clinging to her perspectives like a lifeline. She adds to this end of history idea, not about years, but any large change, when we imagine what it will be like to navigate an unexpected change and its aftermath, we tend to assume that we'll be the same person from beginning to end. Research indicates that we greatly underestimate how much we'll change in the future, even though we fully acknowledge that we've changed considerably in the past.

In a recent development, am I just going to keep reading you quotes? Yes, I am. Because these are literally professional studiers of brains, and they said this better than I can. You can think of this as the audiobook interlude. "The unique stresses and demands of being thrust into a newly introduced reality can uncover unexpected insights about ourselves and the world around us. These insights, coupled with the experience of the change itself, can transform us in extraordinary ways." I hear that, and I externally nod. Like, yes, maybe I'll grow on the other side of whatever this unprecedented time is. Also, a small part of me throws an absolute foot-stomping fit. I do not want to. I've barely got it together with the current state of things, and now you're coming at me with, think of all the personal growth you'll get. Like, no, I'm sorry. How many people are actively fantasizing about goat-herding careers right now?

In a recent development, there is some comfort in knowing that the person who will undergo the full experience will be different from the person we are in this very moment. We will become latest people on the other side of change in ways we are capable of shaping. I still don't want to. I don't. I remind myself to take a breath, or six, because, see, the frog is facing physical challenges and doesn't have biohacking tools there in its pot. Our challenges are all in our minds, for better or worse. As my favorite book series says, my head is where 90-plus percent of my problems are. We believe in neuroplasticity. We can change and grow our minds from the inside out. I promise this is related, but did you know in the competitive equine sports world, all horses have the same official birthday? In the Northern Hemisphere, they all turn one year older on January 1st.

In a recent development, that means that if your horse was born on Upcoming Year's Eve, for juvenile racing purposes, they'll be considered 2 years old when they turn 366 days. You can see how a 700-day-old 2-year-old race horse would have an advantage. Breeders often arrange for foals to be born as close to January 2nd as they can. Football in the States has the same effect, actually, where a statistically improbable number of professional footballers are born in the first quartile of the year. Few parents blueprint their kids' births around the football season for some reason. There's something to be said for always being a little ahead of your peer group. You literally win more. If the kids on your football team look up to you because they're barely 6 while you're nearly 7, and coaches look to you to lead the team's comeback when they're behind 3-0, you develop leadership skills and confidence from a very early age.

Sources indicate that I am on the other side. I came to technology late, so I got used to seeking coding advice from literal teenagers from day one of my first professional programming job. Since then, every team I'm on, I've been in the middle quartile in terms of raw technical Leet code acumen. Before anyone starts DMing me about imposter syndrome and telling me to believe in myself, I'm going to stop you, because I'm on the Photoshop engineering team, and I'm solidly in the middle of the pack. It's like being in the bottom third of Man City players, like, I'm one of the worst world-class athletes. Like, it's fine. I'm no slouch. I just keep moving up to better and better leagues. Because I started out behind and have stayed in the middle, I've never developed an ego around being the fastest prototyper or the most effective algorithm tuner. I have learned how to learn.

There's this famous study on which learning tasks people will take if given the option to improve their skills. One task is advertised as majorly effective, the other as so-so. It turns out the researchers could easily influence which participants chose which task. See, in the ineffective task, people could try and fail privately, and the highly effective one involved practicing in front of the group so everyone saw your mistakes. Clearly different paths with different risks and outcomes, and you all might have a sense of which group you would tend towards. How would a researcher influence you to pick one over the other? They gave people reading material about the malleability of the particular skill, debating in this case. One group read that debate is mostly an innate skill, the other that anyone can do it. It just takes training. It takes practice. The people who were in the inborn skill group, they did not participate in the activity that would help them improve, because then everybody would see that they lacked the skill.

The trainable skill group people were like, ok, let's go. Who cares if other people see that I can't do this yet? Showing people you're ignorant of something today can and should be super low stakes. It goes along with believing in neuroplasticity. This study is out of Carol Dweck's research about growth mindset, which had a whole Silicon Valley trend moment. I think it's not as trendy now, but the research is still solid. People who believe that their traits and abilities can significantly change are more likely to engage in behaviors that improve them. One problem that I ran into face first, like a very clean plate glass door one, is that when you start paying attention to whether you have a growth mindset and realize that without the researcher's priming that you would definitely be in the group that's like, better make sure no one finds out I'm a terrible debater.

Sources indicate that it throws you extra, because you, by definition, don't really believe that you can change how fixed your mindset is. These research scientists, I have to believe them because they approach this problem with rigor and with science at Stanford. They say quite plainly that cherished traits can be developed. I want to be better at believing in change and in neuroplasticity, so I'm working on it.

According to recent reports, part of my identity has become someone who learns out loud, and I've modeled learning out loud in public. The first time a principal engineer on the Photoshop team wanted to show me how to use a new AI tool to bolt a tricky feature onto our existing architecture, I recorded our screen share session and posted it for the rest of the team because seeing a tool used in a real-world context is always more instructive than the demo-worthy vacuum. Especially because, like all my comrades who brought their kids to weekend morning soccer practices, we each come to AI and use AI in completely different ways. My favorite take on this is from Dr. Cat Hicks. She is a research psychologist studying software teams and gets riled up in a very data-driven way when people talk about things like measuring team effectiveness. She emphasizes that none of us are having the same experience.

"When you have a highly adaptive, dialogical tool," which means the user is in dialogue with the tool, "where the user is shaping the context and wielding progressive disclosure to probe very different parts of its capabilities, different people will continue to get very different answers. Until we get real about the personalized, adaptive nature of this." People are each running their own individual experiments with new tools, and if we don't tell each other what our own tool uses look like, no one will know that you can put your kid to bed already wearing their football kit. This is not the time to experiment alone until your output seems to resemble other people's. Plus, even if I just complain about a tool, I usually get some really good alternative suggestions. Even though we've all transcended onto this higher plane of mental abstractions, there is still value in showing your actual footwork. Where did your tool fall over? Why did you keep using it anyway?

I actually literally do this in a surprising social context. Otherwise, awkward dance floors. Specifically at weddings or oddly corporate events that have decided to have a dance floor. Basically, collections of people of very mixed abilities who don't know each other super well and yet are celebrating something notable together. I pride myself on understanding the assignment to look like I am enjoying myself in a way that invites other people in. I am very specifically not dancing like no one's watching. I am dancing like there's no downside to looking like a goon. I actually want people to see me and think, what a goon? That actually looks fun. Then I, as an enthusiastically mediocre dancer, will also have more fun because more people will be dancing. I also do this in socio-professional groups. I run a biweekly hallway track meeting for Photoshop developers where we just get together and talk off the record about our most recent formal meeting.

Sometimes there's a lull in the conversation. I'll just jump in with an inane comment, sometimes a spicy question, just to let people know we aren't here trying to impress each other. I'll set the bar and then open the door and get out of the way because I love hearing experienced people hash things out. Being mediocre in public can invite people out with you. It brings out other intermediate-level folks. It brings out some shy experts because you've made it obvious that the bar for participation is one that they can easily clear. Now you're in a group of people sharing information and refining ideas before they've fully calcified, and you make each other better. Don't wait to be an expert to join a conversation about your tools. A caveat, when I tell people my advice to be joyfully imperfect in public, I usually mean it a little bit glibly.

Recent findings suggest that like in the sense of, but obviously not things that are core to your central identity. That would be terrible. No, like I can take up watercolors and show people that I'm an amusingly bad artist, or take up Chinese and let people laugh. When your skill at something is core to your identity, being mediocre in public is like doing a penance for a sin that you didn't even really get to enjoy committing. What I'm trying to do with every fiber of my being is to push this other skill, this meta skill of learning and adapting to change even deeper into my identity and recognizing that this squeaky, uncomfortable like, no, I'm terrible at this. It's like the lactic acid buildup the day after a workout. Is it comfortable? No, it sucks. It is the concrete feeling of getting better.

It has been revealed that some of you have been quietly bemused during this whole, here's how to not give up and survive section, because you are fully into learning the new thing. You are like, I am literally a core contributor on Gas Town, my good lady, what are you on about? This next section is for you. See, given the choice, I would rather dance than talk about the weather. I find it less awkward. Sorry, England. If I had absolute power, every awkward silence would just meld seamlessly into a dance break. Yet, I have not once committed the faux pas of grabbing some poor soul by the hand and dragging them onto the dance floor. I would never. Imagine this? You're sitting there at your linen-covered table trying to remember which wine was yours, and some absolute zealot comes and drags you by the hand onto the dance floor and then cheerfully bops away.

You're welcome. It's not ok. Unless you very promptly find your own groove, as soon as you can get away with it, you will moonwalk right back to the table straight past both glasses of wine because this time you're choosing a table much farther from these diehards who keep trying to force you into places where you don't think you fit. People who are happy on the dance floor need to make it more obvious that this is a good place to be and not just keep shouting that all of the non-dance floor is lava and we're getting left behind. Another aspect of bringing people with you. A few months ago, I used an AI agent to help me plan out decluttering my basement. I described the state of years of kid clutter accumulation, and listed off a couple sample starting ideas like disassembling the massive tower of cardboard box sculptures my kid had made, or sorting and condensing the various containers that were half full of miscellaneous.

Cursor came back with a useful proposal and some excellent advice, which included, do not start with the miscellaneous bins. They will just exhaust you. Better to focus on low-decision weight, high-impact tasks. You all sighed with relief along there with me. Like, "Low-decision weight, high-impact? Yes, this plan will work. It's going to feel so good and productive." It did. I got the tower out. I got rid of expired food and old toiletries. I made so many easy decisions, and I wrapped up the day feeling tired but satisfied and a good day's work. Then I go to work the next day, and the AI agents are like, "Good, you're back. I saved all these high-decision weight tasks for you. You're welcome." It turns out I'm not the only one who's had this, hold up, I feel like I'm doing more work now. We're working harder. Birgitta mentioned this too.

We are tired. Please keep in mind that when you're telling people how great this tool is, it is not zero cost. It is free as in puppy. You can't just drop it on people's doorsteps. If you're walking around insisting that everyone adopts one, you've got to provide material support. One specific practice, Photoshop's strongest AI tooling advocates host weekly office hours. We're constantly re-explaining to each other how to export the right environment variables this week. The support is critical because you're asking people to work harder. If you're patient when you're asking someone if they've sourced their, Oh My Zsh config recently, they're more likely to keep trying your next, "You'll like this one, I promise." They're more likely to try that idea.

Recent findings suggest that I know that some of you are very worried that some of us aren't fully embracing how different our jobs will be in five years. I actually noted that to troll you a little because I know it's an order of magnitude faster. Remember that a source of denial can be a lack of certainty that we have the skills to deal with the change. The more you remind your teams and your colleagues that they have done hard things before, that they can learn and grow, that neuroplasticity is real, the more they can loosen their hold on denial. The more we all believe that we do have the skills to face it, the more likely we are to engage in real protective behaviors. My favorite researcher, Cat Hicks, again, if our teams have a culture of learning, we report more productivity. This next part is me, non-professional scientist, extrapolating, but I think if you have a choice between a team with one expert tool user and a team who believes that they can learn and has faith in the organizational support behind it, choose the team that identifies as learners, the team that thinks they can't use the tool yet.

Sources indicate that why are we here? This is a question whose spiritual pay grade is much higher than mine. I'm going to narrow it to something that I'm actually qualified to speak to, how did we get here? First, approximately one lifetime ago, a lot of people suffered through a lot of months of pregnancy. Some number of years ago, we went from not knowing technology to being paid to be good at it. Some number of weeks ago, we all decided it was a good use of three solid days of our time to sit at a tech conference, and then every single person got it together and left their home. If we had heads-up displays showing each of our logistical contortions we used to get here, we would be high-fiving and pouring each other pints all day. We all decided that, yes, it's worth it to take that skeptically optimistic next step to learn a newly introduced thing from a stranger rather than chatting up friends in the hall.

We've been through a lot to get here, and it's all been in the mad hope of finding that next good thing. We got here, and here and now is oddly harder than anything our industry has encountered, and even this is just a practice round for the next. The beginner's mindset that you're dusting off, the resilience that you did not want to have to shore up, and the communities that you're building now, this is not the last time you'll be calling on them. We're all just brains in training for the next swell, so if you usually avoid things that make you feel like a December-born horse, take a minute to practice being newly introduced at things. Start with watercolors if you want, but also today you could go to a talk whose topic intimidates you. If a popular or mandated tool is giving you blisters, you can say so.

It has been revealed that talk to your peers to commiserate, to your juniors so they know it's not just them, to your management if you've got some political capital burning a hole in your Slack drafts. This is what leadership looks like in this world where everyone's a beginner. It looks like being unafraid to say, don't you know who I am? Yes, I'm someone who learns out loud.

Industry News: Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Donsz

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0.
  • This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.
  • And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can swiftly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:.

The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here, and here.

My work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team.

Industry observers note that on the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0. Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Industry observers note that chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md indicates it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual newly introduced subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

Sources indicate that the goal of the newly introduced trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero", referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one, that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed. Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Note: Chalk and the fresh trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

But what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

The first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide". It indicates "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.". But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Sources indicate that some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties. For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality. To codify these properties, we can use traits. In other words, a trait is a property of a type.

Industry observers note that notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties. The standard library's definition of Clone also includes two methods that can be called to perform this cloning operation.

In a recent development, to check whether the code you wrote is correct, the Rust compiler sometimes has to check that these properties hold. If you're trying to clone a value, the compiler has to check whether that value can be cloned.

Prolog is a cool programming language that works and looks very differently to what you may be used to. However, it is just as powerful (i.e. turing complete) as any other. The way it works has strong parallels to our trait system, let me show you. Here's an example:.

Sources indicate that A Prolog program consists of a set of statements, called "facts", as well as relationships between facts. In the above program, there are two facts: u64 has the property Copy, String has the property Clone, And there's also a relationship between these two properties. If some variable x has the Copy property, it also has the Clone property.

Finally, we can ask the prolog program some questions. For example, Does the type u64 have the Clone property? To answer that question, the runtime of a prolog program has to analyze all the known facts and relations. In this program we haven't remarked that u64 has the Clone property. However, we have said that it has the Copy property. And by using the relationship between Copy and Clone, the solver can derive that both questions (starting with ?-) are true!

The reason Chalk was using a "prolog-like" solver, is because as you can see, the trait system is extremely similar to a logic solver. Both "facts" and "relations" can be written using impl blocks. In fact, I can write the above program as a Rust program:.

Recent findings suggest that neither the fresh solver or the old solver state as plainly as chalk does that they're using a "prolog-like solver". However, given the similarities, both the old solver and the new solver really aren't so different from how you'd implement a prolog runtime.

Trait solving is not the same as type inference. This is a common misconception. Inside the Rust compiler, the two are completely different subsystems. Type inference is the process of replacing blanks with types. Throughout this text I'll refer to some the following example code (with slight variations):.

It has been revealed that we use type inference to determine that the type of the variable a is an integer. The same for b.

It has been revealed that having mentioned that, sometimes during type inference we do have to ask things about traits, and will call into the trait solver. Furthermore, the trait solver sometimes "unifies type variables", which means that while Rust makes a query about traits, we might make some progress on figuring out what the types of some variables are.

In the example code, one place where the trait solver comes into effect is when we call weird_add. On the function there's a where bound. A where bound is a requirement that the Rust compiler must check before allowing a call to that function. In this case, Rust has to make sure that i32 (a type we found through type inference) implements the Add trait. To do that, the solver can use one of a couple of strategies, and we'll look at each. In this case, we'll be looking for an impl block that mentions the i32 type, and we'll find one of those in the standard library!

Recent findings suggest that once the trait solver finds this impl block, it acts as an answer to the question "does i32 implement Add?". We somtimes refer to this answer as a a proof that the statement holds.

The example code contains several more calls to the trait solver. One you may not have thought about is that all local variables in Rust have to implement the Sized trait to be allowed on the stack. The Sized trait codifies that the compiler knows how many bytes of memory the value takes up, so it can be allocated on the stack. So, there will also be a query to the trait solver asking "does i32 implement Sized?".

The proof for this statement doesn't come from an impl block though. I did say that the compiler has several stratagies to derive proofs. In this case, the fact that some primitive types implement Sized is built-in to the compiler. i32 is inherently Sized, and there is no impl block anywhere that says so.

Recent findings suggest that answering Sized queries in general turns out to be quite hard because of the shear volume at which it occurs. To compile rust's standard library, we'll ask "does type implement Sized?" about 800 000 times! Additionally, answering it isn't always this simple. Let's take a slightly more involved example:.

To prove Kitten: Sized, a recursive process takes place. Both fields have to implement Sized too. So in the process of answering this question, the trait solver will produce more questions to be answered. Kitten: Sized leads to String: Sized & f64: Sized. f64 luckily is trivial again, and built into the compiler. String isn't though, and we go one more layer deeper to Vec: Sized, etcetera.

In a recent development, in Rust, generic functions can be type checked standalone. The example using weird_add doesn't need a main function to be checked, and may emit its own type errors.

This is where the trait solver actually does the most work. For example, to type check weird_add, we have to prove that a + b is valid. a + b desugars to a.add(b), and when finding the method add the trait solver gets invoked, since the add method comes from the Add trait.

Previously, proof candidates came either from impl blocks or they were built into the compiler. Not here though! A latest proof strategy is used here instead. When calling weird_add we saw that a where bound acts as a requirement that has to be checked before calling, but that means that inside weird_add we can assume that where bound holds and thus it acts as a proof strategy. Concretely, we know a has the type T, and to answer the question "does T implement Add" we find a where bound that states so.

Sources indicate that add isn't the only trait bound that has to be proven inside weird_add. This is another place where we have to prove that T: Sized. Again we have to look for candidates, and there's no built in one for generic types T, nor is there an impl block, nor a where bound that mentions Sized. So how does that work? Well, it turns out the where bound is implicit. T: Add really means T: Add + Sized, and so proving Sized works the same as proving Add.

According to recent reports, on lobsters I got asked about whether the Add bound is required to add the Sized bound. The T: Sized implicit bound gets added for any generic. Even if there was not already an Add bound, T would still be Sized. Presently, you can opt out of that implicit bound using T: ?Sized (or in the example, T: Add + ?Sized). In the future we may change the syntax for that to T: MetaSized. Look for the keyword "Sized Hierarchy" if you want to learn more. This document should also give you a primer.

Finally, this code will actually give a type error, because there's one more trait to prove. Because b gets mentioned twice, we have to clone or copy values of type T. The function signature really should have been:.

To summarize, trait solving is the process of answering questions about relations between types and traits. These questions are submitted to the trait solver, and the trait solver looks for candidates in the form of:.

When it finds one of these, we say we've found a proof, and if we cannot find one, a type error is emitted.

Industry observers note that sofar, all trait solving came down to finding a single candidate, but that's not always how it works. Let's look at the definition of the From and the Into traits:.

It has been revealed that if the trait solver gets a question like u32: Into (does u32 implement the Into trait), it will find the impl block above. However, the impl block is generic, and has a where bound that notes "T implements Into U IF U implements From T". Luckily there's another impl block that gives that implementation and so the initial statement can be proven.

What this all means, is that while answering a question, the trait solver emits more questions. These subquestions get added to an internal queue in the trait solver, and this queue of questions will be proven one after the other. Like this, some questions can turn into several subquestions, which can even have their own subquestions again.

Also, in the example from above, the second question actually has two proofs! There are two impl blocks that apply, since there's also this blanket implementation for identity conversion:.

Recent findings suggest that some preference takes place here. Since this is a blanket implementation, the other more specific one takes precedence. We can think about the trait solving about answering a tree of candidates that may apply. In this case, the single candidate for u32: Into turns into two, u64: From and T: From.

Something we'll not cover today, but this tree of candidates in reality is not a tree, it can have cycles! This has been the cause of both many bugs, and many rust compiler developers' nightmares.

The trait solver doesn't just deal with traits. An important thing it has to also consider is the associated types of traits. Let's look at the Add trait:.

An implementation of the Add trait can decide what the Output type will be equal to. Remember the definition of Add for integers?

Sources indicate that it states that when you add two i32s, we get back an i32. The reason the trait solver cares about associated types is that sometimes answering questions creates subquestions that mention associated types.

Industry observers note that because we wrote Output = T, the trait solver has to check that the candidate impl block has an Output type that's equal to T. We could've also written a more general function signature to something like:.

Or really to make it works you have to go one step further (click to expand).

Sources indicate that hold on! impl blocks can define inputs they act on, like impl Foo for i32 applies when the input is i32. It can make these inputs variables, like impl Foo for T. And impl blocks can also define outputs thrugh associated types.

According to recent reports, what we've done here, is make impl blocks powerful enough to act as functions, with inputs and outputs. And Alonzo Church proved that a language with only pure functions is in fact turing complete.

This is why Prolog is a fully-fledged turing complete programming language, and so is Rust's type system. People have defined numbers completely in Rust's type system in a crate called typenum, and have gone even further by implementing a chess engine inside the type system.

It has been revealed that trait solving ends up being a subsystem that the compiler spends quite a large portion of its time in. In general, there are two reasons for that:.

This ends up replacing the trait solver more complicated than you might think. People have already written many programs using the old solver, and because the upcoming solver internally makes different assumptions (sometimes in the name of soundness, remember the old solver has many bugs), we end up having programs that take both longer and shorter to compile. Sometimes with a polynomial factor, sometimes even with an exponential factor.

For example, the crate unic-ucd contains code along the lines of:.

Sources indicate that it lists a whole bunch of unicode characters, and each constant inside these slices are themselves string literals. That means each of them has an associated lifetime variable, that at some point gets inferred to 'static since we're assigning to a const. Now the upcoming trait solver, in some cases where the old solver did not, reasons about lifetimes.

It has been revealed that now sometimes, the rust compiler attempts see if two types are equal. This process may have side effects, in that it may make some progress towards inferring other types in the program. Because these side effects are sometimes undesireable, we have a system to "attempt" to unify types, and then roll back the results. To be able to do rollbacks we sometimes keep a trace of all operations we perform, so we can run them in reverse to get back to where we started. However, sometimes this tracking is more expensive than simply making a copy of the state and putting that copy back.

Sources indicate that in this case, during borrow checking, we call into the the trait solver and end up unifying two "lifetime variables", which we roll back. This specific rollback involves a copy, though there was a shortcut. We keep track of a single boolean: "was any lifetime variable modified". If none were, the rollback can be skipped. The old solver wouldn't do such unifications, so the rollback could always be skipped, while in the newly introduced solver we couldn't do so.

Recent findings suggest that often, there are very few lifetime variables in scope, so doing a rollback isn't so bad. However, the example above lists every unicode character in existence, so the list is rather long. And for every item in the list, we'd do such a rollback, that copied all lifetime variables (for which there is one per element in the list). So N undos copying a list of N lifetime variables, that's a quadratic factor! So this crate would compile just fine with the old solver, and be 200 times slower with the new solver. Oops!

There are two important strategies we use to make the trait solver faster. First of all, there's caching, and a lot of it. For example, in the following example we prove that i32: Sized three times:.

We'd like to make it so we only need to figure out whether a specific type is Sized once, and so we cache the result.

The second optimization we use a lot is not caching funnily enough. Accessing the cache can be rather expensive (we'll get to why). So in this case, since i32 is trivially Sized, we can answer the question faster by never looking in the cache. For more complicated types this is not true.

In a recent development, A naive cache would be a mapping from questions asked to the trait solver, to answers (errors or proofs). So, something like HashMap, but this wouldn't perform so well. Let's look at this example:.

Here we've renamed the variables T and U between foo and bar. We'll prove two question, that T: Into and later U: Into. Because of the renamings these two proofs are the same, but the questions are technically different. If we don't do something about variable renaming, we'd have cache misses all the time.

Another matter is that this cache wouldn't even work. By now, we've learned that candidates for proofs can come from three sources:.

The first two play nicely, because the same impl blocks and compiler built-ins are around for all questions submitted to the trait solver. Howver, where bounds are different for every function, and thus a proof that a type implements a trait inside of one function, may not be reusable inside another function.

Recent findings suggest that in the example above, we prove that T: Into twice. Inside foo that's ok, but not inside of bar. So if we naively cached that T: Into we wouldn't notice that bar is incorrect.

We call the set of bounds that are in-scope during trait solving the ParamEnv (parameter environment), and so the cache would really have to look like HashMap<(ParamEnv, Question), Answer>. Since for every function, the ParamEnv is different, we'd have even more cache misses.

To improve our chances of a cache hit, we perform a process called "Canonicalization". During canonicalization, we do two things. First we'll rename all variables with numbers. So, T: Into will become ?0: Into (variable 0 implements Into variable 1). Since this process is consistent, another renamed input like U: Into also gets this numbering and is compatible.

Industry observers note that in addition, we'll try very hard to figure out which where bounds in the ParamEnv actually matter. If there are bounds that won't affect the result of the query, we can avoid putting them in the cache key, making cache hits more likely.

According to recent reports, so, in the rust compiler, the cache really looks more like a HashMap<(Paramenv, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer> Note that the answer of every query now has to be de-canonicalized. We call this "instantiation". When we turn T: Into into ?0: Into, and cache its result, and we later look for U: Into, we have to turn the answer (that mentions variables 0 and 1) into U and T respectively. In other words, by canonicalizing we make cache hits much more likely, but the process isn't free. Hence not caching is sometimes worth it for simple questions.

Industry observers note that now is this worth it? Below I've plotted the hit rate of the new solver's cache for various popular crates, and one internal rust compiler benchmark.

As you can see, we can often avoid almost 80% of all trait solving by caching. The last two bars are for a crate called wg-grammar. It is a crate that used to be particularly slow with the upcoming trait solver. Part of my job this year used to be specifically optimizing it.

Recent findings suggest that the problem was that there's one more property that has to be part of the cache key: which opaque types are in scope. An opaque type is a type you write as a "return position impl trait". For example:.

Sources indicate that foo returns impl IntoIterator. By doing so, callers of this function don't get to know what specific type is returned. Only that they can iterate over whatever they get back. Inside of this function foo, the trait solver will infer which specific type gets returned (a Vec), but in other functions calling foo, this information is not available. So, this is another piece of information that may affect answers from function to function, just like the ParamEnv.

Sources indicate that so, the real cache has one more input: HashMap<(ParamEnv, OpaqueTypes, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer>. What that really means is that the following two functions both submit the question i32: Clone to the trait solver, but cannot reuse the cache entry:.

Recent findings suggest that this ends up mattering a lot in async code, or code like parser-generators that tend to return -> impl Parser from functions. That's unfortunate, because the fact that opaque types are different ends up almost never affecting the outcome of a question. Sure, we can come up with examples where it does, but in practice it almost never does.

So, the fix here is to remove opaque types from the cache key to the cached value like so: HashMap<(ParamEnv, CanonicalQuestion), (CanonicalAnswer, OpaqueTypeState)>. Then, every time we answer a question that may be different because of opaque types, we record in the opaque type state under what condition it may affect the answer, and continue assuming the answer is unaffected (this is often the case). Then, when we get a cached answer in a specific environment, we look at the opaque type state, to see whether the answer might be affected by current context. It almost never is, but if it ends up mattering, we retry the question but now no longer assuming opaque types don't matter.

Recent findings suggest that this sometimes makes performance worse (we sometimes do double work), but since its so rare, we get an improvement over all by having more cache hits. In the graph from above, there are two bars for wg-grammar. One where the hit rate is 73% and one where the hit rate is 79%. This 6% difference translates to some the wg-grammar crate first taking 28 seconds to compile, and afterwards only 14 seconds. That's 2x faster!

(click to expand for me going into a little more detail about this).

Technically even when we use opaque type tracking, the list of opaques is still part of the key. We just set it to be an empty list. That means that in the rerun, we un-empty it and we get a different cache key. Now because we keep the cache entry with the empty list around too, when a new query comes along it will also empty the list, find a cache hit that matches this empty list but with tracking information (so it's not redoing work getting that tracking). Then, if it decides it needs to rerun, it adds back the list of opaques and could totally get a cache hit again if we've tried with those exact opaques before.

Sources indicate that of note is also that sometimes we run multiple dependent queries without their opaques like this. We can only un-empty the list once we get back up to the root at the point where we emptied the list to see if they may be unnecessary. To make sure we don't spend too much time running giant query trees we have a bailing mechanism built in to the tracking. Once a query and it's dependencies try to access opaques more than 3 times (or when they do so in very specific ways) we assume that it's unlikely for opaques not to influence the outcome of the query in any way, and we bail out of the "erased" attempts (recording in each dependent result that it's likely a rerun is necessary) and rerun without every knowing the original (erased) result, since it's unlikely to be correct. Future queries will see that this happened in the tracking information, and never attempt to erase opaque types. They know that the attempt is likely wasted.

Now there's an even more subtle thing going on. Sometimes assuming that opaques are empty (in a specific path related to coroutines) leads to query cycles. So, in that case we are forced to do this bailing and to rerun with opaque types even if the answer would've maybe been correct with the erased environment, because the compiler would crash if it encountered the cycle and we want to avoid those at all costs. In this case we may end up rerunning with opaque types, get to the exact same point, and continue to return the exact same result as we would have when we erased the environment previously. This is sadly unavoidable.

This, and more optimizations meant that wg-grammar used to take almost 200 Billion cpu cycles to compile, and now only about 7 Billion.

Now this is my second blog post about trait solver optimization. The other one is a little more technical, and goes into all the different things we did over the past year to bring the newly introduced trait solver towards stabilization. Go read it next if you're interested, and thank you for reading! If you're still interested in learning more about this, I'm happy to answer any questions if you reach out.

In a recent development, also, hell yea! you made it to the end. Here's my cat.

Improving Hugging Face Model Access for Kaggle Users

📅 14 May 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community.
  • Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.
  • You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community. That’s why we’re excited to announce our prepares to bring our platforms and communities closer to better serve AI developers everywhere.

Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.

You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa. Start by visiting a Hugging Face model page like Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B. To use it in a Kaggle Notebook, you can click on “Use this model” and select “Kaggle” to open up a Kaggle notebook with a pre-populated code snippet to load the model. You can do the same from a Hugging Face model page on Kaggle by clicking the “Code” button.

Industry observers note that when you run a notebook on Kaggle that references a model hosted on Hugging Face Hub, we will automatically generate a Hugging Face model page if one doesn’t exist already. You don’t need to make any special changes to your code. Additionally, when you make your notebook public, it will automatically show on the “Code” tab of the Kaggle model page.

Discover Hugging Face models and explore all the community examples in public notebooks in one place on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/models. As more Hugging Face models are used on Kaggle, the number of models and associated code examples you can explore for inspiration will grow.

In a recent development, when browsing Hugging Face models on Kaggle, we want to make it easy for you to navigate back to Hugging Face to explore additional details, metadata, community usage in Hugging Face Spaces, discussion, and more. Simply click “Open in Hugging Face” on the Kaggle model page.

Sources indicate that if you use a private Hugging Face model in your Kaggle notebook, authenticate via your Hugging Face account as normal (add your HF_TOKEN in the “Add-ons > Secrets” menu in the notebook editor). A Hugging Face model page won’t be generated on Kaggle.

If you want to access a consent-gated model in your Kaggle notebook, you’ll need to request access to it using a Hugging Face account and follow the prompts on your browser's Hugging Face model page as normal. Hugging Face has documentation to guide you through this process. Otherwise, the integration will work the same as for non-gated models.

Sources indicate that we’re actively working on a solution to seamlessly use Hugging Face models in Kaggle competitions that require offline notebook submissions. While this will take a few more months to complete, we believe the wait will be worth it.

You can read Kaggle’s position on “AI Competitions as the gold standard for empirical rigor for GenAI evaluation” to understand why it’s so vital for us to get this part of the integration right! But tl;dr – Kaggle is highly sensitive to data leakage and its impact on model contamination. Our goal is to design this integration to preserve the integrity of our competitions and their vital role in the industry, while enabling seamless access for Kaggle competitors to build with the best models from Hugging Face!

We’d love to hear your feedback in the meantime - share your thoughts and ideas here!

A living trust is a legal arrangement where you (the grantor) transfer ownership of your assets to a trust entity that you also control (as trustee). It sounds circular, and in practice, during your lifetime, nothing changes about how you use your money and property. The magic happens when you die or become incapacitated.

The three key roles in a living trust:.

Sources indicate that during your lifetime: You are both the grantor and the trustee. You control everything. You can add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, modify terms, or dissolve the trust entirely. Your Social Security number is the trust's tax ID — there is no separate tax return. For practical purposes, nothing changes about your daily financial life.

If you become incapacitated: Your successor trustee immediately takes over management of trust assets. No court petition needed. No guardianship proceeding. No delay. This is a major advantage over a will, which provides zero protection during incapacity.

When you die: Your successor trustee distributes assets according to your trust document. No probate court. No public record. No waiting 6-18 months. Beneficiaries can typically receive assets within days or weeks.

A living trust essentially creates a private, self-executing transfer system that operates outside the court system entirely. For FI families who have spent years building wealth, this means your heirs receive the full value of your estate without probate eating into it.

According to recent reports, the terms "revocable" and "irrevocable" describe whether you can change or dissolve the trust after creating it. This distinction has major implications for control, taxes, and asset protection.

Revocable living trust — the standard choice for most families:.

You retain full control. You can amend the trust, add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, or dissolve it completely at any time. Because you maintain control, the IRS treats trust assets as yours — they are included in your taxable estate, and creditors can reach them. The primary benefit is probate avoidance and incapacity protection, not asset protection or tax reduction.

Irrevocable trust — the advanced tool for specific situations:.

According to recent reports, once created, you generally cannot change or revoke it. You give up control of the assets placed inside. In exchange, you get benefits that a revocable trust cannot provide.

When an irrevocable trust makes sense:.

In a recent development, for most FI families: A revocable living trust is the right starting point. It provides the two biggest benefits — probate avoidance and incapacity protection — while letting you maintain complete control.

The re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a latest deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage organization (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

Ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a fresh bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.
