In a recent development, A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance organization of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

In a recent development, online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

In a recent development, transfer real estate by recording fresh deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Sources indicate that draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and update both documents every 3-5 years.

A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Recent findings suggest that yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

A living trust is one of the most effective tools for protecting the wealth you have built on the path to financial independence. It avoids probate, provides incapacity protection, maintains complete privacy, and ensures your heirs receive assets quickly and efficiently. The key is actually funding the trust — transferring asset titles into it. For FI families with a net worth above $500K, the $1,500-$5,000 setup cost pays for itself many times over in avoided probate fees and time savings for your heirs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SPONSORED FEATURE: Agentic AI turns inference into a round-the-clock production job. Here's what it takes to keep the tokens flowing in the datacenter you already have.

Recent findings suggest that agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure. According to Goldman Sachs, token consumption is set to jump 24-fold to 120 quadrillion tokens per month between this year and 2030. Enterprises, wary of frontier model sticker shock, are now building their own GPU estates to cope.

According to recent reports, those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production. The indicators of success for such companies are different than those for a frontier model provider, and so are the constraints. DIY AI infrastructure at the enterprise level has to earn ROI quickly, meaning that enterprises must focus on sustained operation. That makes engineering criteria such as uptime, heat and power, service windows, and deployment times doubly vital. The performance benchmarks that hyperscalers focus on won't matter nearly as much to the average bank or retailer.

ASUS is presenting the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, built on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, as a worked example of sustained AI inference infrastructure. It confirmed two models at NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October: the 3U hybrid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BHFS and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BLFS.

In a recent development, agents represent a hockey stick curve for token consumption because an agent isn't a single prompt. It loops until the job's done, often spawning other versions of itself in the process. This is how it breaks a goal into steps and works through them iteratively.

According to recent reports, while training is a batch workload, agent inference is a production service that runs around the clock and only gets bigger. NVIDIA is making each generation of systems more powerful than the last to keep up with the demands of both.

According to recent reports, running at scale, day after day, is another matter. A useful way to think about the infrastructure that does it is as a token factory: it takes in power, data and GPU compute and turns out tokens. What counts is throughput, meaning how many tokens, and how many people, the same power and floor space can serve, hour after hour.

It has been revealed that enterprises are moving ahead quickly with their AI factory projects. According to Deloitte's AI infrastructure survey, published in March, 64 percent of respondents have started limited or at-scale AI factory deployments, while 88 percent expect to do so by 2028. They are spending more on AI infrastructure to do it: 86 percent expect their budgets to increase over the next three years.

In a recent development, enterprises have different problems from hyperscalers and frontier model companies, though. Model builders often get to design greenfield campuses around their GPUs. Conversely, enterprises are often working with small operations teams in existing datacenters that may not have been built with AI in mind. That means they need to think harder about maintenance windows, existing management tooling and predictable deployment. And they'll often be retrofitting halls whose racks rarely draw more than 30 kW.

Sources indicate that in token factory terms, the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System is the core compute engine. Each system puts eight NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPUs on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, linked by sixth-generation NVLink. ASUS has designed its equipment to support the constraints above. Its customers can choose between the hybrid and fully liquid-cooled models, and they can opt for partial or full rack configurations by buying multiple trays. This enables them to match their facilities' needs.

The other difference between model providers and enterprises lies in which numbers they care about. Peak performance is different from sustained performance. The first is a specification sheet number, while the second is what the GPU actually delivers hours into a heavy workload.

Recent findings suggest that production inference tends to run continuously, especially when it uses agents, as opposed to training, which is a sporadic job. So the sustained figure is the one that buyers pay for. Heat becomes a real concern here because when cooling can't keep up, GPUs throttle their clocks to protect themselves. In a token factory, a throttled GPU is a slower production line.

Industry observers note that the more advanced the architecture becomes, the higher the stakes get. NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU has raised them to their highest point, delivering up to 400 petaflops of NVFP4 inference per eight-GPU board, according to NVIDIA's sparse specification. This is screamingly fast, but the increased heat per board means less margin before throttling.

According to recent reports, ASUS designed both models to put direct-to-chip liquid cooling on every GPU. Only the 3U unit leaves the CPUs on air cooling. ASUS also claims it puts every configuration through a 168-hour stress test.

Recent findings suggest that as boards increase their compute density, pushing up the power and heat requirements, planning naturally has to move out of the server room and into the facility. That's the case whether you're talking about an entire NVL72 rack or a stack of eight-GPU servers like the ASUS systems.

There are other things to consider beyond heat. Few datacenters run racks drawing more than 30 kilowatts, notes the Uptime Institute. Yet a single liquid-cooled tray of the ASUS systems draws up to 23.9 kilowatts, and a full rack of nine has a power budget of about 216 kilowatts.

Floor loading and power distribution matter as much as cooling.

In a recent development, NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU raises the stakes again. The eight-GPU format enables organizations to buy their computing power in more granular steps. That's where the two ASUS systems come into their own. With few enterprises needing a training cluster at NVL72 scale, the advantage is that an HGX box lets them buy AI compute in digestible pieces.

The ASUS systems also come with a 54V busbar and cable-free board-to-board design. ASUS says this simplifies assembly and improves reliability.

According to recent reports, so that's space, power and heat. But a GPU board won't produce many tokens if the network, storage or operational tooling can't feed it properly. Agent workloads move context and data all the time, so east-west bandwidth and local storage are key to effective utilization. Any latest equipment should ideally slot straight into the enterprise's existing management and monitoring tooling.

ASUS ships the whole rack, including servers, networking, power and storage, as a single blueprint. ASUS pre-validates this AI Factory reference architecture at rack scale so that organizations can plan for future growth. That includes dedicated management nodes and a management switch.

It has been revealed that inside each tray, ASUS has sized the data paths to keep the GPUs fed. Eight OSFP ports on NVIDIA ConnectX-9 give every GPU 800Gb/s of east-west bandwidth to the rest of the cluster, and an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU adds two 400GbE ports. Within the board, the eight GPUs talk to each other over NVLink at 3,600GB/s, ASUS says. The 2U tray takes up to 4TB of DDR5 system memory and has eight E1.S NVMe bays for fast local data access, while the 3U model offers a choice of U.2 or E1.S drives.

The other matter for enterprises putting AI inference into production is service and maintenance. In a liquid-cooled box, routine fixes can mean draining a coolant loop, which is downtime, and lost token output, that most enterprises can't afford, especially when dealing with non-batch workloads such as inferencing. So ASUS set out to make components quicker to swap.

It has been revealed that on the 2U fully liquid-cooled model, ASUS did it with independent, tool-less CPU and GPU sleds, each with its own direct-to-chip cooling. On the 3U hybrid, ASUS says the air-cooled CPU sled cuts maintenance time by up to 50 percent.

Sources indicate that services aren't just about server maintenance. They're also about decreasing the time to value for AI. Most enterprises won't have in-house rack-scale GPU integration skills, which is why pre-validation and design services are so crucial.

Industry observers note that ASUS claims its services run from early facility assessment through to operations. Its professional services cover five offerings: infrastructure design, deployment, performance optimization, AI platform development and lifecycle management. For rapid deployment, ASUS uses its own automation platform, the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center (AIDC).

It has been revealed that so, with an enterprise token factory judged on how reliably it keeps producing rather than on peak FLOPS, in-house AI deployment teams will be back to focusing on the basics, albeit while dealing with an innovative technology. That means they'll be asking questions about sustained performance, heat and power in existing facilities. They'll be looking at integration at the rack level and with management software, along with service windows and deployment time. ASUS is positioning itself as a partner that can answer those questions with the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, which it's making available this quarter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.
  • Transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model.
  • Industry observers note that transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 new architectures added every week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

Transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model. Since then, we've continuously aimed to add state-of-the-art architectures, initially focused on NLP, then growing to Audio and computer vision. Today, transformers is the default library for LLMs and VLMs in the Python ecosystem.

Industry observers note that transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 new architectures added every week. We have aimed for these architectures to be released in a timely manner; having day-0 support for the most sought-after architectures (Llamas, Qwens, GLMs, etc.).

Over time, Transformers has become a central component in the ML ecosystem, becoming one of the most complete toolkits in terms of model diversity; it's integrated in all popular training frameworks such as Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, TRL, Nanotron, etc.

Recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...) for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

As an example, here is how you would work with the transformers backend in vLLM:.

That's all it takes for a fresh model to enjoy super-fast and production-grade serving with vLLM!

Read more about it in the vLLM documentation.

We've also been working very closely with llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

We are super proud that the transformers format is being adopted by the community, bringing a lot of interoperability we all benefit from. Train a model with Unsloth, deploy it with SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp to run locally! We aim to keep supporting the community going forward.

To make it easier for the community to use transformers as a reference for model definitions, we strive to significantly reduce the barrier to model contributions. We have been doing this effort for a few years, but we'll accelerate significantly over the next few weeks:.

As a model user, in the future you should see even more interoperability in the tools that you use.

This does not mean that we intend to lock you in using transformers in your experiments; rather, it means that thanks to this modeling standardization, you can expect the tools that you use for training, for inference, and for production, to efficiently work together.

As a model creator, this means that a single contribution will get your model available in all downstream libraries that have integrated that modeling implementation. We have seen this many times over the years: releasing a model is stressful and integrating in all important libraries is often a significant time-sink.

By standardizing the model implementation in a community-driven manner, we hope to lower the barrier of contributions to the field across libraries.

We firmly believe this renewed direction will help standardize an ecosystem which is often at risk of fragmentation. We'd love to hear your feedback on the direction the team has decided to take; and of changes we could do to get there. Please come and see us over at the transformers-community support tab on the Hub!

Awesome news! Transformers being the default access point for as many models on day 0 as well as in being able to use the inference engine of choice is an epic goal!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an newly introduced pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this blogpost, we present the key highlights and rationales about the Falcon-Edge series - a collection of powerful, universal, and fine-tunable language models available in ternary format, based on the BitNet architecture.

Drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an newly introduced pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants. This comprehensive approach produces a non-BitNet model in bfloat16 format, the native BitNet model, and a pre-quantized BitNet variant specifically engineered for effortless fine-tuning, enabling people and developers to precisely tailor these models to their specific applications and needs.

Recent findings suggest that available now in two sizes—1 Billion and 3 Billion parameters—each size comes in both base and instruction-tuned models. Discover the Falcon-Edge series on our dedicated Hugging Face collection.

In a recent development, large Language Models (LLMs), by design, are inherently large and resource-intensive. As demand grows to deploy these models efficiently on edge devices, research into model compression has accelerated. Recent efforts, such as those by DeepSeek and Llama 4, explore training with reduced precision formats—down to FP8—to improve deployment scalability. On the other hand, many state-of-the-art methods emphasize post-training quantization. In contrast to these approaches, BitNet introduces a fundamentally different paradigm: unlike reduced-precision training which still relies on floating-point formats, and post-training quantization which adjusts weights after full-precision training, BitNet operates with the lowest possible precision — ternary weights ({-1, 0, 1}) — directly during training, enabling an end-to-end ultra-efficient model design.

In a recent development, these ternary weights are paving the way for a “matmul-free” LLM design that is notably faster and remarkably memory-efficient in practice. The primary challenge of this innovative approach is the necessity for pre-training BitNet models, which can be computationally demanding and costly for typical customers.

According to recent reports, leveraging the learnings from pre-training data strategies from our center, we pre-train our model on an internal data mixture for approximately 1.5 Tera Tokens. We use the classic WSD learning rate scheduler for pre-training.

We evaluate our models (base and instruct versions) on the former Hugging Face leaderboard v2 benchmark and report the normalized results below in comparison with other models of similar size:.

Additional results (leaderboard v1) on comparing our instructed models with Microsoft’s upcoming BitNet model:.

Falcon-Edge demonstrates on-par and better performances than models of comparable sizes on the leaderboard v2 tasks, demonstrating that it is possible to train powerful BitNet models on desired domains while being competitive enough on other tasks.

If we look closer at the formula of the BitNet linear layer for inference (in terms of Python code):.

The normalization activation_norm_quant quantizes the activations in int8 format, then the activation is computed back in half precision by diving it by x_scale. Since the model has been trained with fake 8-bit activation quantization, we argue that it is possible to approximate that:.

Therefore, instead of quantizing the model post-training, injecting the weight scale after quantizing the weights should lead to a good enough “approximation” of the non-BitNet version of the model:.

We confirm this by running end-to-end evaluations on the bfloat16 variant of our 1B and 3B base models and below are the results:.

The bfloat16 counterparts of the models can be loaded directly via Hugging Face transformers by passing revision="bfloat16" in the from_pretrained function:.

To the best of our knowledge, except from the most recent release from Microsoft previous BitNet releases only focus on releasing the final quantized model, making it usable only for inference. Similarly to the release from Microsoft, we propose to extend the accessibility of research and application of BitNet models by releasing their pre-quantized weights. That way, users can either perform fine-tuning on their target domain, or do continuous pre-training of the BitNet checkpoint as long as nn.Linear layers are replaced by BitnetLinear layers, and by making sure to quantize the model post training in BitNet format. Since the weights corresponds to the pre-quantized weights, performing text generation without replacing the nn.Linear layers with BitnetLinear layers will produce gibberish output.

The pre-quantized weights can be downloaded via Hugging Face's transformers library by specifying the revision argument to be prequantized:.

It has been revealed that this way, we will help fostering an ecosystem around first powerful 1-bit fine-tunes by the community. We provide to community the tools to get easily started and fine-tune their own version of powerful BitNet models by packaging all needed utility methods for performing fine-tuning on the pre-quantized weights on a Python package called onebitllms that we will cover in the next section.

In this release, we also introduce onebitllms - a lightweight Python package that can be plugged into your favorite LLM fine-tuning tools in order to fine-tune any pre-quantized BitNet model. At this time of writing onebitllms exposes these main functionalities:.

Currently, only full-finetuning is supported through this framework, while in this release the model sizes are relatively small, supporting Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for BitNet models remains an exciting and impactful open question for upcoming BitNet models.

To get started, simply install the package directly through pip or from source, and take a look at examples/ folders inside the source code.

With this package, we hope to accelerate research and development around ternary format LLMs, and hope to see many derivations of Falcon-Edge and other future powerful BitNet models developed by the community.

We believe this release opens up multiple interesting directions - among all the possible follow up directions, we currently think that the following open questions will make BitNet models much more impactful in the near future:.

If you find this work useful for your research and work, please consider citing our work, as well as citing all the foundational work behind BitNet models:.

Making more open models easily accessible to Azure customers, for secure deployment alongside company private data, will enable enterprises to build AI applications and agents while being fully in control of their technology and data.

We’re enabling companies to take control of their AI destiny, deploying the best open models securely within their Azure account, to build AI applications they can trust and verify.

-- Clement Delangue, CEO and cofounder at Hugging Face.

In a recent development, let’s head over to Azure AI Foundry, and select the Model Catalog. Here you can now find over 10,000 models under the Hugging Face Collection.

Models in the Collection include the most popular, trending models on Hugging Face for a wide range of tasks to work with text, audio and images - including text generation, feature extraction, fill-mask, translation, identifying sentence similarity, image classification, image segmentation, text to image generation, image to text conversion, automatic speech recognition and audio-classification.

To make the Hugging Face Collection on Azure AI Foundry enterprise-ready, we are only featuring models:.

In addition, Microsoft and Hugging Face will continuously test inference containers for vulnerabilities to maintain and patch them as needed.

Now let’s say you want to deploy for instance the popular Microsoft Phi-4 Reasoning Plus open model.

According to recent reports, first, let’s select the model in the Hugging Face Collection in Azure AI Foundry, and click the “Deploy button”. The form allows you to select a VM, instance count and deployment parameters, and start the deployment process with just another click!

Now, if you prefer browsing models on the Hub, you can also start from the model page - the “Deploy on Azure ML” option will take you to the same deployment option within Azure AI Machine Learning Studio.

We are really excited about all the upcoming Hugging Face models and modalities now directly available within Azure AI Foundry, but we’re not going to stop there!

In the weeks and months to come, you can expect a rolling thunder of updates:.

If you’re on Azure, it’s time to build with open models!

InfoQ Homepage News Vercel Rolled out Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks across Humans and Coding Agents.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that vercel has launched Vercel Board, an experimental, headless message board where people and coding agents coordinate tasks across tools and harnesses. Vercel claims Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can work on the same board as if they were a single harness.

According to recent reports, each Vercel team gets a default board, named General, organized into channels and threads. Developers and agents read and write through the `vercel board` CLI or the `@vercel/board` JavaScript SDK. A skill, installed with npx skills add vercel/board --skill board, teaches coding agents the CLI. Agents name themselves with --as or BOARD_PROFILE, but still act with the operator's or project's credentials.

In a recent development, A task is a thread whose state the board keeps. A worker claims a ready task, posts updates, and completes or fails it. A claim is a lease of up to five minutes and must be renewed; if it expires, the task returns to the queue. When two workers claim the same task, one succeeds and the other fails with task_claimed. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits until its fix completes while independent work proceeds in parallel. Watchers on a Vercel deployment can run when a reply is posted or a label changes, waking the deployment so no process has to stay running.

Sources indicate that sync, configured in the SDK and delivered through Vercel Connect, can attach a board channel to Slack, GitHub, or Linear. Slack and Linear sync both ways; GitHub imports pull requests and issues and does not write back unless the project sends those messages. Grants control who can read, post, and manage each channel. For an agent in a Vercel Sandbox, sandboxPolicy() can grant limited board access without putting a credential inside the sandbox. Vercel says it rebuilt v0's software factory on Board, and that the factory now merges over 50% of its pull requests.

Official documentation warns that Board grants do not apply on Slack, GitHub, or Linear, so a private Slack channel synced into an open board channel is readable by the whole Vercel team.

Austin King (@MadeWithOzten) replied to Vercel's announcement asking to:.

Do this self-hosted and open source - Rust, Yjs Sync,.

then wrote that he had bought openboard.lol.

For a self-hosted open source Vercel board like thing.

Aaron Delz (@AaronDelz) said he already kept a shared checklist with his agent, and liked that a Board task can be completed with the pull request attached:.

Same rule my agents run on: no saying 'done' without the evidence.

Similar coordination shows up elsewhere. OpenCrawl is an open source, self-hostable board that also records agent sessions. GitHub Agent HQ can assign issues and pull requests to Copilot, Claude, or Codex. Linear's cloud coding agent turns scoped issues into draft pull requests with Claude Code or Codex. Claude Code agent teams coordinate multiple Claude Code sessions around a shared task list, and the Agent2Agent protocol standardizes delegation between agents rather than hosting a board.

Board remains experimental infrastructure on a Vercel team. Setup steps and the CLI and SDK references are in Vercel's Board documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

nanoVLM is the simplest way to get started with training your very own Vision Language Model (VLM) using pure PyTorch. It is lightweight toolkit which allows you to launch a VLM training on a free tier colab notebook.

We were inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT, and provide a similar project for the vision domain.

In a recent development, at its heart, nanoVLM is a toolkit that helps you build and train a model that can understand both images and text, and then generate text based on that. The beauty of nanoVLM lies in its simplicity. The entire codebase is intentionally kept minimal and readable, making it perfect for beginners or anyone who wants to peek under the hood of VLMs without getting overwhelmed.

In this blog post, we cover the core ideas behind the project and provide a simple way to interact with the repository. We not only go into the details of the project but also encapsulate all of it so that you can quickly get started.

You can start training a Vision Language Model using our nanoVLM toolkit by following these steps:.

Here is a Colab notebook that will help you launch a training run with no local setup required!

As the name suggests, a Vision Language Model (VLM) is a multi-modal model that processes two modalities: vision and text. These models typically take images and/or text as input and generate text as output.

Generating text (output) conditioned on the understanding of images and texts (inputs) is a powerful paradigm. It enables a wide range of applications, from image captioning and object detection to answering questions about visual content (as shown in the table below). One thing to note is that nanoVLM focuses only on Visual Question Answering as the training objective.

If you are interested in learning more about VLMs, we strongly recommend reading our latest blog on the topic: Vision Language Models (Better, Faster, Stronger).

"Talk is cheap, show me the code" - Linus Torvalds.

In a recent development, in this section, we’ll guide you through the codebase. It’s helpful to keep a tab open for reference as you follow along.

Industry observers note that below is the folder structure of our repository. We have removed helper files for brevity.

We model nanoVLM after two well known and widely used architectures. Our vision backbone (models/vision_transformer.py) is the standard vision transformer, more specifically Google’s SigLIP vision encoder. Our language backbone follows the Llama 3 architecture.

The vision and text modalities are aligned using a Modality Projection module. This module takes the image embeddings produced by the vision backbone as input, and transforms them into embeddings compatible with the text embeddings from the embedding layer of the language model. These embeddings are then concatenated and fed into the language decoder. The Modality Projection module consists of a pixel shuffle operation followed by a linear layer.

Pixel shuffle reduces the number of image tokens, which helps reduce computational cost and speeds up training, especially for transformer-based language decoders which are sensitive to input length. The figure below demonstrates the concept.

According to recent reports, all the files are very lightweight and well documented. We highly encourage you to check them out individually to get a better understanding of the implementation details (models/xxx.py).

One could also swap out the backbones with other variants of SigLIP/SigLIP 2 (for the vision backbone) and SmolLM2 (for the language backbone).

Using nanoVLM as the toolkit, we have trained a model and published it to Hub. We have used the google/siglip-base-patch16-224 and HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M as backbones. The model was trained this for ~6h on a single H100 GPU on ~1.7M samples of the cauldron.

This model isn't intended to compete with SoTA models, but rather to demystify the components and training process of VLMs.

In this blog post, we walked through what VLMs are, explored the architecture choices that power nanoVLM, and unpacked the training and inference workflows in detail.

By keeping the codebase lightweight and readable, nanoVLM aims to serve as both a learning tool and a foundation you can build upon. Whether you’re looking to understand how multi-modal inputs are aligned, or you want to train a VLM on your own dataset, this repository gives you a head start.

If you try it out, build on top of it, or just have questions we’d love to hear from you. Happy tinkering!

I’ve been working on a fork of Nano-vLLM called Nano-vLLM-v1, which re-engineers the core architecture to closely reproduce the vLLM v1 scheduler and introduces Chunked Prefill for better performance.

The goal was to build a lightweight, readable, yet highly efficient inference engine that stays true to the original vLLM design while being easy to understand and extend.

Check it out here: https://github.com/slwang-ustc/nano-vllm-v1/tree/main.

It has been revealed that I’d love for the community to try it out, give feedback, or contribute! The code is designed to be readable and modular, making it easy to experiment with new features or optimizations.

If you’re interested in lightweight, high-performance LLM inference without the complexity, give it a star ⭐ and let me know what you think!

The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis.
  • I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens upcoming window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window).
  • Sources indicate that but that's easier stated than done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving, and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens upcoming window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

Sources indicate that but that's easier stated than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens fresh window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

Sources indicate that it might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:.

According to recent reports, proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

According to recent reports, my chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a latest formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):.

So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:.

It has been revealed that this design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

In a recent development, A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens upcoming window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

Sources indicate that I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens upcoming window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

#150558. Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers

📅 21 May 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (922 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that large diffusion models like Flux (a flow-based text-to-image generation model) can create stunning images, but their size can be a hurdle, demanding significant memory and compute resources.
  • Before we dive into the technical details of how various quantization backends in Hugging Face Diffusers work, why not test your own perception?
  • We created a setup where you can provide a prompt, and we generate results using both the original, high-precision model (e.g., Flux-dev in BF16) and several quantized versions (BnB 4-bit, BnB 8-bit).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that large diffusion models like Flux (a flow-based text-to-image generation model) can create stunning images, but their size can be a hurdle, demanding significant memory and compute resources. Quantization offers a powerful solution, shrinking these models to make them more accessible without drastically compromising performance. But the major question always is: can you actually tell the difference in the final image?

Before we dive into the technical details of how various quantization backends in Hugging Face Diffusers work, why not test your own perception?

We created a setup where you can provide a prompt, and we generate results using both the original, high-precision model (e.g., Flux-dev in BF16) and several quantized versions (BnB 4-bit, BnB 8-bit). The generated images are then presented to you and your challenge is to identify which ones came from the quantized models.

It has been revealed that often, especially with 8-bit quantization, the differences are subtle and may not be noticeable without close inspection. More aggressive quantization like 4-bit or lower might be more noticeable, but the results can still be good, especially considering the massive memory savings. NF4 often gives the best trade-off though.

In a recent development, building on our previous post, "Memory-efficient Diffusion Transformers with Quanto and Diffusers", this post explores the diverse quantization backends integrated directly into Hugging Face Diffusers. We'll examine how bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, Quanto and native FP8 support make large and powerful models more accessible, demonstrating their use with Flux.

Before diving into the quantization backends, let's introduce the FluxPipeline (using the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev checkpoint) and its components, which we'll be quantizing. Loading the full FLUX.1-dev model in BF16 precision requires approximately 31.447 GB of memory. The main components are:.

bitsandbytes is a popular and user-friendly library for 8-bit and 4-bit quantization, widely used for LLMs and QLoRA fine-tuning. We can use it for transformer-based diffusion and flow models, too.

All benchmarks performed on 1x NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU.

Note: When using PipelineQuantizationConfig with bitsandbytes, you need to import DiffusersBitsAndBytesConfig from diffusers and TransformersBitsAndBytesConfig from transformers separately. This is because these components originate from different libraries. If you prefer a simpler setup without managing these distinct imports, you can use an alternative approach for pipeline-level quantization, an example of this method is in the Diffusers documentation on Pipeline-level quantization.

For more information check out the bitsandbytes docs.

torchao is a PyTorch-native library for architecture optimization, offering quantization, sparsity, and custom data types, designed for compatibility with torch.compile and FSDP. Diffusers supports a wide range of torchao's exotic data types, enabling fine-grained control over model optimization.

For more information check out the torchao docs.

Quanto is a quantization library integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem via the optimum library.

Note: At the time of writing, for float8 support with Quanto, you'll need optimum-quanto<0.2.5 and use quanto directly. We will be working on fixing this.

For more information check out the Quanto docs.

GGUF is a file format popular in the llama.cpp community for storing quantized models.

For more information check out the GGUF docs.

In a recent development, FP8 Layerwise Casting is a memory optimization technique. It works by storing the model's weights in the compact FP8 (8-bit floating point) format, which uses roughly half the memory of standard FP16 or BF16 precision. Just before a layer performs its calculations, its weights are dynamically cast up to a higher compute precision (like FP16/BF16). Immediately afterward, the weights are cast back down to FP8 for efficient storage. This approach works because the core computations retain high precision, and layers particularly sensitive to quantization (like normalization) are typically skipped. This technique can also be combined with group offloading for further memory savings.

For more information check out the Layerwise casting docs.

Most of these quantization backends can be combined with the memory optimization techniques offered in Diffusers. Let's explore CPU offloading, group offloading, and torch.compile. You can learn more about these techniques in the Diffusers documentation.

Note: At the time of writing, bnb + torch.compile also works if bnb is installed from source and using pytorch nightly or with fullgraph=False.

Recent findings suggest that model CPU Offloading (enable_model_cpu_offload): This method moves entire model components (like the UNet, text encoders, or VAE) between the CPU and GPU during the inference pipeline. It offers substantial VRAM savings and is generally faster than more granular offloading because it involves fewer, larger data transfers.

bnb + enable_model_cpu_offload:.

In a recent development, group offloading (enable_group_offload for diffusers components or apply_group_offloading for generic torch.nn.Modules): It moves groups of internal model layers (like torch.nn.ModuleList or torch.nn.Sequential instances) to the CPU. This approach is typically more memory-efficient than full model offloading and faster than sequential offloading.

FP8 layerwise casting + group offloading:.

Note: torch.compile can introduce subtle numerical differences, leading to changes in image output.

torch.compile: Another complementary approach is to accelerate the execution of your model with PyTorch 2.x’s torch.compile() feature. Compiling the model doesn’t directly lower memory, but it can significantly speed up inference. PyTorch 2.0’s compile (Torch Dynamo) works by tracing and optimizing the model graph ahead-of-time.

Explore some benchmarking results here:.

You can find bitsandbytes and torchao quantized models from this blog post in our Hugging Face collection: link to collection.

Here's a quick guide to choosing a quantization backend:.

Quantization significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using large diffusion models. Experiment with these backends to find the best balance of memory, speed, and quality for your needs.

#150555. Latest Update: Taking Email Back

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1647 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Linux-magazine ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Taking Email Back

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Linux-magazine

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.
  • Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line.
  • Industry observers note that the software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.

Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way.

Industry observers note that the software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and plans to move to Aerogramme around January 2027.

In a recent development, the collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains.

Industry observers note that email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence.

In a recent development, two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services.

The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development.

It has been revealed that in the 1990s, running your own mail server was ordinary. Universities and small companies did it, and so did Mauro De Gennaro. In 1993, as a teenager, he fetched mail for consumers of his bulletin board over UUCP: the dial-up protocol Unix machines used to exchange mail. He has worked on mail software for most of the three decades since. When he looked at the open source stack again about six years ago, he saw "it's the same software that companies and servers have been using for over 20 years.".

It has been revealed that he counts 12 separate programs to run a conventional self-hosted setup. Each has its own configuration format and logs, written by different people in different styles. The software works well, he notes, but was "designed and documented for other developers." Bundles such as Mailcow and Mail-in-a-Box install the whole set at once: “They abstract the complexity," De Gennaro says, "but they do not remove it." Since all of it was designed for a single machine, running it as a cluster server is possible in the same way it's possible to take a Fiat Cinquecento and turn it electric: "It was not designed for that." Google rolled out Gmail into that friction in 2004, with a gigabyte of free storage, and let companies run their own domain's mail on it. "Then they started billing," De Gennaro says. The users were captive, and moving email is disruptive enough that few of them left.

Sources indicate that ben Bucksch joined the Mozilla mail team in the late 1990s, where his first contribution made email links clickable; he also served in leadership for the Thunderbird Council and invented AutoConfig, which lets a mail client set up an account from nothing but an email address. In his telling, the lock-in started within the client.

IT departments think about email as servers; “what people want is to keep their workflow," Bucksch notes. Microsoft shaped those workflows with Outlook's calendar and corporate features: Outlook works properly only with Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft is pushing Exchange customers into its cloud. By some estimates, about 75 percent of professional mailboxes are on Office 365. "If we want to free the lock-in," he says, "we need to start with the client.".

It has been revealed that dufour and Armaël Guéneau of Deuxfleurs locate the problem in operations. IMAP is the protocol most clients use to read mail. An IMAP server has to serve webmail that queries the server for every view, desktop clients such as Thunderbird that synchronize whole mailboxes, and phones that do some of each. Implementing it is hard; the reliability people expect is harder. When the tax office sends you an email, Dufour says, "it must work." The expertise to run mail at that level, Guéneau says, "tends to be captured by hyperscalers.".

As Dufour tells it, Google didn't adapt existing mail software; it built Gmail on top of its distributed storage. Open source mail software was designed for one machine first, so adding distribution later, he says, requires "really huge trade-offs.".

Recent findings suggest that reclaiming email is more complex than deciding to run your own server and navigating the software. Your service has to fluently speak with the large providers and support migration without disrupting service. And, of course, it needs sustainable funding.

Today, publicly funded teams are working on solving each of those three problems.

Recent findings suggest that stalwart, the server from De Gennaro’s team, focuses on streamlining the software to replace 12 programs with one: Installation takes two commands and a six-screen web wizard. It speaks every common mail and collaboration protocol: SMTP for sending, IMAP and POP3 for reading, JMAP for web-based mail, and CalDAV and CardDAV for calendars and contacts. Spam filtering, sender authentication, and TLS encryption are built in. Give it a token for a DNS provider such as Cloudflare or Route 53, and the server publishes its own mail records. Behind the wizard are nearly 3,000 settings across 176 screens, which most operators never touch. De Gennaro calls Stalwart "the software at the other end of your email client or calendar client.".

Recent findings suggest that stalwart 1.0 was released in October 2026 after five and a half years of development. NGI Zero funded the project with two grants: one for the mail server, and one for calendars, contacts, and file storage.

Industry observers note that for users who can’t leave Outlook features behind, there’s Parula. Keeping the application logic strictly separate from a thin interface layer, and a well thought-out common logic, so a newly introduced protocol takes “just a few thousand lines of code,” Bucksch and his team at Beonex GmbH built an Outlook-like interface alongside a modern interface, a chat-style view and a classic three-pane view. It runs on a JMAP server or any other mail server and offers shared team mailboxes, delegated access so an assistant can run a manager’s calendar, and free/busy lookups for team meetings. It speaks IMAP, JMAP, and POP3, plus four from Microsoft: Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync, Microsoft Graph, and Outlook Web Access.

Aerogramme, an IMAP server that doesn't keep any state of its own, answers the operations problem in the storage. It doesn’t send or receive mail, so it needs a separate mail transfer agent such as Postfix; then it encrypts each mailbox on Garage, compatible with Amazon’s S3 interface. Garage replicates every piece of data in three locations, so users can still read and write their mail if a site goes offline. This design for power cuts and residential Internet connections gave up perfect synchronization, but it spreads maintenance work among five to ten members rather than requiring one big server host to give up all his weekends.

Recent findings suggest that the research problem, Dufour says, is mapping the mail, calendar, and contact protocols cleanly onto object storage. Aerogramme is still on the way, with internal deployment planned for January 2027 and a public beta a few months later. To get there, a second grant funded through NGI Zero is supporting a hunt for edge cases where a network delay or a failure halfway through writing could lose a message.

Industry observers note that the three projects already interoperate with each other and with other email programs on the NLnet list funded by NGI Zero. Parula lists Stalwart as a supported server; Stalwart can keep its messages in Garage. Bucksch and De Gennaro both name Mox as another server built as a single package. Different teams, working separately, have split the email problem and built solutions that fit back together.

Improvements to SMTP will provide better guarantee of confidentiality.

Version 1.0.0 of the Tarmail mail server has just been released. The developers claim that their software is particularly resilient against exploits, spam and email worms.

Upcoming mail protocol will shut out the NSA and prevent snooping on metadata.

IndiMail, an email solution made of open source components, now includes greylisting spam filtering in version 1.6.

📅 21 May 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1221 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Falcon-Arabic: A Breakthrough in Arabic Language Models

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are excited to introduce Falcon-Arabic, a 7B parameter Language Model that sets a newly introduced benchmark for Arabic NLP.
  • Falcon-Arabic redefines the boundaries of what is possible for Arabic Language Models.
  • Recent findings suggest that in recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed Artificial Intelligence, powering tools for translation, content creation, virtual assistance, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check out our official blogpost (EN, AR).

We are excited to introduce Falcon-Arabic, a 7B parameter Language Model that sets a newly introduced benchmark for Arabic NLP. Built on the Falcon 3 architecture, Falcon-Arabic is a multilingual model that supports Arabic, English, and several other languages. It excels in general knowledge, Arabic grammar, mathematical reasoning, complex problem solving, and understanding the rich diversity of Arabic dialects. Falcon-Arabic supports a context length of 32,000 tokens, allowing it to handle long documents and enabling advanced applications like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in-depth content creation, and knowledge-intensive tasks.

Falcon-Arabic redefines the boundaries of what is possible for Arabic Language Models. It significantly outperforms other Arabic LLMs in its size category and even models up to four times larger across both Arabic-native models and those adapted from other languages. This makes Falcon-Arabic not only a state-of-the-art model in terms of performance, but also a uniquely efficient and accessible solution for developers and researchers working with the Arabic language.

Recent findings suggest that in recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed Artificial Intelligence, powering tools for translation, content creation, virtual assistance, and more. Yet much of this progress has focused on highly represented languages like English, leaving languages such as Arabic underrepresented. Arabic presents unique challenges it's morphologically rich, diglossic (spanning both Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and diverse regional dialects), and used across a vast and culturally varied population. Developing robust Arabic LLMs is essential to ensure Arabic-speaking communities are fully included in the AI revolution.

With this goal in mind, we’re introducing Falcon-Arabic a specialized adaptation of the Falcon 3 model family, developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in the UAE. The Falcon models have earned global recognition for their multilingual strength and open-source approach. Falcon-Arabic builds on this legacy, bringing advanced language understanding and generation to Arabic. By training the model to handle both Modern Standard Arabic and key dialects, Falcon-Arabic fills a critical gap in language technology enabling more natural, intelligent, and inclusive Arabic AI across the Gulf, Middle East, and North Africa.

It has been revealed that building Falcon-Arabic started with a strategic decision: rather than training a model from scratch, we chose to adapt a strong multilingual foundation. In the Arabic LLM landscape, three main approaches exist: training from scratch (e.g., Jais-native), adapting multilingual models (like Allam or Fanar), or using models that natively support Arabic alongside other languages (such as Qwen or LLaMA). Observing the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard, it became clear that adapted and multilingual models consistently outperformed others in both efficiency and capability. To build on that momentum, we selected Falcon 3-7B, a model that strikes a practical balance between performance and resource efficiency within the Falcon 3 family developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII).

Industry observers note that the core challenge was adapting Falcon 3-7B, which originally lacked Arabic support at the tokenizer and embedding level. We addressed this by extending the tokenizer’s vocabulary with 32,000 Arabic-specific tokens, and applying a novel embedding initialization strategy based on textual similarity. This technique mapped latest Arabic tokens to semantically related embeddings from the existing vocabulary, allowing the model to inherit prior knowledge and accelerate learning particularly around sentiment, abstract concepts, and reasoning patterns. This gave Falcon-Arabic a head start in understanding and generating high-quality Arabic text.

It has been revealed that with the tokenizer and embeddings in place, we began continuous pretraining on high-quality, 100% native Arabic datasets, avoiding the use of machine-translated content to minimize cultural bias and preserve linguistic authenticity. Training followed a multi-stage curriculum: early stages focused on general knowledge and dialect-rich Arabic content to stabilize the model and reinforce logical capabilities, while later phases emphasized math, code, and reasoning. The result is a model that not only speaks Arabic fluently across dialects, but also retains Falcon’s multilingual and reasoning strengths pushing the boundaries for Arabic-first AI.

We evaluated Falcon-Arabic on OALL v2, the leading benchmark for Arabic Language Models. It includes six multiple-choice tasks such as Arabic MMLU (native and translated), Arabic Exams, Alghafa, MadinahQA, Aratrust and one generative benchmark, Alrage. Falcon-Arabic outperforms all existing Arabic LLMs in its size range and even surpasses models up to 4× larger. It leads in key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, Exams, MadinahQA, and Aratrust, setting a new standard for Arabic-first Language Models.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base-details.

Recent findings suggest that after finalizing the base model training, we performed a post-training alignment phase to fine-tune Falcon-Arabic’s responses according to human preferences. This phase began with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using a combination of high-quality public datasets and internally collected native Arabic instruction data, covering a range of tasks and conversational scenarios.

Sources indicate that to further enhance alignment, we applied Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) a reinforcement learning-based method that tunes the model to prefer outputs that humans rate as more helpful, safe, and relevant. This two-step process ensures that Falcon-Arabic Instruct not only understands Arabic well but responds in a way that aligns with real user expectations.

Recent findings suggest that as shown in the results plots, Falcon-Arabic Instruct leads the pack, outperforming all other Instruct-aligned Arabic LLMs in its size class and even models significantly larger across multiple benchmarks. The model demonstrates strong performance in both instruction following and open-ended dialogue, setting a new standard for Arabic conversational AI.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct-details.

In a recent development, falcon-Arabic sets a newly introduced benchmark for Arabic Language Models. With only 7B parameters, it delivers state-of-the-art performance outperforming models of similar size and even those several times larger across key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, MadinahQA, and Aratrust. It combines fluency in Modern Standard Arabic, strong understanding of regional dialects, and robust reasoning and multilingual capabilities, making it ideal for a wide range of applications: from Arabic-first chatbots and educational tools to content generation, code assistance, and document understanding.

To give you a hands-on feel for what Falcon-Arabic can do, we built a simple demo that showcases its capabilities in machine translation even though the model hasn’t been fine-tuned specifically for that task. The tool runs purely on Falcon-7B-Arabic-Instruct, and the results are surprisingly strong across various translation directions. You can try it yourself through the demo linked just below. In fact, we used the same setup to translate this blog post into Arabic for our Arabic-speaking audience. Check it out here 🚀. And if you're curious to explore more, we also provide access to a live playground where you can interact with Falcon-Arabic Instruct and experience its performance across different tasks ✨.

Like all Large Language Models, Falcon-Arabic inherits some common limitations. These include occasional hallucinations (producing plausible but incorrect outputs), sensitivity to how prompts are phrased, and varying performance across very long contexts. While Falcon-Arabic is designed to reduce these concerns especially for Arabic tasks consumers should still apply critical thinking when interpreting results, particularly in high-stakes or fact-sensitive use cases.

If you find this work helpful for your research or projects, please consider citing it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News DoorDash Scales Dispatch 10x While Maintaining 99.99% Peak Availability.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

DoorDash has rebuilt its real-time dispatch platform to handle growing delivery demand, replacing a monolithic optimization engine with a distributed architecture that separates coordination from computation. The redesign delivers 10 times higher throughput and more than 99.99% availability during peak periods, while enabling the manufacturer to run machine learning and reinforcement learning models within dispatch workflows.

The previous dispatch engine tightly coupled business logic, logistics state management, and computationally intensive routing algorithms. As delivery volume increased, its optimization workload became increasingly difficult to process within the time available for dispatch decisions. The underlying algorithms had roughly quadratic time complexity, and during peak periods, demand approached four times the system's processing capacity. The engine consequently relied on fallback heuristics and sometimes made assignment decisions using incomplete information.

As the DoorDash engineering team explained:.

The fatal bottleneck wasn't just raw machine capacity; it was the speed of reality.

Rather than address the bottleneck through conventional horizontal scaling, DoorDash redesigned the execution model around two independently scalable tiers. The engineering team described the motivation:.

To scale into the future, the system didn't just need more capacity; it demanded a fundamentally newly introduced execution model.

The newly introduced platform separates execution into two independently scalable tiers. A stateful coordinator manages dispatch lifecycles, maintains global logistics state, and validates business rules. Stateless compute workers handle mathematical optimization, vehicle-routing heuristics, and model inference.

The coordinator distributes localized portions of logistics data to workers using payload sharding over gRPC. This avoids broadcasting the entire global state to every worker and reduces network overhead. Workers process their assigned optimization tasks independently, while the coordinator manages orchestration and result aggregation.

Evolution from DoorDash's monolithic dispatch engine to its distributed architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

The redesign addresses computational complexity through hierarchical decomposition. Rather than solving one global optimization problem, the coordinator partitions logistics data into geographic clusters and delivery trajectories. Workers process smaller problems in parallel, and a reconciliation layer combines results across partitions.

It has been revealed that doorDash used shadow testing before directing live dispatch decisions to the latest platform. Production requests were duplicated, with the legacy engine determining assignments while the new platform's outputs were logged for comparison. Teams evaluated matching quality, delivery times, and resilience under load. After establishing parity, they used controlled switchback experiments and fallback mechanisms during rollout.

Shadow testing compares legacy and latest dispatch outputs (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

It has been revealed that doorDash reports a tenfold increase in dispatch throughput, with more than 99.96% of runs completing within 20 seconds. During Super Bowl Sunday, the platform maintained more than 99.99% availability despite a 10% week-over-week increase in peak volume.

The architecture also introduces a hybrid L1/L2 model serving. Latency-sensitive inference runs locally within compute workers using ONNX Runtime, avoiding remote procedure call overhead. More complex evaluations use isolated remote model-serving clusters, keeping heavier workloads away from the coordinator's state-management path.

DoorDash has also deployed multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust dispatch objective weights based on localized marketplace feedback, including merchant congestion and courier utilization. The agents adapt the trade-off between delivery speed and batching efficiency at individual stores. The approach was evaluated through production switchback experiments and accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.
