📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CNBC reported on November 26, 2026 that Nvidia chip sellers have told neocloud operators, which rent out accelerated computing capacity, they will not supply GPUs if any of the resulting computing capacity will be rented to Chinese companies, citing two people familiar with the private communications.

According to recent reports, the condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the company had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds.

The disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases.

According to recent reports, the seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS said the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments.

The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations.

In a recent development, aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case.

In a recent development, exporters and foreign data centers are expected to check customers for direct or indirect ownership or control by persons located or headquartered in those destinations, including through an ultimate parent. A data center’s refusal or inability to provide sufficient compliance information is a red flag that must be resolved before proceeding.

Sources indicate that A later change from a permitted end use to a prohibited one can require BIS authorization. Data centers already providing covered compute before publication must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date to continue without facing future export restrictions.

Computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end users that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries.

Industry observers note that the reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. Under the reported condition, a neocloud’s hardware access depends on the customers its capacity will serve, wherever the data center is located.

KV Cache from scratch in nanoVLM

📅 04 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch).
  • Autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time.
  • This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch). This gave us a 38% speedup in generation. In this blog post we cover KV Caching and all our experiences while implementing it. The lessons learnt are general and can be applied to all autoregressive language model generations. Implementing from scratch on a small codebase is a great learning experience, come along for the ride!

Autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time. During inference, the model processes a given input sequence, predicts the next token, appends it to the sequence, and repeats this process until some stopping criterion:.

This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.

Sources indicate that this repetition also leads to computational redundancy. In this post, we explore KV Caching, an optimisation technique that mitigates this inefficiency.

Before diving into caching, let’s revisit how attention operates in transformer models. A Transformer language model consists of stacked layers, each composed of:.

To understand where KV Caching helps, we focus on the self-attention mechanism, specifically within a single attention head.

Let’s walk through a simple PyTorch implementation to visualise the key computations.

For a sequence of T T T input embeddings represented as X∈RT×D X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D} X∈RT×D, self-attention is computed as:.

Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤⋅Mdk)V \text{Attention}(X; Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top \cdot M}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤⋅M​)V.

Here’s a minimal PyTorch equivalent using a causal mask:.

Sources indicate that in autoregressive generation, the model generates one token at a time. With each step, it recomputes Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V for the entire sequence, even though the earlier tokens haven’t changed.

These checks show that for all but the newest token, K K K and V V V are identical to previously computed values.

Sources indicate that most of the attention computation is repeated needlessly. This gets more expensive as sequences grow.

To eliminate this inefficiency, we use KV Caching:.

This changes generation from full-sequence re-computation to a lightweight, incremental update.

✅ In practice, this cache is a per-layer dictionary with keys "key" and "value", each of shape (batch_size, num_heads, seq_len_cached, head_dim).

This is the foundation of how modern LLMs can generate long outputs efficiently.

In a recent development, now that we understand the theory behind KV Caching, let’s see how it’s implemented in practice inside our nanoVLM repository. This is an ideal testbed, as it's a super concise and self-contained codebase.

KV caching is enabled across three key components in our model:.

In the LanguageModelGroupedAttention class, we modify the forward function to accept and update a cache of keys and values (block_kv_cache).

Previously, the model recomputed K K K and V V V at every generation step. Now we only compute Knew K_{\text{new}} Knew​, Vnew V_{\text{new}} Vnew​ for the current token, and append them to the cached values.

In a recent development, in the LanguageModel class, we introduce layer-wise cache tracking. The start_pos argument helps the model compute correct rotary positional encodings for newly generated tokens.

The biggest architectural change is in the generate() method of the VisionLanguageModel.

We split generation into two stages:.

By separating these phases, we avoid redundant computation and dramatically speed up inference, especially for long prompts.

Industry observers note that KV caching eliminates unnecessary computation during autoregressive generation, enabling faster and more efficient inference, especially in long sequences and real-time applications. This is a trade-off between speed and memory, and its drawbacks can be more complex code and restricting fancier inference schemes, like beam-search, etc. KV caching is a popular method for speeding up LLM inference, making it possible to run them on consumer hardware, and now you know how it works too!

Latest Update: AI Could Soon Edit Live Videos in Real Time

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context.
  • For example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time.
  • Microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context. Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered editing could reshape that connection by changing speech before it reaches viewers.

For example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time. Such capabilities could support clearer communication, but they also raise questions about whose words audiences actually hear. Understanding the differences between original and AI-edited video can help explain what editable video could mean for viewer trust.

Microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch. Its scope covers both recorded presentations and near-real-time changes to live events. The proposed system could remove filler words, correct mispronunciations and replace other speech, including colloquial expressions or words it identifies as inappropriate. It would also adjust the speaker’s lip movements to match the replacement audio.

Audience profiles could influence those choices. The filing describes profiles containing details such as age, language, cultural background and education level, which could guide speech replacements. Viewers could therefore receive different versions of the same event, with wording tailored to their profiles.

According to recent reports, the proposed process begins with capturing a speaker’s audio and video during a live event. An AI agent identifies words to change, guided by editing settings or audience profiles. Generative AI then creates replacement speech and adjusts the corresponding video frames, including lip movements, to match.

Recent findings suggest that these changes would happen within a short broadcast buffer. The filing describes a roughly one-to-10-second delay, giving the system time to process speech before presenting the modified stream. To keep the result flowing naturally, the system would smooth audio and visual transitions around each replacement. Some implementations could also patch captions to reflect the edited speech and retain original recordings for later reference.

In a recent development, multilingual presentations could let viewers hear speech in their preferred language while seeing lip movements that match the translation. Educational broadcasts and training sessions could use this approach to reach audiences across language barriers. Audience-based adjustments could also help explain unfamiliar terms in language suited to viewers’ knowledge.

Speakers who stutter could choose to use optional editing support during presentations or live broadcasts. That choice should remain with the speaker, including control over which speech patterns the system changes. Removing a hesitation can make speech easier to follow while preserving the message, although pauses sometimes convey uncertainty or emphasis. Meanwhile, replacing a factual claim changes the substance of the statement and requires a different level of scrutiny and speaker approval.

Existing AI tools already offer parts of the proposed system’s capabilities, including translated speech, synchronized lip movements and live voice modification. Their uses and limitations help show how Microsoft’s proposal compares with available products and research demonstrations.

HeyGen’s Video Translation tool works with uploaded footage, translating speech into a selected language and synchronizing the speaker’s lips with the fresh audio. Its Dynamic Duration option lets individual segments stretch or compress by up to 20%, allowing more natural pacing when translations are longer or shorter. This flexibility helps accommodate differences in phrasing between languages.

In a recent development, the workflow processes an existing recording before the creator shares the translated version. Microsoft’s proposed system would instead modify an incoming live broadcast within a short delay, making changes while the event continues.

In a recent development, krisp’s AI Accent Conversion processes speech during live conversations, adjusting pronunciation to help listeners understand the speaker more easily. It aims to preserve the person’s voice and tone while modifying how words sound. This could support communication in customer service calls and meetings where unfamiliar accents create listening challenges.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction lies in what changes. Accent conversion focuses on pronunciation while preserving the words and their meanings. Microsoft’s proposed system goes further by allowing word replacements and corresponding video edits, potentially changing the statement itself.

Microsoft’s VASA-1 explores how AI can turn a still portrait into a moving, speaking face using an accompanying audio clip. Beyond matching mouth movements to speech, it generates changes in expression and head position that make the face appear more lifelike. It offers another example of how AI can create convincing footage from limited source material.

Recent findings suggest that its ability to animate a portrait also creates opportunities for impersonation, particularly when someone pairs a recognizable face with fabricated speech. Those concerns led Microsoft to withhold public access, with no full release planned until it has confidence in its ability to ensure regulation-compliant use. This position reflects the challenge of making useful avatar technology available while limiting applications that could falsely portray someone saying something.

When AI changes speech while preserving a speaker’s appearance, viewers could attribute the replacement words to that person. A speaker might approve pronunciation corrections without agreeing to changes that reshape an opinion or factual claim. Consent therefore needs to cover the scope of editing, especially when the finished video presents generated words as the speaker’s own.

According to recent reports, generated talking faces and synthetic voices extend this concern beyond alterations to existing footage. They could make someone appear to deliver a statement without participating in the recording. Some people already struggle to recognize sarcasm or identify a skit. When staged content already confuses, the prospect of widespread deepfake misinformation becomes a reasonable concern. Research demonstrates that all age groups are susceptible to digital manipulation.

Convincing impersonations could damage reputations or distort public debate. Their growing plausibility could also give people an excuse to dismiss authentic recordings as AI fabrications, making genuine evidence harder to establish.

According to recent reports, broadcasters and creators should clearly disclose AI edits and provide access to original recordings, especially when changes affect meaning. These steps help audiences understand what changed and give speakers control over statements presented in their name. Independent platforms like C2PA Content Credentials can support transparency by documenting media origins and editing history. They function like a nutrition label for digital content, allowing anyone to inspect the available history using compatible tools.

For consequential clips, viewers should compare the footage with sources and independent reporting. Realistic faces, matching lip movements and familiar voices alone offer limited grounds for trust.

AI video editing could improve cross-language communication and give speakers more control over how they present themselves. Microsoft’s proposed system and research demonstrations represent different stages of development. As audiovisual edits become more convincing, disclosure and verifiable original recordings will become more important for maintaining trust.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate.
  • We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!
  • According to recent reports, in short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate. Along the way, we created the largest benchmarking suite for GUI agents performances 👉 let us introduce ScreenSuite.

We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!

GUI Agents in action - courtesy of OSWorld.

According to recent reports, in short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world. (more thorough definition here).

In a recent development, in particular, a “GUI Agent” is an agent that lives in a GUI. Think “an agent that can do clicks and navigate on my desktop or my phone”, à la Claude Computer Use.

This means in essence that the AI model powering the agent will be given a task like “Fill the rest of this Excel column”, along with screen captures of the GUI. Using this information, it will then decide to take action on the system : click(x=130, y=540) to open a web browser, type(”Value for XYZ in 2025"), scroll(down=2) to read further… To see a GUI agent in action, you can try our Open Computer Agent, powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B.

A good GUI agent will be able to navigate a computer just like we would, thus unlocking all computer tasks : scrolling through Google Maps, editing a file, buying an item online. This involves a variety of capabilities that can be hard to evaluate.

The literature, for instance Xu et al. (2025) or Qin et al. (2025), generally splits GUI agent abilities amongst several categories:.

So our first contribution is to gather and unify a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks spanning the full range of these GUI agent capabilities.

If you look at the last category listed above, evaluating Multi-step agentic capabilities is especially challenging as it requires virtual machines to run the agent’s environment, be it Windows, Android, Ubuntu... To address this, we provide support both for E2B desktop remote sandboxes, and we created from scratch a new option to easily launch Ubuntu or Android virtual machines in Docker!

In a recent development, we’ve carefully designed our benchmark suite with modularity and consistency in mind, ensuring strong alignment across tasks and environments. When required, especially for online benchmarks, we leverage smolagents as framework layer to streamline agent execution and orchestration.

To support reproducibility and ease of use, we’ve built custom Dockerized containers that allow local deployment of full Ubuntu Desktop or Android environments.

Unlike many existing GUI benchmarks that rely on accessibility trees or other metadata alongside visual input, our stack is intentionally vision-only. While this can result in different scores on some established leaderboards, we deem that it creates a more realistic and challenging setup, one that better reflects how humans perceive and interact with graphical interfaces.

Sources indicate that – All agentic frameworks (Android World, OSWorld, GAIAWeb, Mind2Web) use smolagents and rely solely on vision, without any accessibility tree or DOM added (in contrast with evaluation settings reported in other sources). – Mind2Web (Multimodal) originally used element-name-based multi-choice selection based on the accessibility tree and screenshots, but was later adapted to click precision within bounding boxes using vision only, which significantly increases task difficulty.

We’ve evaluated leading VLMs on the benchmark.

Our scores are in general agreement with the scores reported in various sources! With the caveat that we evaluate on vision only, causing some differences, see implementation details above.

It has been revealed that 💡 Note that ScreenSuite does not intend to exactly reproduce benchmarks published in the industry: we evaluate models on GUI agentic capabilities based on vision. As a result, on benchmarks like Mind2Web where other benchmarks gave the agent a view of information rich context like DOM or accessibility tree, our evaluation setting is much harder, thus ScreenSuite does not match other sources.

The multistep benchmarks requires a bare-metal machine to run and deploy desktop/mobile* environment *emulators (see README.md).

Running consistent and meaningful evaluations easily allows the community to quickly iterate and make progress in this field, as we’ve seen with Eleuther LM evaluation harness, the Open LLM Leaderboard and the Chatbot Arena.

We hope to see much more capable open models in the coming month that can run a wide range of tasks reliably and even run locally!

Canada Invests $700 Million More to Expand AI Compute Access Fund

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Canadian government expanded the AI Compute Access Fund with an additional $700 million on November 26, 2026, bringing it to $1 billion and opening a sector-specific call for health and life sciences projects.
  • Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon announced the next phase in Toronto.
  • In a recent development, solomon also announced more than $52 million for 45 companies under the fund’s initial phase, lifting cumulative commitments to more than $118 million across 89 Canadian companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Canadian government expanded the AI Compute Access Fund with an additional $700 million on November 26, 2026, bringing it to $1 billion and opening a sector-specific call for health and life sciences projects.

Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon announced the next phase in Toronto. The expansion adds to the fund’s initial $300 million and is intended to help Canadian organizations develop, test and commercialize AI products by offsetting cloud-compute costs. Eligible work includes model training, inference and fine-tuning.

In a recent development, solomon also announced more than $52 million for 45 companies under the fund’s initial phase, lifting cumulative commitments to more than $118 million across 89 Canadian companies. Those earlier-phase awards are distinct from the expansion and cover health care, agriculture, manufacturing, finance and transportation projects.

It has been revealed that the updated program guide covers up to 80% of eligible cloud-compute costs from sovereign providers and up to 50% from Canadian-based providers. Sovereign suppliers must operate infrastructure in Canada, process and store data there, be incorporated and registered in Canada, be Canadian-owned, and keep governance and decision-making authority in the country.

Canadian-based providers must meet the infrastructure, data and incorporation requirements. The ownership and governance tests do not apply to that category. Multinational companies with Canadian-registered entities can therefore qualify when the infrastructure and data remain in Canada. The rate structure offers a larger potential subsidy for choosing a provider with Canadian ownership and control without excluding multinational suppliers’ Canadian operations.

Eligible proposals must include $100,000 to $5 million in compute costs and end no later than March 31, 2030. Applicants can be Canadian-registered for-profit companies, nonprofit corporations or charities, including qualifying postsecondary institutions; they generally need fewer than 500 full-time-equivalent employees, Canada-based research and development teams and a commercialization plan. Contributions may be non-repayable, conditionally repayable or repayable, depending on the project’s assessed benefits and risk.

Health and life sciences applicants must submit a statement of interest by 11:59 p.m. ET on December 17, 2026. Those invited to proceed must file full applications by 11:59 p.m. ET on January 4, 2027, with compute contracts, invoices or other documentation in place or in progress. A selected applicant whose agreement is still in progress must finalize it before signing a contribution agreement.

Assessment covers market potential, organizational and financial capacity, technology readiness, expected economic and public benefits, and alignment with government priorities. Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada states it will endeavour to make funding decisions within 90 business days after the call closes. The department will also use AI tools to support analysis of application information, conduct risk-related research and assist with program administration, while retaining final authority over recipient selection.

An official recipient backgrounder shows the range of supported work. Vancouver-based Apera AI is developing 4D vision and simulation-driven models for factory robots, while Toronto-based RetiSpec is working on a non-invasive retinal-imaging tool intended to detect early Alzheimer’s disease. Gotcare, also in Toronto, is building an AI-enabled home-healthcare management system focused on rural and underserved populations.

Recent findings suggest that the sector calls sit within the government’s AI for All strategy, which names five priority areas: health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing and robotics. The strategy describes Canada’s sovereign compute capacity as nascent and notes most Canadian small and medium-sized businesses lack an affordable domestic option, leaving them reliant on foreign cloud platforms for training, testing and deployment.

The government is also connecting the renewed fund to its commitment to bring 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute online. The expanded program is intended to create demand for Canadian providers and support investment in domestic AI infrastructure, linking commercialization assistance to a broader infrastructure objective.

That makes the reimbursement gap central to the policy: companies receive the strongest support when their computing is owned, operated and governed in Canada. The open question is whether the demand created by these subsidies can support enough affordable domestic capacity while helping Canadian AI products reach the market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today at GTC Paris, we are excited to announce Training Cluster as a Service in collaboration with NVIDIA, to make large GPU clusters more easily accessible for research organizations all over the world, so they can train the foundational models of tomorrow in every domain.

Many Gigawatt-size GPU supercluster projects are being built to train the next gen of AI models. This can make it seem that the compute gap between the “GPU poor” and the “GPU rich” is promptly widening. But the GPUs are out there, as hyperscalers, regional and AI-native cloud providers all quickly expand their capacity.

How do we then connect AI compute capacity with the researchers who need it? How do we enable universities, national research labs and companies all over the world to build their own models?

This is what Hugging Face and NVIDIA are tackling with Training Cluster as a Service - providing GPU cluster accessibility, with the flexibility to only pay for the duration of training runs.

To get started, any of the 250,000 organizations on Hugging Face can request the GPU cluster size they need, when they need it.

To get started, you can request a GPU cluster on behalf of your organization at hf.co/training-cluster.

Training Cluster as a Service integrates key components from NVIDIA and Hugging Face into a complete solution:.

Once your GPU cluster request is accepted, Hugging Face and NVIDIA will collaborate to source, price, provision and set up your GPU cluster per your size, region and duration requirements.

The Telethon Institute of Genomics and Medicine - TIGEM for short - is a research center dedicated to understanding the molecular mechanisms behind rare genetic diseases and developing novel treatments. Training new AI models is a new path to predict the effect of pathogenic variants and for drug repositioning.

Industry observers note that AI offers fresh ways to research the causes of rare genetic diseases and to develop treatments, but our domain requires training new models. Training Cluster as a Service made it easy to procure the GPU capacity we needed, at the right time.

-- Diego di Bernardo, Coordinator of the Genomic Medicine program at TIGEM.

Numina is a non-profit organization building open-source, open-dataset AI for reasoning in math - and won the 2024 AIMO progress prize.

We are tracking well on our objective to build open alternatives to the best closed-source models, such as Deepmind's AlphaProof. Computing resources is our bottleneck today - with Training Cluster as a Service we will be able to reach our goal!

-- Yann Fleureau, cofounder of Project Numina.

Mirror Physics is a startup creating frontier AI systems for chemistry and materials science.

According to recent reports, together with the MACE team, we're working to push the limits of AI for chemistry. With Training Cluster as a Service, we're producing high-fidelity chemical models at unprecedented scale. This is going to be a significant step forward for the field.

-- Sam Walton Norwood, CEO and founder at Mirror.

Training Cluster as a Service is a newly introduced collaboration between Hugging Face and NVIDIA to make AI compute more readily available to the global community of AI researchers.

In a recent development, access to large-scale, high-performance compute is essential for building the next generation of AI models across every domain and language. Training Cluster as a Service will remove barriers for researchers and companies, unlocking the ability to train the most advanced models and push the boundaries of what’s possible in AI.

-- Clément Delangue, cofounder and CEO of Hugging Face.

Industry observers note that integrating DGX Cloud Lepton with Hugging Face’s Training Cluster as a Service gives developers and researchers a seamless way to access high-performance NVIDIA GPUs across a broad network of cloud providers. This collaboration makes it easier for AI researchers and organizations to scale their AI training workloads while using familiar tools on Hugging Face.

-- Alexis Bjorlin, vice president of DGX Cloud at NVIDIA.

We are excited to collaborate with NVIDIA to offer Training Cluster as a Service to Hugging Face organizations - you can get started today at hf.co/training-cluster.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

Today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major update to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

Technical Blog for GR00T N1.5: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-n1_5/.

Now accessible to developers working with a wide range of robot form factors, GR00T N1.5 can be easily fine-tuned and adapted using the affordable, open-source LeRobot SO-101 arm.

This flexibility is enabled by the EmbodimentTag system, which allows seamless customization of the model for different robotic platforms, empowering hobbyists, researchers, and engineers to tailor advanced humanoid reasoning and manipulation capabilities to their own hardware.

Before proceeding to installation, please check if you satisfy the prerequisites.

In a recent development, consumers can fine-tune GROOT N1.5 with any LeRobot dataset. For this tutorial, we will be using the table cleanup task as an example for fine-tuning.

Recent findings suggest that it's important to note that datasets for the SO-100 or SO-101 are not in GR00T N1.5's initial pre-training. As a result of this, we will be training it as a new_embodiment.

Gift Tax Rules: How Much Can You Give Tax-Free?

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code.
  • Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

Industry observers note that the annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

According to recent reports, this limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:.

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:.

In a recent development, the annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

According to recent reports, when you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

According to recent reports, at the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

It has been revealed that the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

According to recent reports, the type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

Spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

The identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron indicates the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

According to recent reports, saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert new audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz says the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

Instead of manually managing complex dependencies, wrestling with compilation flags, or building libraries like Triton or CUTLASS from source, you can use the kernels library to instantly fetch and run pre-compiled, optimized kernels.

#150508. How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation.
  • Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests.
  • This sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation. In short: for the first output token (prefill step), the entire prompt needs to be processed, which can be parallelized efficiently and can saturate GPU utilization. For all later output tokens (decode steps), only a single additional token needs to be processed, which is less compute-intensive but must be done sequentially. When many requests are processed concurrently, any strategy that aims for low latency needs to run prefill steps for newly arriving requests while the decode steps of previously scheduled requests are still ongoing. Concurrent processing of new as well as running requests therefore requires careful balancing between the prefill and decode stages, which presents two major challenges, which we will discuss in the following. One is a readily solvable issue, while the other one constitutes a more fundamental flaw.

Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests. For prefill, however, this approach does not work. Because of the parallelized processing of all prompt tokens, a single prefill step can already saturate GPU utilization. Consequently, in the default chunked-prefill strategy of vLLM, each prefill chunk contains only prompt tokens of a single request. The next request in line has to wait until the previous prefill phase has been finished before its own prefill phase can start.

This sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue. (Note that the sequential processing of prefills is the default characteristic of chunked-prefill and only appears when there already is a concurrent request in its decode phase; hence the name "partial prefill".).

Unfortunately, this challenge can neither be solved with vLLM-side priority scheduling (see the first article of this series) nor with a more sophisticated upstream scheduler. The reason is that the long prompt can be scheduled before any subsequent requests exist, so there is nothing the scheduler could wait for.

A straightforward solution would be to process prefill chunks of different requests in parallel. This might not be resource-optimized, as single-request prefill chunks could already saturate compute-power. Any additional prefill executed in parallel would likely prolong the prefill duration a bit and slow down any concurrent decode-requests even further. This would be acceptable if it reduced the latency of short requests and made the system appear more responsive. This approach fails, however, when the next request in line has a long prompt too. In such a case, two compute-intensive prefills would be batched together and result in a severe slowdown.

Sources indicate that in one of the latest vLLM updates, an improved strategy has been implemented: it allows for parallel prefills of different requests but with a limit to the number of concurrently processed long prompt requests. An example configuration could enable batching of prefills for four requests, but only one of them may be longer than 10,000 prompt tokens. With such a configuration, the behavior for longer requests is still the same as before: long prompts are processed sequentially. Short requests, however, no longer need to wait for the long prefill of a previous request to finish; short prompts can take a fast lane. These requests no longer suffer from long waiting times and show much lower time-to-first-token metrics.

In a recent development, of course, parallel prefills can only reduce waiting times; but the time-per-output-token remains elevated during the concurrent long-prefill operation. In this regard, request-parallel prefills show the same behavior and performance as standard chunked-prefill, just with a shorter time-to-first-token.

According to recent reports, whenever prefill and decode of different requests are executed in the same GPU operation, it takes longer than for an isolated decode step. The user experiences an interruption or a slowing down of the token generation by a subsequent request. In particular, a single request with a long prompt is sufficient to slow down all previously scheduled requests that are already in their decode phases.

This is a fundamental flaw in the concurrent processing of prefill and decode on the same GPUs, because there is little you can do:.

The difference between ideal concurrent processing (which would be no different from isolated requests), actual concurrent processing, and a disaggregated prefill strategy is shown by the following measurements:.

Sources indicate that separating prefill and decode eliminates the slowing-down of token generation in presence of other requests to a large extent, which makes it a very attractive strategy. It comes at the price of a second full-size vLLM deployment (e.g. for Llama-3.3-70B, you would need four H100 GPUs for a prefill worker and another four H100 GPUs for a decode worker if you wanted to support a maximum context length of 130k tokens). Another disadvantage is the uneven GPU utilization: because prefill is compute-intensive but decode is not, the prefill worker will likely saturate GPU utilization before the decode worker does. On the other hand, large clusters could consist of different numbers of prefill and decode workers (depending on load patterns), in order to optimize resource utilization.

In a recent development, disaggregated prefill is not intended to increase total throughput, rather total "goodput" (i.e. the rate of requests that satisfy latency targets). Consequently, it is not the best use of GPU resources if your application is not sensitive to latency of individual requests.

According to recent reports, another caveat: the disaggregated prefill feature in vLLM is still experimental, and some optimizations and features are not accessible yet. For example, there are at the moment lower limits on context length, and the decode worker doesn't use CUDA graphs consistently, causing the slower decode of the long-prompt request in the figure above. Fortunately, these are not fundamental obstacles and are likely going to be solved in future versions of vLLM.

The result here is an acceptance rule, not a measured delivery improvement: declare the record change confirmed only after the observed value matches the intended value. Start with the tempting implementation: concern the write, check that the call succeeded, and label the task finished. That approach leaves a gap between the operation being accepted and the desired configuration being observed. The read-compare-write-read sequence closes that specific gap. It also gives repeated runs a useful outcome: unchanged.

A no-op means the current configuration already matches the requested configuration, so the helper sends no mutation. A confirmation means a mutation was followed by a matching read. Neither establishes that a particular message reached an inbox. For the mail migration, record delivery observations separately; otherwise a dashboard can turn a configuration check into a promise it never tested. DMARC is another distinct concern: RFC 7489 describes message authentication policy and reporting, rather than a replacement for verifying an MX record change.

The notebook-to-prod transition is where this distinction earns its keep. A notebook can display the final value and leave the reader to interpret it. A production job needs a defined result that another component can evaluate without guessing. An agent should receive that compact result instead of inferring success from a long transcript of requests. That keeps the prompt budget focused on the decision, too.

The main example uses reserved example names and an in-memory store. Its record representation is an application fixture, not a vendor request schema; the MX content string is illustrative. A third check models an accepted operation that leaves the old value in place, which must fail verification. This synthetic case tests the helper; it isn't a report about any service.

Exact string comparison is deliberate in this small fixture. It makes the acceptance rule visible. It also sets a boundary: the example doesn't implement provider-specific normalization, an entire MX record set, or concurrency control. Before adapting it, decide what counts as equivalent using the actual record schema, and compare the intended configuration at that scope. Don't reduce a multi-record mail configuration to whichever record happens to appear first.

According to recent reports, A second boundary matters for retries. Skipping an unchanged value reduces redundant writes on a later run; it doesn't by itself make every network retry safe. A real adapter needs explicit HTTP methods, status handling, bounded backoff for rate limits, and the provider's documented idempotency mechanism where applicable. Avoid inventing a request payload merely to make a notebook look complete.

There is no measured deliverability ranking here. The comparison is a selection rule for a tech giant choosing how to manage its existing mail DNS. Monte Carlo Permutation Tests: Stress-Auditing a Trading Strategy

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A backtest gives you a number: total PnL, Sharpe, max drawdown.
  • Consider two strategies with identical trade lists: same 300 trades, same total PnL, same win rate.
  • In a recent development, A Monte Carlo permutation test fixes this cheaply.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A backtest gives you a number: total PnL, Sharpe, max drawdown. The first two are (roughly) order-independent if you're just summing returns. Max drawdown is not. Neither is the probability that your equity curve touches a ruin threshold before the backtest window ends.

Consider two strategies with identical trade lists: same 300 trades, same total PnL, same win rate. One sequence happens to cluster its losses early and its wins late. The other does the reverse. Same totals, radically different drawdowns, radically different risk of blowing up mid-stream. Your backtest only sampled one of the possible orderings — the one that actually happened, or worse, the one your optimization pipeline selected for.

In a recent development, A Monte Carlo permutation test fixes this cheaply. Shuffle the realized trade PnL sequence thousands of times, recompute max drawdown and ruin indicators on every shuffle, then look at the resulting distribution. If your backtest's drawdown sits at the 5th percentile of the shuffled distribution, your headline number is flattering you. If it sits near the median, the strategy's risk is roughly order-neutral and you can trust the backtest more.

The key assumption: the multiset of trade PnLs is fixed, only the order is random. This tests sensitivity to sequencing, not to whether the trades themselves were lucky. It's a stress audit of path risk, not a validation of edge.

Assume you have a vector of per-trade PnL in account currency (or in R-multiples — the math is identical, only the ruin thresholds change units).

In a recent development, the permutation test only cares about the values, not their original order. If you want to audit the actual backtest drawdown, keep the original array around — you'll compare it against the shuffled distribution.

Industry observers note that the naive approach loops over 5000 shuffles in Python and calls np.cumsum each time. That's fine for 300 trades but painful at 5000 trades × 5000 shuffles. Vectorize it: build a matrix of shape (n_sims, n_trades), cumsum along axis 1, then compute running max and drawdown per row.

For 5000 trades and 5000 simulations, that's a 25M-element float64 array — about 200 MB. If memory is tight, chunk the simulations:.

Max drawdown is one number per shuffle. Ruin probability is the fraction of shuffles where the equity curve drops below a threshold at any point. Compute it directly from the drawdown matrix — no extra pass needed.

Pass thresholds in the same units as your PnL. If you're sizing in R-multiples and risking 1% of equity per trade, a 20R drawdown is roughly a 20% equity hit (ignoring compounding). Pick thresholds that map to real operational limits: margin call levels, a hard stop-loss on the strategy, a psychological "I'd shut this down" number.

Sometimes you want this in a script with no numpy dependency — a research notebook on a locked-down box, a quick check in a CI step, or a port to another language. The pure-Python version is 20 lines and fast enough for a few hundred trades.

It has been revealed that random.Random.shuffle mutates the list in place, so you don't rebuild it every iteration — that's the main cost saver. If you need ruin probabilities too, track the minimum equity inside the loop and collect it. For 1000 trades × 5000 sims this takes a few seconds; the numpy version is roughly 50–100× faster.

Recent findings suggest that now the part that actually matters. You have a distribution of 5000 max drawdowns. What do you do with it?

The percentile of your backtest DD tells you how flattering the realized order was. A backtest DD at the 10th percentile means 90% of orderings produce a worse drawdown — the strategy's risk is understated. At the 50th, you're unbiased. At the 90th, your backtest was unusually unlucky and the strategy is probably better than it looks (rare, but it happens with short samples).

A concrete rule that works in practice:.

Recent findings suggest that one caveat worth stating plainly: this test assumes trade PnLs are exchangeable. Real strategies have autocorrelation — volatility clustering, regime shifts, correlated losses during stress. Permutation tests ignore that, so they can understate tail drawdowns when losses cluster. If you suspect serial dependence, the permutation test is a lower bound on path risk, not an upper one. Combine it with a block bootstrap or a regime-conditional analysis if the strategy is sensitive to volatility regimes.

Recent findings suggest that it tells you whether your backtest drawdown is representative of the drawdown distribution over all orderings of the same trades. It does not tell you whether the trades themselves are predictive, whether the sample is large enough, or whether the strategy will work out of sample. Those are separate questions with separate tests.

According to recent reports, what it does well: it catches the specific failure mode where a strategy looks safe because the backtest got a lucky ordering. That failure mode is common, cheap to test for, and expensive to discover live. Five thousand shuffles and a percentile lookup is a small price.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance.
  • Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them.
  • We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance. We saw how bitsandbytes, torchao, and others reduce memory footprints for generating images.

Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them. Therefore, in this post, we tackle efficient fine-tuning of these models with peak memory use under ~10 GB of VRAM on a single GPU. This post will guide you through fine-tuning FLUX.1-dev using QLoRA with the diffusers library. We'll showcase results from an NVIDIA RTX 4090. We'll also highlight how FP8 training with torchao can further optimize speed on compatible hardware.

We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.

The model consists of three main components:.

In our QLoRA approach, we focus exclusively on fine-tuning the transformer component. The text encoders and VAE remain frozen throughout training.

In a recent development, we used a diffusers training script (slightly modified from here designed for DreamBooth-style LoRA fine-tuning of FLUX models. Also, a shortened version to reproduce the results in this blogpost (and used in the Google Colab) is available here. Let's examine the crucial parts for QLoRA and memory efficiency:.

In a recent development, loRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Deep Dive: LoRA makes model training more efficient by keeping track of the weight updates with low-rank matrices. Instead of updating the full weight matrix W W W, LoRA learns two smaller matrices A A A and B B B. The upgrade to the weights for the model is ΔW=BA \Delta W = B A ΔW=BA, where A∈Rr×k A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} B∈Rd×r. The number r r r (called rank) is much smaller than the original dimensions, which means less parameters to update. Lastly, α \alpha α is a scaling factor for the LoRA activations. This affects how much LoRA affects the updates, and is often set to the same value as the r r r or a multiple of it. It helps balance the influence of the pre-trained model and the LoRA adapter. For a general introduction to the concept, check out our previous blog post: Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning.

QLoRA: The Efficiency Powerhouse: QLoRA enhances LoRA by first loading the pre-trained base model in a quantized format (typically 4-bit via bitsandbytes), drastically cutting the base model's memory footprint. It then trains LoRA adapters (usually in FP16/BF16) on top of this quantized base. This dramatically lowers the VRAM needed to hold the base model.

For instance, in the DreamBooth training script for HiDream 4-bit quantization with bitsandbytes reduces the peak memory usage of a LoRA fine-tune from ~60GB down to ~37GB with negligible-to-none quality degradation. The very same principle is what we apply here to fine-tune FLUX.1 on a consumer-grade hardware.

8-bit Optimizer (AdamW): Standard AdamW optimizer maintains first and second moment estimates for each parameter in 32-bit (FP32), which consumes a lot of memory. The 8-bit AdamW uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer states in 8-bit precision, while maintaining training stability. This technique can reduce optimizer memory usage by ~75% compared to standard FP32 AdamW. Enabling it in the script is straightforward:.

Gradient Checkpointing: During forward pass, intermediate activations are typically stored for backward pass gradient computation. Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory by only storing certain checkpoint activations and recomputing others during backpropagation.

Cache Latents: This optimization technique pre-processes all training images through the VAE encoder before the beginning of the training. It stores the resulting latent representations in memory. During the training, instead of encoding images on-the-fly, the cached latents are directly used. This approach offers two main benefits:.

Before we launch the QLoRA fine-tune we can save a huge chunk of VRAM and wall-clock time by caching outputs of text encoders once.

At training time the dataloader simply reads the cached embeddings instead of re-encoding the caption, so the CLIP/T5 encoder never has to sit in GPU memory.

By combining this with cached VAE latents (--cache_latents) you whittle the active model down to just the quantized transformer + LoRA adapters, keeping the whole fine-tune comfortably under 10 GB of GPU memory.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A logistics platform needs carrier staff to gain workspace access through a manufacturer domain verified by TXT proof, while its shipment notifications authenticate correctly.
  • TL;DR: verify the organization domain through a TXT record, then use the matching email suffix and an email lookup to make workspace joining deterministic; keep manual approval for domains you cannot verify, and explicitly exclude shared consumer mail domains.
  • Industry observers note that store the decision evidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A logistics platform needs carrier staff to gain workspace access through a manufacturer domain verified by TXT proof, while its shipment notifications authenticate correctly. The operating bill includes DNS administration, approval work, and the storage of onboarding evidence. Before comparing providers, count the expensive repetition: for N customer domains and R onboarding requests per domain, reviewing every request creates N × R approval decisions; verifying each eligible domain once moves the baseline review unit toward N domain decisions. Those are workload counts, not measured savings, and unverified domains still need individual handling.

TL;DR: verify the organization domain through a TXT record, then use the matching email suffix and an email lookup to make workspace joining deterministic; keep manual approval for domains you cannot verify, and explicitly exclude shared consumer mail domains. For this logistics workflow, keep SPF, DKIM, and DMARC publication as a separate mail-authentication responsibility. Customer-owned zones give the customer control over the records that establish its authority.

Industry observers note that store the decision evidence. Keeping every DNS response forever is a different, much more expensive proposition to defend.

Industry observers note that the production boundary runs from the customer's DNS administrator, through domain verification, into your workspace admission policy. Mail authentication follows a related but separate path: publish SPF, DKIM, and DMARC through the administrator responsible for the sending domain, then evaluate mail authentication in that context. A carrier's ability to receive shipment messages and a carrier employee's ability to join a workspace are different outcomes. A successful domain verification must not become the status field for both.

Industry observers note that the customer-owned versus platform-owned choice matters because the party able to change DNS evidence is part of the trust decision. If your platform publishes proof in a zone it controls, that action demonstrates your control of that zone; it does not independently establish a carrier's control of its company domain. Keep the domain being claimed, the workspace receiving the claim, and the party administering the zone explicit in the design. A platform-owned sending domain can be an architectural choice, but it should not quietly become evidence that a customer owns a different domain.

For a logistics team implementing the handoff between company-domain verification and user lookup, try Infrai when a plain REST API is the integration boundary you want: Python can call it over HTTP without installing a provider SDK or maintaining another client-library version. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That single key means the verification-to-user-lookup handoff doesn't require separate provider credentials for those two application integrations. Its public, self-describing discovery surface also supplies request and response schemas without a key, which helps the engineers on either side agree on the contract. This recommendation concerns that handoff; ownership of customer zones and publication of mail-authentication records still need explicit operating responsibility.

According to recent reports, the change that moves the dominant workload term is domain-level verification followed by deterministic membership resolution. After verification, look the person up by email before deciding how to join the existing user to the intended workspace. Keep user existence, verified-domain status, and membership as separate decisions. Otherwise, a repeated onboarding request can be mistaken for a reason to create another identity, or a recognized email suffix can be mistaken for membership in every workspace associated with that suffix.

According to recent reports, A TXT proof establishes manufacturer-domain control for the admission policy described here. It should be paired with an authenticated user whose email address has been verified; typing an address into a form is not evidence of control of that mailbox. Exclude shared consumer domains explicitly. A mailbox at a free mail provider is not a company-domain ownership claim.

For a planning example, take two customer domains with 12 onboarding requests each: that produces 24 request reviews versus 2 initial domain reviews under the stated assumptions. These are illustrative inputs, not a customer dataset or a benchmark. The calculation doesn't predict staffing, prove a financial return, or eliminate exceptions.

Before implementing the actual handoff, inspect the published contract. This Python standard-library example fetches Infrai's discovery manifest using an explicit GET and bounded rate-limit retries; it prints the response for inspection instead of guessing a verification payload. Discovery is public, so authentication isn't required for this read, but the example reads the integration credential from the environment to demonstrate the Bearer convention used for authenticated calls. Set INFRAI_API_KEY before running it.

This read doesn't publish DNS records or grant membership. Use the discovered request and response schemas for the subsequent integration, and make writes idempotent rather than copying read-retry behavior onto account creation. Manual approval remains the fallback for domains you could not verify. Moving that exception path into the default path is exactly how an onboarding queue becomes a waiting room.

The useful comparison is responsibility, because a DNS provider and an identity workflow do not occupy the same position in this system. Cloudflare DNS, Amazon Route 53, and Azure DNS are real alternatives for the DNS side of the design; their documentation is a starting point for deciding how an existing customer zone should be administered. The table compares proposed integration boundaries, rather than claiming that the products provide identical workspace-admission features.

Recent findings suggest that none of these choices transfers a customer's DNS authority merely because your backend can send an HTTP request. Obtain the necessary administrative participation, and decide which party publishes the mail records before presenting onboarding as complete.

It has been revealed that keep the existing DNS provider when it already fits. The reason to add a shared API surface is a concrete reduction in integration contracts around verification and identity, not a reason to migrate every carrier's zone.

According to recent reports, for a proposed evidence policy, retain the claimed domain, workspace binding, verification decision, decision time, and the policy version that interpreted it. These are application-owned audit fields, not claims about any provider's response schema. Retain enough user-resolution evidence to explain which verified email led to the membership decision, while treating that information as access-controlled customer data. The retention question is whether an operator can reconstruct the authorization decision, rather than whether the system can accumulate a complete history of DNS observations.

In a recent development, A useful storage model is D × E × T: domains under management, evidence collected per domain per interval, and retained intervals. This is an accounting model, not a measured storage bill. Reducing retained observations changes E or T; changing which customers own their zones does not automatically change either one. Keep the decision record longer than disposable observation details if the support and audit requirements justify that distinction. Set the actual periods against those requirements rather than copying a generic number of days.

Sources indicate that name the failures before choosing retention. A stale ownership decision means the old evidence no longer describes current control. A wrong workspace binding means valid domain evidence was attached to the wrong tenant. An ambiguous email lookup means identity resolution has not produced a deterministic user. A shared-domain admission error means a consumer email suffix was treated as company authority. These are application design risks, and each requires a different piece of evidence; a large archive of TXT responses cannot repair a missing workspace binding.

Mail adds a separate diagnostic question. A DMARC investigation concerns mail authentication and policy, so the evidence relevant to it must not be replaced with a workspace verification flag. RFC 7489 is the reference for that protocol boundary. Do not promise delivery merely because a carrier's staff can now sign in.

Sources indicate that the practical default is customer-domain TXT verification, email-based lookup, and automatic joining for eligible matching addresses, with manual approval for unverified domains. Use a direct DNS provider when zone administration is the principal job; consider a shared REST surface when verification and identity handoff create the extra integration work. Keep mail authentication visible as its own completion condition.

According to recent reports, the deliberate deletion is repetitive raw DNS observations after their diagnostic retention period, while preserving the decision record for the period your access-review obligations require. That sacrifices the ability to replay every earlier observation during a later dispute. Recovery may require fresh domain proof and another conversation with the customer's DNS administrator; the retained decision should still explain why access was granted at the time. Accept that cost explicitly. Otherwise, retention becomes an unbounded substitute for a recovery proposal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data. Its simplicity, flexibility, and expansive model zoo make it a powerful tool for rapid development.

Recent findings suggest that but once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical. That’s where SGLang comes in.

It has been revealed that designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend. This means you can pair the flexibility of transformers with the raw performance of SGLang.

Let’s dive into what this integration enables and how you can use it.

SGLang now supports Hugging Face transformers as a backend, letting you run any transformers-compatible model with high-performance inference out of the box.

No native support needed — SGLang automatically falls back to Transformers when needed, or you can set impl="transformers" explicitly.

Let’s walk through a simple text generation example with meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct to compare both approaches.

transformers library is great for experimentation, small-scale tasks and training, but it's not optimized for high-volume or low-latency scenarios.

Industry observers note that SGLang takes a different track, prioritizing efficiency with features like RadixAttention (a memory-efficient attention mechanism). Inference with SGLang is noticeably faster and more resource-efficient, especially under load. Here’s the same task in SGlang using an offline engine:.

Or you can spin a server and send requests:.

Note that SGLang also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, making it a drop-in replacement for external services.

It has been revealed that with the newly introduced transformers backend integration, SGLang can now automatically fall back to using transformers models it doesn’t natively support. This means in practice:.

This unlocks faster inference and optimized deployment (e.g enabling RadixAttention) without sacrificing the simplicity and versatility of transformers ecosystem.

Note that specifying the impl parameter is optional. If the model is not natively supported by SGLang, it switches to transformers implementation on its own.

In a recent development, any model on the Hugging Face Hub that works with transformers using trust_remote_code=True and properly implements attention is compatible with SGLang. You can find the exact requirements in the official documentation. If your custom model meets these criteria, all you need to do is set trust_remote_code=True when loading it.

Kyutai Team’s Helium isn’t yet natively supported by SGLang. This is where transformers backend shines, enabling optimized inference without waiting for native support.

There are several key areas we are actively working on to enhance this integration:.

Performance Improvements: transformer models currently lag behind the native integration in terms of performance.Our primary objective is to optimize and narrow this gap.

VLM Integration: we are also working toward adding support for Vision-Language Models (VLM) to broaden the range of capabilities and use cases.
