💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Sharpe ratio's standard error formula assumes i.i.d.
  • The fix is cheap: correct the Sharpe ratio by the Lo factor before you run any significance test.
  • Lo (2002) derives the asymptotic variance of the Sharpe estimator under serial dependence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Sharpe ratio's standard error formula assumes i.i.d. returns. That assumption is almost always false for real strategies: smoothed marks, overlapping holding periods, illiquid positions, and momentum effects all leave a lag-1 autocorrelation in the return series. When returns are autocorrelated, the effective sample size is smaller than the nominal one, and significance tests fire far too often. With rho = 0.2, a nominal 5% test rejects the null at 18–25% in simulation. That is not a small calibration error; it is the difference between "maybe real" and "coin flip.".

The fix is cheap: correct the Sharpe ratio by the Lo factor before you run any significance test.

Lo (2002) derives the asymptotic variance of the Sharpe estimator under serial dependence. For an AR(1)-style dependence with lag-1 autocorrelation rho, the corrected Sharpe is:.

The rule I use: apply the correction whenever |rho| > 0.1. Below that threshold the adjustment is within noise of the estimate itself, and applying it adds churn without information. Above it, ignoring the correction is a methodological error, not a modeling choice.

Recent findings suggest that the (1 - rho)/(1 + rho) factor is the AR(1) special case. For q-th order dependence, the full Lo variance uses a weighted sum of autocorrelations:.

Industry observers note that for most daily-frequency strategies, lag-1 dominates and the closed form above is enough. Use the general form when you have overlapping windows (e.g., 5-day returns sampled daily), where lag-k dependence out to k = 4 is structural, not noise.

Do not eyeball this from a chart. Compute it, and compute it on the return series you actually test, not on cumulative PnL. Cumulative PnL is a random walk under the null and will show high autocorrelation regardless of the strategy.

Two practical checks before you trust the number:.

Keep the correction in one place so every downstream test uses the same number.

Then wire it into your evaluation path:.

In a recent development, the SharpeReport object carries both numbers and a flag. Log the flag. If a strategy's headline Sharpe only survives because the correction was never applied, you want that visible in the report, not buried in a notebook.

Recent findings suggest that the point estimate correction is what people remember, but the test is where the false positives come from. The corrected Sharpe has standard error approximately:.

Note the direction: positive autocorrelation inflates the standard error by the same factor that deflates the point estimate. Both effects push you toward "not significant," which is the honest conclusion. A quick t-statistic:.

Run this on raw and corrected Sharpe with the same rho and the same n. If the raw version clears 3.0 and the corrected one does not, the strategy does not clear 3.0.

Negative autocorrelation is the less-discussed case, and it is worth walking through because the correction moves the number up, which invites overconfidence.

Suppose a mean-reversion strategy on a liquid futures contract highlights an annualized Sharpe of 1.40 over 500 daily observations, with lag-1 autocorrelation of -0.33. That is a large negative value. Check it against the ACF before proceeding:.

Recent findings suggest that the pattern — strong lag-1, weak lag-2, near-zero beyond — is consistent with a genuine AR(1) mean-reverting component rather than an artifact. Now apply the correction:.

Sources indicate that A Sharpe of 1.40 becomes 1.97. That is a 41% uplift, and it is legitimate under the AR(1) model: negative dependence means each observation carries more independent information than its index suggests, so the effective sample is larger than 500.

But the standard error moves too:.

Sources indicate that with rho = -0.33, the SE factor is sqrt(0.67 / 1.33) ≈ 0.71, so the standard error shrinks by about 29%. The t-statistic rises, but not by the 41% the point estimate suggests. The two adjustments partially offset. This is the honest reading: negative autocorrelation helps, but less than the headline correction implies.

Two caveats on negative rho specifically:.

The autocorrelation correction is the single most common missing step in strategy evaluation, and it interacts badly with multiple testing.

Consider a grid search over 200 parameter combinations. You keep the best in-sample Sharpe. Two things then compound:.

Sources indicate that the result is a strategy that looks significant at p < 0.01 on the raw numbers and is pure noise. The autocorrelation correction does not fix selection bias on its own, but it is a prerequisite. Deflating a Sharpe that was never corrected for dependence deflates the wrong quantity.

A minimal evaluation harness that handles both:.

The expected_max_z line is a crude proxy for the multiple-testing hurdle, not a substitute for a proper deflated Sharpe. It is there to make the point concrete: once you correct for rho, the bar the best candidate must clear goes up, and the number of candidates that clear it goes down. Usually to zero, which is the correct answer for most grid searches.

The Drawdown Breaker Blind Spot: Realized PnL Hides Unrealized Bleeding

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most drawdown guards are built on a simple, reasonable-sounding premise: track losses, and when losses pile up, stop trading.
  • It has been revealed that the problem is that this guard is blind to the exact moment it matters most: while positions are open and bleeding.
  • This post dissects the blind spot, walks through a scenario where every guard reads fine while the account is drowning, and presents a dual-viewport design: realized drawdown and pool-wide mark-to-market unrealized PnL tracked separately, with the unrealized view gating new entries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most drawdown guards are built on a simple, reasonable-sounding premise: track losses, and when losses pile up, stop trading. The implementation almost always looks at the same number — realized PnL. A trade closes, the result is booked, the counter increments. Three losses in a row? Cool off. Daily loss limit hit? Flatten and stop.

It has been revealed that the problem is that this guard is blind to the exact moment it matters most: while positions are open and bleeding. An unrealized loss of 4% sitting in three open positions is invisible to a realized-PnL guard. The counter still reads zero. Every safety number is green. Then the positions close — and the drawdown "suddenly" appears, fully formed, in one tick of the counter.

This post dissects the blind spot, walks through a scenario where every guard reads fine while the account is drowning, and presents a dual-viewport design: realized drawdown and pool-wide mark-to-market unrealized PnL tracked separately, with the unrealized view gating new entries.

Consider a typical consecutive-loss breaker:.

This code is correct for what it measures. The issue is what it doesn't measure. on_trade_closed only fires when a trade closes. Between the open and the close, consecutive_losses and realized_pnl_today are frozen. If you have five positions open and all five are down 1.5% each, the breaker sees zero losses, zero realized drawdown, and happily approves a sixth entry.

The guard is not wrong. It is answering a different question than the one you think you're asking. "How much have I lost?" and "How much am I presently down?" are different quantities, and the gap between them is where accounts die.

It's not laziness. Realized PnL is easy: it's a single scalar that updates on a discrete event. Unrealized PnL is a moving target that requires a mark price per position, updates continuously, and has to handle stale quotes, funding, and partial fills. The realized-only guard is the 80% solution that ships in an afternoon. It's just missing the 20% that contains the worst days.

Here's the concrete version. Suppose the account is 100,000 units of quote currency, the consecutive-loss breaker is set to 3, and the daily loss limit is 2%. Position sizing is 20,000 notional per entry, so a 1.5% adverse move on a position is a 300-unit unrealized loss (0.3% of equity).

09:30 — Two positions open. Both drift against you. Unrealized: −600. Realized today: 0. consecutive_losses: 0. Breaker: open for business.

Industry observers note that 10:15 — The market trends against the book. A third and fourth position open (the breaker approved them, because nothing has closed). Unrealized across four positions: −2,400 (2.4% of equity). Realized today: still 0. consecutive_losses: still 0. can_open_new returns True.

According to recent reports, 11:00 — A fifth entry. Unrealized: −3,600. The daily loss limit is 2%, but it's computed on realized PnL, so it reads 0%. The breaker is structurally incapable of firing.

13:00 — Stops trigger across the book in a correlated move. All five close within twenty minutes. Realized today: −3,900. consecutive_losses: 5. The breaker finally fires — after the entire drawdown has been realized, and after it approved two entries during the bleed.

At 11:00, the account was down 3.6% on a mark-to-market basis. Every guard reported it was down 0%. The pool was drowning while the dashboard revealed a calm surface. This is the blind spot: the guard's measurement point (trade close) is downstream of the risk event (adverse mark-to-market drift on open exposure).

The design change is to stop treating "drawdown" as one number. Track two:.

The realized view answers "how bad has it been?" The unrealized view answers "how bad is it right now?" Entries should require both to be acceptable.

Sources indicate that the mark-to-market gate is checked on entry, not on a timer. You don't need a background thread recomputing the pool every millisecond. You need the check to run at the one moment it can still do something: before a upcoming order goes out. If the pool is down 1.6% and the cap is 1.5%, the next entry is refused — regardless of what the realized counter claims.

The two limits are separate knobs with separate meanings. max_unrealized_dd is typically tighter than the realized limit, because unrealized losses are still recoverable and you want to stop adding risk early. max_realized_dd can be looser, because realized losses are sunk and the response there is cooldown, not prevention. Conflating them into one number forces a bad compromise.

It has been revealed that the obvious pushback: mark-to-market is noisy, and a tight unrealized cap will block entries on harmless intraday wicks. Two mitigations, both cheap:.

Feed SmoothedMark.enhancement(price) into guard.mark(symbol, smoothed) and the gate becomes resistant to single-tick noise while still tracking real adverse drift.

The guard change fixes the behavior; you also want the diagnostic so you can see the blind spot forming. Log both viewports on every entry decision, and log the gap:.

The gap column is the interesting one. When realized_dd − unrealized_dd grows large and negative — realized flat, unrealized deeply negative — you are inside the blind spot of a realized-only guard. If you ever run a realized-only breaker in parallel (legacy system, comparison study), this log tells you exactly how many entries it approved that the dual-viewport guard would have refused, and what those entries cost on a mark-to-market basis.

Industry observers note that be clear about the scope. The unrealized gate does not prevent the first position from going against you, and it does not replace per-position stops. It addresses one specific failure mode: the guard that approves latest risk while existing risk is already underwater. Correlation is the amplifier here — five positions that all bleed together look like five independent decisions to the entry logic and like one concentrated bet to the mark-to-market pool. The pool view catches that; the per-trade view never will.

Sources indicate that the general principle generalizes beyond drawdown breakers: any risk control whose measurement event is downstream of the risk event has a blind window. Realized PnL is downstream of unrealized PnL. Trade close is downstream of trade open. The fix is always the same — measure at the point where the risk actually lives, and gate at the point where you can still act.

Industry observers note that gemma 3n was announced as a preview during Google I/O. The on-device community got really excited, because this is a model designed from the ground up to run locally on your hardware. On top of that, it’s natively multimodal, supporting image, text, audio, and video inputs 🤯.

Sources indicate that today, Gemma 3n is finally available on the most used open source libraries. This includes transformers & timm, MLX, llama.cpp (text inputs), transformers.js, ollama, Google AI Edge, and others.

This post quickly goes through practical snippets to demonstrate how to use the model with these libraries, and how easy it is to fine-tune it for other domains.

Here is the Gemma 3n Release Collection.

According to recent reports, two model sizes have been released today, with two variants (base and instruct) each. The model names follow a non-standard nomenclature: they are called gemma-3n-E2B and gemma-3n-E4B. The E preceding the parameter count stands for Effective. Their actual parameter counts are 5B and 8B, respectively, but thanks to improvements in memory efficiency, they manage to only need 2B and 4B in VRAM (GPU memory).

Recent findings suggest that these models, therefore, behave like 2B and 4B in terms of hardware support, but they punch over 2B/4B in terms of quality. The E2B model can run in as little as 2GB of GPU RAM, while E4B can run with just 3GB of GPU RAM.

Sources indicate that in addition to the language decoder, Gemma 3n uses an audio encoder and a vision encoder. We highlight their main features below, and describe how they have been added to transformers and timm, as they are the reference for other implementations.

Sources indicate that the easiest way to vibe check the model is with the dedicated Hugging Face Space for the model. You can try out different prompts, with different modalities, here.

Install the latest version of timm (for the vision encoder) and transformers to run inference, or if you want to fine tune it.

The easiest way to start using Gemma 3n is by using the pipeline abstraction in transformers:.

Initialize the model and the processor from the Hub, and write the model_generation function that takes care of processing the prompts and running the inference on the model.

Since the model supports all modalities as inputs, here's a brief code explanation of how you can use them via transformers.

Support for videos is done as a collection of frames of images.

Gemma 3n comes with day 0 support for MLX across all 3 modalities. Make sure to upgrade your mlx-vlm installation.

In addition to MLX, Gemma 3n (text only) works out of the box with llama.cpp. Make sure to install llama.cpp/ Ollama from source.

Check out the Installation instruction for llama.cpp here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/install.md.

Finally, we are also releasing ONNX weights for the gemma-3n-E2B-it model variant, enabling flexible deployment across diverse runtimes and platforms. For JavaScript developers, Gemma3n has been integrated into Transformers.js and is available as of version 3.6.0.

For more information on how to run the model with these libraries, check out the usage section in the model card.

Industry observers note that given the size of the model, it’s pretty convenient to fine-tune it for specific downstream tasks across modalities. To make it easier for you to fine-tune the model, we’ve created a simple notebook that allows you to experiment on a free Google Colab!

We also provide a dedicated notebook for fine-tuning on audio tasks, so you can easily adapt the model to your speech datasets and benchmarks!

With this release, we also introduce the Hugging Face Gemma Recipes repository. One will find notebooks and scripts to run the models and fine tune them.

According to recent reports, we would love for you to use the Gemma family of models and add more recipes to it! Feel free to open Challenges and create Pull Requests to the repository.

We are always excited to host Google and their Gemma family of models. We hope the community will get together and make the most of these models. Multimodal, small sized, and highly capable, make a great model release!

If you want to discuss the models in more detail, go ahead and start a discussion right below this blog post. We will be more than happy to help!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy.
  • Sources indicate that validation does not require a perfect product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Sources indicate that validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you strategy to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Recent findings suggest that side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

In a recent development, one of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Manufacturer). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

The biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

The 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Sources indicate that batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

Sources indicate that the FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice claims to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

It has been revealed that but here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the notable thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Sources indicate that open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Industry observers note that pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Sources indicate that create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

According to recent reports, your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

It has been revealed that once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and organization handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

It has been revealed that report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Sources indicate that start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Sources indicate that dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP promptly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

The whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking latest ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

Industry observers note that the custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it shows in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

Industry observers note that one frame highlights the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

The system proves itself where the company actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hi all, this is the sixth post in a small series about the Amazon main image rules that actually get listings suppressed.
  • A preflight report is only useful if you know what each line is measuring, and what to do when a line is not green.
  • Sources indicate that the pair below is a real output from the tool, from the examples on the site.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi all, this is the sixth post in a small series about the Amazon main image rules that actually get listings suppressed. The first covered the full preflight check list, the second covered source resolution, the third covered frame fill, the fourth was a teardown of a sneaker photo failing three ways, and the fifth was about the content rules no report can check. This one is about reading the report itself.

A preflight report is only useful if you know what each line is measuring, and what to do when a line is not green. So here is a real report from the tool, line by line, on a real photo: a ceramic mug shot on a beige background.

Sources indicate that the pair below is a real output from the tool, from the examples on the site. Before: the mug on a beige background, and the product only covered 31 percent of the original frame. After: only the product, background removed and composited on exact pure white RGB 255,255,255, centered at 85 percent frame fill, rebuilt at 2000x2000.

According to recent reports, the report marked the photo PASS overall. But PASS overall is not the whole story. Here is every line, and what it means.

It has been revealed that the report found the product and isolated it from the background. The bounding box covered 31 percent of the original frame, which is why the before photo looks small and lost: the camera was too far away, and the frame was mostly beige wall.

According to recent reports, what FAIL would look like here: no clear product found, because the photo is a flat lay of five items, or the product blends into a background of the same color. The fix is a reshoot with the product alone in the frame, on a background that contrasts with it.

In a recent development, the output is 2000x2000px, which is the size Amazon wants for zoom. This line is about the delivered file, not your source photo. A tool that outputs 1000px will fail this line no matter how good your source was.

All 8 edge and corner samples came back pure white. This is the line most sellers skip, and the one that quietly suppresses listings: a background that looks white on your screen can sample at 250 or 247 at the edges, and that is not pure white. The report samples the edges because that is where a leftover tint hides.

What FAIL would look like here: a warm gray cast from indoor lighting, or a soft shadow the background removal left behind. The fix is a clean cutout composited on exact 255,255,255, not a brightness slider pushed until it looks white.

Industry observers note that delivered as .jpg. Amazon main images must be JPEG, so a PNG or WebP output fails this line even if everything else is perfect.

According to recent reports, this is the most interesting line in the whole report. The source photo was 900x900px, and it was upscaled to 2000px. The report marked it WARN, not FAIL, because 900px is above the 500px floor where a source fails outright, but below the 2000px that would be sharp at full size.

Industry observers note that WARN means: this image will pass, but it will not be as sharp as a photo shot at 2000px or more. If this is your hero image, the one buyers see first, reshoot it at full resolution. If it is a secondary angle and the budget is spent, a WARN is acceptable and you can ship it.

Sources indicate that the rule behind the line: a source under 500px on the longest side fails, because no upscaling can invent the detail Amazon's zoom needs. That was the whole second post in this series.

The product's longest side fills 85 percent of the frame, centered. This is the line the third post in this series was about: Amazon wants the product to dominate the frame, and the original 31 percent bounding box is exactly why the before photo would never have worked as a main image.

Read it in this order. First, fix any FAIL, because a FAIL is a rule broken. Second, read the WARN lines and decide whether the photo matters enough to reshoot. Third, remember what the report cannot see: the content rules from the last post, text, props, lifestyle elements, watermarks. A report that is all green still needs your eyes on the frame.

And one habit that saves the most time: never edit the report to make it green. If the background line fails, fix the photo, not the file. A report you faked will not protect the listing, and Amazon checks the image, not your PDF.

Industry observers note that the checks are technical only: pure white background, 2000x2000 JPEG output, frame fill, and source resolution. Content rules stay with the seller. A PASS report means the technical rules passed, not that the image is compliant.

Industry observers note that if you have a suppressed listing right now, I am happy to run one photo through the preflight and show you the report, free, in the comments. Tell me which line you are unsure about, and we can work out what it means for your photo.

Tool: https://mainimagepass.site.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a state-of-the-art 8B Vision Language Model (VLM) designed for intelligent document processing, offering high accuracy and multimodal understanding. Available on Hugging Face, it excels in extracting and understanding information from complex documents like invoices, receipts, contracts, and more. With its powerful OCR capabilities and efficient performance on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, this model delivers industry-leading accuracy for text and table extraction, as well as chart, diagram, and table parsing. Whether you’re automating financial document processing or improving business intelligence workflows, Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for fast, scalable deployments.

Check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL! People can also post-train the model further with their own datasets using NVIDIA NeMo.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR). With its high accuracy, low model footprint, and multimodal capabilities, Llama Nemotron Nano VL enables the seamless extraction and understanding of information from complex documents. This includes PDFs, images, tables, charts, formulas, and diagrams, making it an ideal solution for automating document workflows across various industries like finance, healthcare, legal, and government.

According to recent reports, llama Nemotron Nano VL demonstrates exceptional accuracy on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, which tests models on real-world OCR and document understanding tasks. These tasks include text recognition, table extraction, and element parsing across various document types. The model’s advanced capabilities enable it to deliver better performance than current leading VLMs in real-world enterprise scenarios.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL builds upon Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and C-RADIOv2-VLM-H, a Vision Transformer (ViT) that serves as the backbone for visual feature extraction. This allows the model to handle a wide variety of visual elements in documents, including charts, graphs, and other complex visual representations.

C-RADIOv2-VLM-H Vision Transformer (ViT): The core visual understanding component of the model, C-RADIO allows for high-resolution processing of documents containing complex visual elements. This serves as a vision backbone, excelling across visual domains and enabling the model to process multi-image understanding with high resolution. This technology underpins the model’s ability to handle complex documents containing visual elements such as images, diagrams, charts, and tables.

It has been revealed that C-RADIO is trained on multi-resolution data using multiple distillation techniques. Multiplicative noise was applied to our weights during training to improve generalization.

Sources indicate that llama Nemotron VL further adopts a design that dynamically aggregates encoded patch features, enabling support for high-resolution input without sacrificing spatial continuity. This strategy efficiently processes documents with arbitrary aspect ratios while preserving both local detail and global context. It enables fine-grained analysis of dense visual content—such as small fonts, multi-column layouts, and intricate charts—without compromising computational efficiency or coverage. The model can also preserve the information better and have less distortion, due to the innovation in high-resolution tiling.

By empowering Llama-3.1 8B LLM with this strong vision foundation, Llama Nemotron Nano VL delivers unparalleled accuracy in parsing and interpreting documents.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using several OSS datasets along with data from NVIDIA’s VLM-based OCR solution, NeMo Retriever Parse. This provides capabilities in text and table parsing, along with grounding, enabling the Llama Nemotron Nano VL to perform at an industry-leading level in document understanding tasks. Synthetic table extraction datasets that were used for training this OCR solution were also used for training Llama Nemotron Nano VL 8B VLM to enable more optimal table understanding and extraction.

In a recent development, llama Nemotron Nano VL excels in tasks like text recognition and visual reasoning, and demonstrates advanced chart and diagram understanding capabilities. Llama Nemotron Nano VL allows for predicting bounding box coordinates in normalized space to enable grounding like tasks and text-referring.

Industry observers note that this strong performance is underpinned by high-quality in-domain data combined with a diverse training distribution across document types, languages, and layouts. A robust data strategy ensures coverage across challenging use cases through selective curation, targeted augmentation, and formatting techniques that clarify task intent and reduce ambiguity—resulting in models that generalize effectively to real-world applications.

Industry observers note that llama Nemotron Nano VL undergoes a two-stage training regimen: pre-training followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The initial pre-training phase focuses on achieving cross-modal alignment between the language and vision domains. This is accomplished through the training of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector, which serves as an interface between the two modalities.

For the training process, Llama Nemotron Nano VL leverages a comprehensive and diverse collection of datasets. This aggregated dataset, comprising a total of ~1.5M samples, includes publicly available, synthetically generated, as well as internally curated datasets. A summary of the datasets utilized during the pre-training stage is presented in Figure 1.

Sources indicate that in the Supervised Fine-Tuning stage, Llama-Nemotron-Nano-VL is trained end-to-end on a combination of synthetic, public, and internally curated datasets. The data encompasses a wide spectrum of tasks, including but not limited to: OCR, text grounding, table parsing, and general document-based VQA.

The document understanding capabilities of Llama Nemotron Nano VL can be largely attributed to the OCR-focused SFT data blend. Besides simple OCR, many of the datasets involve tasks such as predicting the correct reading order, reconstructing markdown formatting along with semantic classes (such as Captions, Titles, Section headers) and bounding boxes of individual text blocks. The model is also trained to parse mathematical formulas in LaTeX format and to extract tables in LaTeX, HTML, or markdown formats, depending on the prompt.

It has been revealed that to ensure robustness across various domains, we apply affine and photometric augmentations to the document images. To improve the table and chart parsing performance further, we enable swapping of tables and charts embedded into the full-page documents between the datasets. This enables the model to handle diverse document layouts and structures.

A large portion of the internally-created datasets are based on Nemo Retriever Parse training data. These include NVPDFTex - a collection of arxiv documents with ground-truth labels consisting of formatted text in reading order, with bounding boxes and semantic classes of text, as well as LaTeX tables and equations; Common Crawl pdfs that are labeled by human annotators; rendered text from Wikipedia with markdown formatting and tables, as well as a number of synthetic datasets targeted at improving table parsing capabilities and dense OCR. In addition, the training blend includes a number of publicly-available datasets, such as DocLayNet, FinTabNet and PubTables-1M, in which we refine the groundtruth labels.

Industry observers note that figure 2 below demonstrates the task distribution of the training data. As can be seen, a significant portion of the training samples involve OCR along with grounding and table parsing, as well as OCR-adjacent VQA tasks.

Recent findings suggest that llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using NVIDIA Megatron and utilizes efficient Transformer implementations in NVIDIA Transformer Engine. For multimodal dataloading, we use Megatron Energon. We provide example Megatron training and inference scripts along with hyperparameters and other instructions to enable custom training of VLMs.

Industry observers note that to ensure the output is formatted precisely as you need, we recommend including detailed instructions within your prompts. We've provided some examples below to illustrate how this works for various tasks:.

Sources indicate that OCRBench v2 is an advanced benchmark designed to evaluate OCR models across a diverse range of real-world document types and layouts. It includes over 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs to rigorously assess a model’s capabilities in visual text localization, table parsing, diagram reasoning and key-value extraction.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL outperforms other VLMs on this benchmark and also achieves strong accuracies in benchmarks such as ChartQA and AI2D, making it a compelling option for enterprises aiming to automate document workflows such as:.

Its combination of high accuracy, strong layout aware reasoning, and efficient deployment on a single GPU makes it an ideal choice for large-scale enterprise automation.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for various document processing tasks across multiple industries. Here are some of the key use cases where the model excels:.

Automating the extraction of line items, totals, dates, and other key data points from invoices and receipts. This is crucial for accounting, ERP integration, and expense management.

Extracting structured data from passports, IDs, and tax forms for regulatory compliance and KYC processes.

Automatically identifying key clauses, dates, and obligations in legal documents.

Extracting patient data, claim information, and policy details from medical records and insurance forms.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL provides developers with the tools to automate document processing workflows at scale. It is available through the NVIDIA NIM API and for download on Hugging Face, where you can begin building production-ready document understanding applications. Users can also use NVIDIA NeMo to finetune the model on their own dataset.

Gate.io API Pagination Trap: from+to+limit Cannot Coexist

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you've wired up Gate.io's futures candlestick endpoint, you've probably hit this: you build a request with a start time, an end time, and a page size, and the server replies HTTP 400.
  • Here's the endpoint in question (USDT-margined perpetual futures):.
  • It has been revealed that the rule the docs bury: from, to, and limit are mutually constrained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you've wired up Gate.io's futures candlestick endpoint, you've probably hit this: you build a request with a start time, an end time, and a page size, and the server replies HTTP 400. You strip out to, retry, and it works. You add it back, it breaks. The error message doesn't mention to at all — it usually complains about something generic like an invalid parameter or an empty result set, which sends you chasing the wrong thing for an hour.

Here's the endpoint in question (USDT-margined perpetual futures):.

Query parameters that matter for history:.

It has been revealed that the rule the docs bury: from, to, and limit are mutually constrained. from+limit works. from+to works. to+limit works. All three together returns 400. And there's a second constraint that bites later: any single call returns at most the most recent 10,000 data points, regardless of how wide your range is.

It has been revealed that let's pin down the failure so it's not folklore. The code below is the minimal reproduction — no retry logic, no abstractions.

The message varies and is never "you sent too many parameters." That's the trap: the API validates combinations, not individual fields, and the error text doesn't say which combination it rejected.

One more detail worth knowing: from and to are in seconds, but the timestamps inside the returned candle objects are also in seconds. Mixing in milliseconds (easy to do if you're used to other exchanges) silently produces empty arrays or absurd ranges rather than an error.

It has been revealed that the fix is to pick one paging axis and stick to it. from+limit is the most robust because it's forward-only: you always ask for "the next N candles starting at timestamp T," and you advance T using the data you got back.

Sources indicate that the rule: next page's from = last candle's timestamp + interval seconds. Not +1 second in general — +1 only works for the 1s interval. For 1m it's +60, for 1h it's +3600. If you use the interval length, you never re-request the boundary candle and you never skip one.

A few things this loop gets right that naive versions don't:.

The 10,000-point cap is per call, not per range, and it's applied to the most recent data in the window you asked for. This has a nasty consequence: if you request from = now - 30 days with limit = 1000 on 1m, you get the 1,000 most recent minutes of that window — not the first 1,000 minutes. Your pagination loop's first page is fine, but the semantics of "most recent within the window" mean that a naive loop which advances from will eventually get stuck asking for data older than what the server will serve in a single call.

The clean way to handle it is to split the overall range into windows of at most 10,000 intervals, and paginate inside each window. That way each from+limit call is guaranteed to fall inside the server's per-call ceiling.

Industry observers note that if you're pulling months of 1m data, this is dozens of HTTP round-trips. That's expected — there is no bulk export endpoint, and hammering the server with parallel requests will get you rate-limited. Serialize, add a small sleep between windows, and cache to disk.

The Gate.io case is one instance of a general problem: undocumented parameter interactions. When you hit a 400 and the message is unhelpful, don't guess — bisect.

The idea: start with a request you know works, then add parameters one at a time, and when it breaks, remove one at a time to confirm which combination is fatal. For a small parameter set this is a few requests.

Sources indicate that for three optional parameters this is at most 8 requests and it tells you definitively that {from, to, limit} is the failing triple and {from, limit} is the maximal working pair. That's far faster than reading docs that don't mention the rule.

According to recent reports, when the parameter space is larger — say, ten optional query params — exhaustive subsets are 1,024 requests, which is too many. Switch to a greedy bisection: add params one at a time in the order you suspect matters; when adding one breaks the request, mark it as conflicting with the current set and try it alone against the required params. That's O(n) in practice.

Run it, and you get a working parameter set plus the list of params that broke it. In the Gate.io case, rejected would contain whichever of from/to/limit was added third — which is exactly the information the error message withheld.

Industry observers note that the general lesson transfers: when an API's parameters interact, the docs often describe each field in isolation and leave the constraints implicit. Build a small probe harness once, and every new endpoint becomes a five-minute investigation instead of an afternoon of guessing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training dense embedding, reranker (cross encoder), and sparse embedding models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more.
  • Finetuning sparse embedding models involves several components: the model, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training dense embedding, reranker (cross encoder), and sparse embedding models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a sparse encoder/embedding model and explain why you might want to do so. This results in sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq, a cheap model that works especially well in hybrid search or retrieve and rerank scenarios.

Finetuning sparse embedding models involves several components: the model, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong sparse embedding models.

In addition to training your own models, you can choose from a wide range of pretrained sparse encoders available on the Hugging Face Hub. To help navigate this growing space, we’ve curated a SPLADE Models collection highlighting some of the most relevant models.We list the most prominent ones along with their benchmark results in Pretrained Models in the documentation.

Recent findings suggest that the broader term "embedding models" refer to models that convert some input, usually text, into a vector representation (embedding) that captures the semantic meaning of the input. Unlike with the raw inputs, you can perform mathematical operations on these embeddings, resulting in similarity scores that can be used for various tasks, such as search, clustering, or classification.

According to recent reports, with dense embedding models, i.e. the common variety, the embeddings are typically low-dimensional vectors (e.g., 384, 768, or 1024 dimensions) where most values are non-zero. Sparse embedding models, on the other hand, produce high-dimensional vectors (e.g., 30,000+ dimensions) where most values are zero. Usually, each active dimension (i.e. the dimension with a non-zero value) in a sparse embedding corresponds to a specific token in the model's vocabulary, allowing for interpretability.

Let's have a look at naver/splade-v3, a state-of-the-art sparse embedding model, as an example:.

In this example, the embeddings are 30,522-dimensional vectors, where each dimension corresponds to a token in the model's vocabulary. The decode method returned the top 10 tokens with the highest values in the embedding, allowing us to interpret which tokens contribute most to the embedding.

We can even determine the intersection or overlap between embeddings, very useful for determining why two texts are deemed similar or dissimilar:.

A key component of neural sparse embedding models is query/document expansion. Unlike traditional lexical methods like BM25, which only match exact tokens, neural sparse models generally automatically expand the original text with semantically related terms:.

According to recent reports, for example, in the code output above, the sentence "The weather is lovely today" is expanded to include terms like "beautiful", "cool", "pretty", and "nice" which weren't in the original text. Similarly, "It's so sunny outside!" is expanded to include "weather", "summer", and "sun".

This expansion allows neural sparse models to match semantically related content or synonyms even without exact token matches, handle misspellings, and overcome vocabulary mismatch problems. This is why neural sparse models like SPLADE often outperform traditional lexical search methods while maintaining the efficiency benefits of sparse representations.

However, expansion has its risks. For example, query expansion for "What is the weather on Tuesday?" will likely also expand to "monday", "wednesday", etc., which may not be desired.

Recent findings suggest that in short, neural sparse embedding models fall in a valuable niche between traditional lexical methods like BM25 and dense embedding models like Sentence Transformers. They have the following advantages:.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "sparse embedding model" and "sparse encoder model" interchangeably.

The majority of (neural) sparse embedding models employ the aforementioned query/document expansion so that you can match texts with nearly identical meaning, even if they don't share any words. In short, the model has to recognize synonyms so those tokens can be placed in the final embedding.

Most out-of-the-box sparse embedding models will easily recognize that "supermarket", "food", and "market" are useful expansions of a text containing "grocery", but for example:.

Industry observers note that whereas we wish for it to expand to "headache", the common word for "cephalalgia". This example expands to many domains, e.g. not recognizing that "Java" is a programming language, that "Audi" makes cars, or that "NVIDIA" is a firm that makes graphics cards.

Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.

Training Sentence Transformer models involves the following components:.

Now, let's dive into each of these components in more detail.

Recent findings suggest that sparse Encoder models consist of a sequence of Modules, Sparse Encoder specific Modules or Custom Modules, allowing for a lot of flexibility. If you want to further finetune a Sparse Encoder model (e.g. it has a modules.json file), then you don't have to worry about which modules are used:.

But if instead you want to train from another checkpoint, or from scratch, then these are the most common architectures you can use:.

Splade models use the MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling modules. The former loads a pretrained Masked Language Modeling transformer model (e.g. BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ModernBERT, etc.) and the latter pools the output of the MLMHead to produce a single sparse embedding of the size of the vocabulary.

This architecture is the default if you provide a fill-mask model architecture to SparseEncoder, so it's easier to use the shortcut:.

According to recent reports, inference-free Splade uses a Router module with different modules for queries and documents. Usually for this type of architecture, the documents part is a traditional Splade architecture (a MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling module) and the query part is an SparseStaticEmbedding module, which just returns a pre-computed score for every token in the query.

This architecture allows for fast query-time processing using the lightweight SparseStaticEmbedding approach, that can be trained and seen as a linear weights, while documents are processed with the full MLM transformer and SpladePooling.

Inference-free Splade is particularly useful for search applications where query latency is critical, as it shifts the computational complexity to the document indexing phase which can be done offline.

When training models with the Router module, you must use the router_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map the training dataset columns to the correct route ("query" or "document"). For example, if your dataset(s) have ["question", "answer"] columns, then you can use the following mapping:.

In a recent development, additionally, it is recommended to use a much higher learning rate for the SparseStaticEmbedding module than for the rest of the model. For this, you should use the learning_rate_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map parameter patterns to their learning rates. For example, if you want to use a learning rate of 1e-3 for the SparseStaticEmbedding module and 2e-5 for the rest of the model, you can do this:.

Contrastive Sparse Representation (CSR) models, introduced in Beyond Matryoshka: Revisiting Sparse Coding for Adaptive Representation, apply a SparseAutoEncoder module on top of a dense Sentence Transformer model, which usually consist of a Transformer followed by a Pooling module. You can initialize one from scratch like so:.

Or if your base model is 1) a dense Sentence Transformer model or 2) a non-MLM Transformer model (those are loaded as Splade models by default), then this shortcut will automatically initialize the CSR model for you:.

Unlike (Inference-free) Splade models, sparse embeddings by CSR models don't have the same size as the vocabulary of the base model. This means you can't directly interpret which words are activated in your embedding like you can with Splade models, where each dimension corresponds to a specific token in the vocabulary.

Beyond that, CSR models are most effective on dense encoder models that use high-dimensional representations (e.g. 1024-4096 dimensions).

If you're unsure which architecture to use, here's a quick guide:.

The SparseEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use local data in various formats such as CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL.

Note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets in the Hugging Face Hub.

In a recent development, some datasets, like nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual, have multiple subsets with different data formats. You need to specify the subset name along with the dataset name, e.g. dataset = load_dataset("nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual", "de", split="train").

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in certain file formats:.

Recent findings suggest that you can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict if your local data requires pre-processing. This allows you to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

Each key in the dictionary becomes a column in the resulting dataset.

Industry observers note that it's crucial to ensure that your dataset format matches your chosen loss function. This involves checking two things:.

For example, if your loss function accepts (anchor, positive, negative) triplets, then your first, second, and third dataset columns correspond with anchor, positive, and negative, respectively. This means that your first and second column must contain texts that should embed closely, and that your first and third column must contain texts that should embed far apart. That is why depending on your loss function, your dataset column order matters.

Consider a dataset with columns ["text1", "text2", "label"], where the "label" column contains floating point similarity scores. This dataset can be used with SparseCoSENTLoss, SparseAnglELoss, and SparseCosineSimilarityLoss because:.

According to recent reports, if the columns in your dataset are not ordered correctly, use Dataset.select_columns to reorder them. Additionally, remove any extraneous columns (e.g., sample_id, metadata, source, type) using Dataset.remove_columns, as they will be treated as inputs otherwise.

It has been revealed that loss functions measure how well a model performs on a given batch of data and guide the optimization process. The choice of loss function depends on your available data and target task. Refer to the Loss Overview for a comprehensive list of options.

According to recent reports, to train a SparseEncoder, you either need a SpladeLoss or CSRLoss, depending on the architecture. These are wrapper losses that add sparsity regularization on top of a main loss function, which must be provided as a parameter. The only loss that can be used independently is SparseMSELoss, as it performs embedding-level distillation, ensuring sparsity by directly copying the teacher's sparse embedding.

Most loss functions can be initialized with just the SparseEncoder that you're training, alongside some optional parameters, e.g.:.

The SparseEncoderTrainingArguments class allows you to specify parameters that influence training performance and tracking/debugging. While optional, experimenting with these arguments can help improve training efficiency and provide insights into the training process.

In the Sentence Transformers documentation, I've outlined some of the most useful training arguments. I would recommend reading it in Training Overview > Training Arguments.

Here's an example of how to initialize SparseEncoderTrainingArguments:.

Industry observers note that note that eval_strategy was introduced in transformers version 4.41.0. Prior versions should use evaluation_strategy instead.

Recent findings suggest that you can provide the SparseEncoderTrainer with an eval_dataset to get the evaluation loss during training, but it may be useful to get more concrete metrics during training, too. For this, you can use evaluators to assess the model's performance with useful metrics before, during, or after training. You can use both an eval_dataset and an evaluator, one or the other, or neither. They evaluate based on the eval_strategy and eval_steps Training Arguments.

Here are the implemented Evaluators that come with Sentence Transformers for Sparse Encoder models:.

Additionally, SequentialEvaluator should be used to combine multiple evaluators into one Evaluator that can be passed to the SparseEncoderTrainer.

Sources indicate that sometimes you don't have the required evaluation data to prepare one of these evaluators on your own, but you still want to track how well the model performs on some common benchmarks. In that case, you can use these evaluators with data from Hugging Face.

In a recent development, when evaluating frequently during training with a small eval_steps, consider using a tiny eval_dataset to minimize evaluation overhead. If you're concerned about the evaluation set size, a 90-1-9 train-eval-test split can provide a balance, reserving a reasonably sized test set for final evaluations. After training, you can assess your model's performance using trainer.evaluate(test_dataset) for test loss or initialize a testing evaluator with test_evaluator(model) for detailed test metrics.

If you evaluate after training, but before saving the model, your automatically generated model card will still include the test results.

When using Distributed Training, the evaluator only runs on the first device, unlike the training and evaluation datasets, which are shared across all devices.

Industry observers note that the SparseEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. We only have to specify the trainer with the model, training arguments (optional), training dataset, evaluation dataset (optional), loss function, evaluator (optional) and we can start training. Let’s have a look at a script where all of these components come together:.

In this example I'm finetuning from distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased, a base model that is not yet a Sparse Encoder model. This requires more training data than finetuning an existing Sparse Encoder model, like naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil.

It has been revealed that after running this script, the sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq model was uploaded for me. The model scores 0.5241 NDCG@10 on NanoMSMARCO, 0.3299 NDCG@10 on NanoNFCorpus and 0.5357 NDCG@10 NanoNQ, which is a good result for an inference-free distilbert-based model trained on just 100k pairs from the Natural Questions dataset.

The model uses an average of 184 active dimensions in the sparse embeddings for the documents, compared to 7.7 active dimensions for the queries (i.e. the average number of tokens in the query). This corresponds to a sparsity of 99.39% and 99.97%, respectively.

All of this information is stored in the automatically generated model card, including the base model, language, license, evaluation results, training & evaluation dataset info, hyperparameters, training logs, and more. Without any effort, your uploaded models should contain all the information that your potential customers would need to determine whether your model is suitable for them.

The Sentence Transformers trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

These are automatically used without you having to specify anything, as long as the required dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Top-performing models are often trained using multiple datasets simultaneously. The SparseEncoderTrainer simplifies this process by allowing you to train with multiple datasets without converting them to the same format. You can even apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps for multi-dataset training:.

Each training/evaluation batch will contain samples from only one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is determined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. The valid options are:.

Let's evaluate our newly trained inference-free SPLADE model using the NanoMSMARCO dataset, and see how it compares to dense retrieval approaches. We'll also explore hybrid retrieval methods that combine sparse and dense vectors, as well as reranking to further improve search quality.

After running a slightly modified version of our hybrid_search.py script, we get the following results for the NanoMSMARCO dataset, using these models:.

The Sparse and Dense rankings can be combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which is a simple way to combine the results of multiple rankings. If a Reranker is applied, it will rerank the results of the prior retrieval step.

The results indicate that for this dataset, combining Dense and Sparse rankings is very performant, resulting in 12.3% and 18.7% increases over the Dense and Sparse baselines, respectively. In short, combining Sparse and Dense retrieval methods is a very effective way to improve search performance.

It has been revealed that furthermore, applying a reranker on any of the rankings improved the performance to approximately 66.3 NDCG@10, showing that either Sparse, Dense, or Hybrid (Dense + Sparse) found the relevant documents in their top 100, which the reranker then ranked to the top 10. So, replacing a Dense -> Reranker pipeline with a Sparse -> Reranker pipeline might improve both latency and costs:.

Vector databases provide the essential infrastructure for storing, indexing, and retrieving sparse embeddings at scale. Popular options include Qdrant, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, and Seismic, among others.

HubSpot private apps can't be created anymore: what to use for server-side integrations

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you've tried to create a private app in HubSpot recently and the option wasn't there, you're not doing anything wrong.
  • Private apps were the simple way to give a script access to your HubSpot data: create the app, pick scopes, copy a token.
  • For a typical marketing or sales operations script (read deals, read contacts, send events somewhere else), a Service Key covers it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've tried to create a private app in HubSpot recently and the option wasn't there, you're not doing anything wrong. HubSpot changed how server-to-server integrations get their credentials, and most tutorials online still describe the old path.

Private apps were the simple way to give a script access to your HubSpot data: create the app, pick scopes, copy a token. That flow is now closed for new legacy apps. HubSpot's direction is two credential types: project-based apps built with the developer platform, and Service Keys for straightforward data integrations.

For a typical marketing or sales operations script (read deals, read contacts, send events somewhere else), a Service Key covers it.

It's sent like any Bearer token:.

That call is also the fastest way to get the internal IDs of your pipeline stages, which is what your code should compare against (never the stage labels, someone will rename them).

The one real limitation: Service Keys don't support webhooks. Webhooks need a project-based app built with the HubSpot CLI.

Industry observers note that for most integrations, polling is the more robust option anyway. Every few minutes, search for records modified since the last run:.

Nothing breaks today. Put two things on the calendar: replace the token with a Service Key, and move your endpoints to the date-versioned paths. Both are small changes if your code keeps the base path and the credential in configuration, not scattered through the script.

A common use for these scripts is closing the loop between HubSpot and Meta Ads: when a deal is qualified or won, an event goes to the Conversions API so campaigns learn which leads actually turn into customers. That's layer 4 of the 4-Layer Tracking Kit, which builds the whole path with a Service Key, the 2026-03 API and polling, including the HubSpot API pitfalls that return status 200 and do nothing.

Do my existing HubSpot private app tokens stop working?

It has been revealed that no. Tokens from legacy private apps that already exist keep working. What changed is that existing accounts can no longer create new legacy private apps. HubSpot has declared the end of support for legacy apps and for the v1 to v3 APIs in September 2027, so plan the migration before then.

What replaces private apps for a simple server-to-server script?

A Service Key. You create it in the account settings, give it only the scopes the script needs, and send it as a Bearer token. For a script that reads deals and contacts, read-only CRM scopes are enough.

Can I receive HubSpot webhooks with a Service Key?

It has been revealed that no. Webhooks require a project-based app built with the HubSpot CLI. With a Service Key, the robust alternative is polling the search API every few minutes for records modified since the last run.

#150477. Meta Conversions API deduplication: why your cost per conversion just halved

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (414 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Meta Conversions API deduplication: why your cost per conversion just halved

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (414 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You turn on the Conversions API, and a few days later cost per conversion drops by half.
  • Sources indicate that the campaign's spend doesn't change; the number of conversions it reports does.
  • Industry observers note that meta compares events from the pixel and the Conversions API.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You turn on the Conversions API, and a few days later cost per conversion drops by half. It looks like the best week of the account. Usually it isn't: Meta is counting the same conversion twice, once from the browser and once from the server.

Sources indicate that the campaign's spend doesn't change; the number of conversions it reports does. Twice the conversions for the same spend means half the cost per conversion. Optimization also starts learning from inflated counts, which is worse than the reporting problem.

Industry observers note that meta compares events from the pixel and the Conversions API. When the event name and the event_id match, it keeps one. In the pixel, the ID goes in the options object:.

Sources indicate that on the server, it goes in the event_id field of the event. With server-side GTM, the GA4 hit carries it from the browser and the Conversions API tag forwards it.

Generate the ID once, where the event is born, and hand the same value to every destination:.

Two rules come with it: one try/catch per destination, so a failure in one doesn't silently stop the others, and no second ID generated in GTM or on the server.

Recent findings suggest that deduplication is one of 13 silent failure modes covered in the free field guide 13 Silent Tracking Failures. The full setup, from the page to HubSpot deal stages flowing back to Meta, is in the 4-Layer Tracking Kit.

How does Meta deduplicate browser and server events?

When the pixel and the Conversions API send the same event with the same event name and the same event_id, Meta keeps one. In the pixel the ID goes in the eventID option; on the server it goes in the event_id field.

Where should the event_id be created?

Industry observers note that once, where the event is born, on the page. The same value goes to the pixel and to the dataLayer, and from there to the server. Generating it twice, in two places, is the same as not having it.

Do CRM events need deduplication?

Sources indicate that not with the browser, because there's no browser counterpart. They still need a stable event_id per record and stage, so a script that runs twice doesn't send the same conversion twice.

📅 04 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (573 w)
