Announcing NeurIPS 2025 E2LM Competition: Early Training Evaluation of Language Models

📅 04 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.
  • Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!
  • Recent findings suggest that the development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.

Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!

Recent findings suggest that the development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated. This phase is commonly referred to as the early stages of training. During this period, researchers primarily monitor two key metrics: the training loss curve and evaluation scores. However, existing evaluation benchmarks often fail to provide meaningful or discriminative signals during these initial stages where LLMs are trained on a few tokens ~200B tokens, making it challenging to derive conclusive insights from ongoing experiments.

In this competition, we want to build together fresh benchmarks to effectively capture relevant signals in early training stages of LLMs, specifically for scientific knowledge domain.

According to recent reports, the competition will be hosted on a dedicated Hugging Face organization - to register to the competition please follow this registration link 👉 https://e2lmc.github.io/registration. Participants will have to submit their solutions, which will be based on lm-evaluation-harness library through a HuggingFace Space. An active leaderboard will be maintained during the competition to track promising submissions. The size of the models make them easily runnable for everyone, on free-tier Google Colab GPUs. We also provide a comprehensive starting kit including several notebooks to get started with the competition.

It has been revealed that each submission will be evaluated using three different scores: signal quality score (ScoreSQ), ranking consistency score (ScoreRC) amd compliance with scientific knowledge score (ScoreCS). These criteria will be combined into a global score used for the final ranking. Additionally, two validation procedures will be systematically applied to all submissions: (i) verification of alignment with established scientific knowledge domains, and (ii) detection of potential information leakage, specifically the presence of the answer within the question prompt.The overall score is computed as a weighted sum:.

In a recent development, where, αSQ, αRC and αCS are weighting coefficients that reflect the relative importance of each criterion. We set the weights as α1 = 0.5, α2 = 0.1 and α3 = 0.4, thereby placing greater emphasis on signal quality and compliance to scientific knowledge, which we consider the most important metrics in evaluating submissions.

Recent findings suggest that participants will be able to compute the signal quality subscore locally using the provided model checkpoints of three Small Language Models 0.5B, 1B and 3B (ranging from 0 to 200 BT) along with the accompanying scoring algorithm (provided in a notebook in the starting kit). In contrast, the other two subscores cannot be computed independently, as the corresponding checkpoints—from 200 GT to 1 T tokens, as well as the 0.5 billion parameter model trained exclusively on web data—will remain hidden throughout the competition. Nonetheless, the global score will be automatically computed upon submission through the Hugging Face competition space, allowing participants to track their overall performance. This setup is intended to prevent overly customized solutions specifically tailored to the released checkpoints.

Further details about each evaluation metric, along with full scoring results on state-of-the-art benchmarks, are available in the competition proposal.

  • Sources indicate that sound familiar?
  • In a recent development, in this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You've got everything ready - data, model, a beefy GPU setup. You hit "run" and... wait. And wait some more. Your GPUs are barely breaking a sweat while your wallet's getting lighter by the hour.

Sources indicate that sound familiar? We've been there. After some detective work on our nanoVLM project, we discovered the real culprit wasn't our model or hardware, it was our data pipeline being incredibly wasteful.

In a recent development, in this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages. In each stage we add or remove from the previous step and comment on what went right and what did not.

It has been revealed that to make it easier to follow the data preparation tasks, we created a separate repo laser-focused on the data pipeline only. We hope this will be much easier to understand that reading the code once integrated with the nanoVLM repository. In addition, this could be useful to bootstrap other data pipelines!

Repository: https://github.com/ariG23498/mmdp.

Industry observers note that to follow along, all you need to do is clone the repository. It contains the final data preparation tasks, but it's designed to showcase each step of the way.

Recent findings suggest that before optimizing anything, we need to understand what we are working with. Our multimodal dataset has images, text prompts, and responses.

In a recent development, getting familiar with your training data is crucial for success. The previous script reveals a random sample each time you run it; you may want to copy the snippet to a notebook and run it multiple times to get a feeling about the data.

Our first training attempt used the obvious (and very frequent) approach:.

The results were painful. Look at this visualization:.

Sources indicate that see all that gray? That's padding. That's the GPU processing absolutely nothing while you pay for compute time. We were wasting roughly 60% of our batch on empty tokens.

Our next move was simple. Set a global maximum length and stick to it. If a sample was too long, we'd just drop it.

According to recent reports, as you might have noticed that the batch now has one sample less. This is due to the filtering process. This helped, but we were still padding everything to the same fixed length regardless of actual content. Better than before, but still wasteful.

Now we’re ready to rethink batching entirely. Padding is the enemy, and we need a strategy to minimize it while maximizing how much data we can fit into each batch. Enter the knapsack problem, a classic from computer science that’s perfect for this.

It has been revealed that imagine you’re packing a backpack for a hike. It can only hold so much weight, and you want to cram in as many useful items as possible. In our case:.

To test this idea, we start with a toy dataset: just a list of numbers from 1 to 25, each representing a sequence length. This lets us experiment without the complexity of images and text.

Most PyTorch datasets are map-style (you access them with dataset[i]). But for dynamic batching, we need something more flexible. So, we built an iterable-style dataset by subclassing torch.utils.data.IterableDataset. This lets us generate batches on the fly and handle tricks like sharding data across multiple workers:.

Packing sequences can be slow, especially if we’re sorting or shuffling. To keep things moving, we use a producer-consumer pattern using Python queues:.

The producer thread packs batches and puts them in a queue, while the main thread pulls them out as needed. This overlap keeps the pipeline flowing smoothly.

First, we try a simple greedy packing strategy:.

This walks through the data sequentially, adding items to a pack until it’s full, then starting a fresh one. It’s fast but not perfect. Here’s what the batches look like:.

Notice how later batches get sparse? We’re leaving gaps.

Let’s try a smarter approach: bin-packing (specifically, First Fit Decreasing):.

This sorts sequences by length (longest first) and tries to fit each one into the first pack that has room. If none fits, it starts a latest pack. The result?

These batches are much tighter, with less wasted space. It’s like playing Tetris with your data, fitting pieces together snugly.

Now for the real deal, applying knapsack packing to our multimodal dataset.

According to recent reports, we’re back to images, prompts, and responses, and we need to pack them efficiently while respecting both token limits and image budgets. Image budgeting is done so that images per sample are balanced. We would like to avoid the case where one GPU needs to process way more images than another.

According to recent reports, our new ConstantLengthDataset class handles the heavy lifting. Here’s how it works, compared to Stage 4:.

The ConstantLengthDataset does it all:.

Look at that! The gray (padding) is minimal, and the batches are dense with useful data. It’s like packing a suitcase so well you can still zip it up without sitting on it.

The image might seem unintuive at the first glance, but let us look at the image side by side with constrained padding.

Sources indicate that here you will notice that the samples in knapsack are more evenly distributed. We also do not run into the concern of having less samples in the batch due to filtering.

What started as a simple "why is training so slow?" investigation led to a complete rethink of how we handle multimodal data.

The balanced knapsack strategy for data pipeline comes from the Eagle 2: Building Post-Training Data Strategies from Scratch for Frontier Vision-Language Models paper from NVIDIA.

Happy training (and may your GPUs stay busy)!

1-Wall Floor Proposal Scale Calibration & Parametric Wall Resizing in Pure TypeScript

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when someone snaps a photo of a hand-drawn floor blueprint or traces an existing PDF listing sheet, the geometry starts out in arbitrary pixel coordinates.
  • In PlanCaliber, all three operations—1-wall scale calibration, centerline/clear-interior parametric wall resizing, and collinear wall-chain dragging—run deterministically in pure TypeScript with zero external geometry kernels (src/lib/cad/healer.ts).
  • Here is the exact math and edge-case protection behind each one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when someone snaps a photo of a hand-drawn floor blueprint or traces an existing PDF listing sheet, the geometry starts out in arbitrary pixel coordinates. Turning that rough sketch into true-scale architectural inches (1/4" = 1'-0") and then letting the user type exact laser-measure dimensions—without warping walls into trapezoids, stretching a 30-inch range into a 41-inch monster, or folding an adjacent bathroom inside-out—is one of the trickiest UX and geometry problems in browser-based CAD.

In PlanCaliber, all three operations—1-wall scale calibration, centerline/clear-interior parametric wall resizing, and collinear wall-chain dragging—run deterministically in pure TypeScript with zero external geometry kernels (src/lib/cad/healer.ts).

Here is the exact math and edge-case protection behind each one.

After tracing a sketch or PDF, a homeowner or appraiser rarely knows the exact pixel-to-inch scale—they know one real tape-measure reading (for example, "this exterior garage wall is 22'-0"").

Naively multiplying every number in the document by factor = targetLengthIn / curLen breaks physical reality:.

Instead, rescalePlanToWall anchors scaling at the initiative's bounding-box origin (ox, oy), scales coordinates uniformly, preserves wall thicknesses and fixed appliance sizes, and snaps architectural openings to 2" rough increments and modular cabinets to 3" stock increments:.

Why anchor around (ox, oy) rather than (0, 0)? Because scaling around the world origin flings the floor plan off-screen if the user panned away from (0, 0) before calibrating. Anchoring to the plan's minimum corner keeps the drawing planted right in the viewport.

According to recent reports, when a contractor reads a blueprint, walls are typically dimensioned centerline-to-centerline or exterior face-to-face. When a homeowner measures a room with a laser tape measure, they measure clear interior drywall-to-drywall.

If a user types 12'-0" (144") in clear mode on a bedroom wall framed between a 6" exterior wall and a 4.5" interior partition, the true CAD centerline span is not 144"—it is:.

144" + (6" / 2) + (4.5" / 2) = 149.25" (12'-5 1/4").

setWallLength inspects every perpendicular wall (|dir · od| < 0.25) attached to either endpoint and accumulates half of each intersecting wall's thickness:.

Moving just wall.endId along (dirX, dirY) turns a rectangle into a trapezoid. Even worse: if a bedroom sits next to a 4'-0" hallway and the user widens the bedroom by +5'-0", shifting only the shared partition wall pushes it past the far hallway wall, inverting the hallway polygon into a negative-area self-intersecting bowtie.

PlanCaliber solves both in two clean graph passes:.

Right after applying dirX * delta and dirY * delta, every door and window on a stretched or shrunk wall updates its offset proportionally ((op.offsetIn / oldL) * newL) and runs through clampOpeningsInPlace so no jamb ever overlaps a corner (>= 3" minimum return).

In a real planar floor-strategy graph, interior partition T-junctions split a 48'-0" exterior south wall into three separate segments (say 16'-0", 14'-0", and 18'-0"). If the user grabs the middle segment to deepen the whole house by 2'-0", dragging only that single segment punches a jagged step into the exterior envelope.

collectCollinearWallChainVertices computes the seed wall's unit normal (nx, ny) = (-dy/len, dx/len) and floods across connected same-kind (exterior or interior) segments whose endpoints lie within 0.5" of the line and whose direction dot-product with the normal is <= 0.02:.

Restricting the flood by w.kind === seed.kind is essential: an interior partition that happens to align with a jogged exterior wall stays independent unless the user edits it explicitly.

You can test the full workflow right in the browser with no account required:.

Note: PlanCaliber exports are preliminary architectural space-planning and drafting documents; field-verify all measurements on site and consult a licensed architect or structural engineer where permits require stamped drawings.

Three Mighty Alerts Supporting Hugging Face’s Production Infrastructure

📅 08 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Infrastructure team at Hugging Face is excited to share a behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of Hugging Face's production infrastructure, which we’ve had the privilege of helping to build and maintain.
  • In this blog post, we’ll dive into the details of three mighty alerts that play their unique role in supporting our production infrastructure, and explore how they've helped us maintain the high level of performance and uptime that our community relies on.
  • Industry observers note that oftentimes, with cloud computing architectures, where data flows between private and public networks, implementing a NAT (Network Address Translation) gateway stands as a steadfast best practice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Infrastructure team at Hugging Face is excited to share a behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of Hugging Face's production infrastructure, which we’ve had the privilege of helping to build and maintain. Our team's dedication to designing and implementing a robust monitoring and alerting system has been instrumental in ensuring the stability and scalability of our platforms. We’re constantly reminded of the impact that our alerts have on our ability to identify and respond to potential issues before they become major incidents.

In this blog post, we’ll dive into the details of three mighty alerts that play their unique role in supporting our production infrastructure, and explore how they've helped us maintain the high level of performance and uptime that our community relies on.

Industry observers note that oftentimes, with cloud computing architectures, where data flows between private and public networks, implementing a NAT (Network Address Translation) gateway stands as a steadfast best practice. This gateway acts as a strategic gatekeeper, monitoring and facilitating all outbound traffic towards the public Internet. By centralizing egress traffic, the NAT gateway offers a strategic vantage point for comprehensive visibility. Our team can easily query and analyze this traffic, making it an invaluable asset when working through security, cost optimization or various other investigative scenarios.

Sources indicate that cost optimization is a critical aspect of cloud infrastructure management, and understanding the pricing dynamics is key. In data centers, pricing structures often differentiate between east-west traffic (typically communication within the same rack or building) and north-south traffic (communication between further away private networks or the internet). By monitoring network traffic volume, Hugging Face gains valuable insights into these traffic patterns. This awareness allows us to make informed decisions regarding infrastructure configuration and architecture, ensuring we limit incurring needless costs.

One of our key alerts is designed to notify us when our network traffic volume surpasses a predefined threshold. This alert serves multiple purposes. Firstly, it acts as an early warning system, alerting us to any unusual spikes in traffic that might indicate potential challenges or unexpected behavior. Secondly, it prompts us to regularly review our traffic trends, ensuring we stay on top of our infrastructure's growth and evolving needs. This alert is set at a static threshold, which we have fine-tuned over time, ensuring it remains relevant and effective. When triggered, it often coincides with periods of refactoring our infrastructure.

For instance, when integrating third-party security and autoscaling tools, we've observed increased telemetry data egress from our nodes, triggering the alert and prompting us to optimize our configurations.

On another occasion, adjustments to our infrastructure lead to mistakenly avoiding a private, low-cost path between product-specific infrastructure (ex. traffic destined to the Hub from a Space to interact with repository data). To elaborate further, the most impactful workloads in terms of cost savings we’ve found are those that access object storage. Fetching objects directly prices cheaper than going through CDN-hosted assets for our LFS repository storage and additionally does not require the same security measures that our WAF provides compared to public requests arriving at our front door. Leveraging DNS overrides to switch traffic through private network paths and public network paths has become a valuable technique for us, driven by the CDKTF AWS provider.

As a final note, while we have configuration-as-code ensuring the desired state is always in effect, having an additional layer of alerting around helps in case mistakes are made when expressing the desired state through code.

According to recent reports, the logging infrastructure at Hugging Face is a sophisticated system designed to collect, process, and store vast amounts of log data generated by our applications and services. At the heart of this system is the Hub application logging pipeline, a well-architected solution that ensures Hub model usage data is efficiently captured, enriched, and stored for reporting and archival purposes. The pipeline begins with Filebeat, a lightweight log shipper that runs as a daemonset alongside our application pods in each Kubernetes cluster. Filebeat's role is to collect logs from various sources, including application containers, and forward them to the next stage of the pipeline.

Once logs are collected by Filebeat, they are sent to Logstash, a powerful log processing tool. Logstash acts as the data processing workhorse, applying a series of mutations and transformations to the incoming logs. This includes enriching logs with GeoIP data for geolocation insights, routing logs to specific Elasticsearch indexes based on predefined criteria, and manipulating log fields by adding, removing, or reformatting them to ensure consistency and ease of analysis. After Logstash has processed the logs, they are forwarded to an Elasticsearch cluster.

Elasticsearch, a distributed search and analytics engine, forms the core of our log storage and analysis platform. It receives the logs from Logstash and applies its own set of processing rules through Elasticsearch pipelines. These pipelines perform minimal processing tasks, such as adding timestamp fields to indicate the time of processing, which is crucial for log analysis and correlation. Elasticsearch provides a scalable and flexible storage solution, allowing us to buffer logs for operational use and real-time analysis.

Industry observers note that to manage the lifecycle of logs within Elasticsearch, we employ a robust storage and lifecycle management strategy. This ensures that logs are retained in Elasticsearch for a defined period, providing quick access for operational and troubleshooting purposes. After this retention period, logs are offloaded to long-term archival storage. The archival process involves an automated tool that reads logs from Elasticsearch indexes, formats them as Parquet files—an efficient columnar storage format—and writes them to our object storage system.

Sources indicate that the final stage of our logging pipeline leverages AWS data warehousing services. Here, AWS Glue crawlers are utilized to discover and classify data in our object storage, automatically generating a Glue Data Catalog, which provides a unified metadata repository. The Glue table schema is periodically refreshed to ensure it remains up-to-date with the evolving structure of our log data. This integration with AWS Glue enables us to query the archived logs using Amazon Athena, a serverless interactive query service. Athena allows us to run SQL queries directly against the data in object storage, providing a cost-effective and scalable solution for log analysis and historical data exploration.

Another point of fragility is the auto-schema detection mechanism in Elasticsearch. While it is designed to adapt to changing log structures, it can fail when application logs undergo significant field type changes. If the schema detection fails to recognize the latest field types, it may lead to failed writes from Logstash to Elasticsearch, causing log processing bottlenecks and potential data inconsistencies. This issue highlights the importance of proactive log schema management and the need for robust monitoring to detect and address such concerns promptly.

In a recent development, memory management is also a critical aspect of the pipeline's stability. The log processing tier, including Logstash and Filebeat, operates with limited memory resources to control costs. When backpressure occurs, these components can experience Out-of-Memory (OOM) issues, especially during system slowdowns. As logs accumulate and backpressure increases, the memory footprint of these processes grows, pushing them closer to their limits. If not addressed promptly, this can lead to process crashes or further exacerbation of the backpressure problem.

Archival jobs, responsible for transferring logs from Elasticsearch to object storage, have also encountered challenges. On occasion, these jobs can be resource-intensive, with their performance becoming sensitive to node size and memory availability. In cases where junk data or unusually large log entries pass through the pipeline, they can strain the archival process, leading to failures due to memory exhaustion or node capacity limits. This underscores the importance of data validation and filtering earlier in the pipeline to prevent such issues from reaching the archival stage.

According to recent reports, to mitigate these potential failures, we've implemented a powerful alert system with a unique motivation: validating end-to-end log flow. The alert is designed to compare the number of requests received by our Application Load Balancer (ALB) with the number of logs successfully archived, providing a comprehensive view of log data flow throughout the entire pipeline. This approach allows us to rapidly identify any discrepancies that might indicate potential log loss or processing complications.

Industry observers note that the alert mechanism is based on a simple yet effective comparison: the number of requests hitting our ALB, which represents the total log volume entering the system, versus the number of logs successfully archived in our long-term storage. By monitoring this ratio, we can ensure that what goes in must come out, providing a robust validation of our logging infrastructure's health. When the alert is triggered, it indicates a potential mismatch, prompting immediate investigation and remediation.

In a recent development, in practice, this alert has proven to be a valuable tool, especially during periods of infrastructure refactoring. For instance, when we migrated our ALB to a VPC origin, the alert was instrumental in identifying and addressing the resulting log flow discrepancies. However, it has also saved us in less obvious scenarios. For example, when archive jobs failed to run due to unforeseen challenges, the alert flagged the missing archived logs, allowing us to promptly investigate and resolve the problem before it impacted our log analysis and retention processes.

While this alert is a powerful tool, it is just one part of our comprehensive monitoring strategy. We continuously refine and adapt our logging infrastructure to handle the ever-increasing volume and complexity of log data. By combining proactive monitoring, efficient resource management, and a deep understanding of our system's behavior, Hugging Face ensures that our logging pipeline remains resilient, reliable, and capable of supporting our platform's growth and evolving needs. This alert is a testament to our commitment to maintaining a robust and transparent logging system, providing our teams with the insights they need to keep Hugging Face running smoothly.

Is a perfect Lighthouse score the goal?

According to recent reports, no. Use it to find the largest problems. A page that scores a little lower but loads its main content rapidly on a phone is better than one tuned to the test.

Not necessarily. Keep it cheap (CSS transforms and opacity), keep it away from the first screen, and respect reduced-motion settings.

It can, if you hand it the specific finding ("LCP element is the hero image, no dimensions") and ask it to change only that section. Vague requests like "make it faster" rarely help.

No. Everything above works with free tools and the AI builder you already use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STUDIO HERRSTRÃM rebuilds the Milkshake brand identity around car culture, a redrawn splash mark, high-vis color and road signs.

Milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its new identity starts in a car. The name was suggested on a car ride, milestones happened in cars, and new music was taken for a car test. The old splash is still there, redrawn as a rounded, blended symbol that reads like metal and liquid merging, and the wordmark runs through it with a zigzag cut that splits Milkshake into two stacked hits. On the posters the name fills the frame until the letters stop being text and start being the picture: acid yellow Milksh across the top, shake across the bottom.

The type system is Gates, a neo-grotesque from Contextype, shown in the specimen with arrows, asterisks, circled letters and roman numerals on a mauve field. The wordmark itself leans forward, its letters cut on a slant that matches the splash, and the supporting lockups borrow their logic from car window stickers and milk carton nutrition labels: small blocks of capitals that hold track names, release dates and the p-line symbol without breaking the grid.

The system proves itself on the objects it touches. A high-vis vest carries the full lockup on its back in black on acid yellow, with reflective bands borrowed from road markings. A neon green acrylic cube hangs outside the shopfront with the black wordmark on its face. A blender wears the whole icon set as stickers: the machine that makes the drink becomes the merch.

Color does the rest. Acid yellow is the signal color, while neon pink and soft lilac take the flavor cues and black keeps the contrast high. The same palette runs the subway poster for Tove Lo's single Me/You (always and forever), dated 18.09.26. Linn Wexell, founder and creative director of Milkshake, states the creative work was smart and on point and the visuals stunning.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

Industry observers note that “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” mentioned Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”.

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Industry observers note that urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

It has been revealed that working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

According to recent reports, “There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” noted Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”.

In a recent development, natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”.

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin mentioned.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who noted they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy noted tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related concerns than average.

In a recent development, another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

Recent findings suggest that “I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”.

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” noted Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Recent findings suggest that fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio noted. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”.

In a recent development, this article was originally published on Stanford News. Read the original article.

Melissa De Witte is the deputy director for social science communications for the Stanford News Service. She attained an M.A. in Media, Culture, & Communication from NYU and a B.Sc. in Sociology from LSE. She was previously the digital communications manager for the Division of Social Sciences at UC Santa Cruz.

#150464. The Overlooked Ways Love Highlights Up in Urban Spaces

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1121 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

The Overlooked Ways Love Highlights Up in Urban Spaces

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings.
  • But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue.
  • My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in major cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

In a recent development, we have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

First, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

Industry observers note that “I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde indicates. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”.

To get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He says: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

In a recent development, A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

Industry observers note that I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

Sources indicate that jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leonardo Pertileâs book design for ADI Design Museumâs Compasso dâOro packs 1,040 pages into twin cloth volumes set in OT Marmo.

Compressing nearly seventy years of Italian industrial design into a 1,040-page brick isnât a subtle problem. Presented by Fondazione ADI, ADI Associazione per il Disegno Industriale, and ADI Design Museum, this Treccani monograph is edited by Beppe Finessi and designed by Leonardo Pertile as twin cloth editions. Brick-red cloth printed in royal blue marks the English Historical Collection with a yellow ribbon, while yellow cloth inked in red identifies the Italian Collezione Storica with a navy ribbon. Neither cover uses product photography. A large blind-debossed compass presses into the woven board under Omnitypeâs pre-release OT Marmo capitals, and opening the red cover flashes yellow endpaper beside three tall floor lamps.

According to the museumâs notes, the publication holds 2,275 images across three parts: ADI Design Museumâs archival role, the 1954â2022 Compasso dâOro Roll of Honour, and critical essays and interviews. Pertile keeps that scale legible by shifting the grid per section so the book design doesnât lose its rhythm. On pages 154 and 155, Anty Panseraâs essay wraps justified columns around four staggered black-and-white ceremony photos. Another spread runs a hand-drawn nebido logo study on millimeter graph paper across the top above justified prose and hanging-indent captions citing Franco Albini, Franca Helg, and Bob Noorda. Turn to pages 474 and 475 for Anno 1967 and the density jumps â Enzo Mariâs concentric Freud Opere sketches and Mario Piazzaâs ruled pull quote face Olivettiâs tight vertical matrix of color-coded marks.

In a recent development, heavy catalogs donât work without quiet spreads. Page 577 pairs an overhead photo of a terracotta sofa and dark-green chaise directly above twin framed floor looks, leaving the plate clear of clutter. That open air widens in the essays and interviews. Alberto Saibeneâs Milano, 1954: cultura e industria opener floats OT Marmo headings high in white space above two narrow columns. On page 967, Beppe Finessiâs interview with Paola Antonelli switches to ragged-right text with outdented BF and PA initials in the margin so speakers scan fast. Itâs disciplined book design that makes a 1,040-page institutional archive easy to open and read.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Workers at a Jack in the Box on Park Street in Alameda went on strike Friday, accusing their employer of issuing bounced paychecks, delaying wages and retaliating against employees.
  • Legal Aid at Work filed a lawsuit last week alleging the pay problems also affected workers at other restaurants operated by the same franchisee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OAKLAND, Calif. (KGO) -- Two separate fights over workers' pay are gaining attention in the East Bay, as fast-food employees in Alameda protest alleged wage theft and Oakland moves closer to deciding the future of a proposed $30 minimum wage.

Workers at a Jack in the Box on Park Street in Alameda went on strike Friday, accusing their employer of issuing bounced paychecks, delaying wages and retaliating against employees.

Legal Aid at Work filed a lawsuit last week alleging the pay problems also affected workers at other restaurants operated by the same franchisee.

"We've had clients borrowing money to cover groceries, borrowing from family," said Samuel Aber, a staff attorney with Legal Aid at Work.

When asked whether the workers could afford to miss paychecks, Aber responded, "No they can't.".

MORE: Alameda County weighs nation's first $30 minimum wage.

ABC7 Eyewitness News reached out to Jack in the Box and the franchise operator for comment but had not received a response.

California has a $20 hourly minimum wage for covered fast-food workers.

Meanwhile, in nearby Oakland, organizers are pushing to gradually raise the city's minimum wage to $30 an hour.

Recent findings suggest that oakland's current minimum wage is $17.34 an hour, compared with $18.45 in San Jose and $19.61 in San Francisco. All three cities adjust their minimum wages annually for inflation.

"One job should be enough," stated Tonisha Scott, an organizer with One Fair Wage, who helped collect signatures for the Oakland initiative.

MORE: With 2027 minimum wage increase, Newsom says CA puts 'working families first'.

After months of gathering signatures, organizers qualified the proposal for city council consideration.

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday, Oakland's Rules and Legislation Committee voted 4-0 to schedule the measure for the full city council on Dec. 1. Councilmembers could adopt the initiative directly, send it to voters in 2028 or request an economic impact study before making a final decision.

Denis Sosinskiy, a postdoctoral scholar at UC Berkeley in labor and employment, mentioned research on minimum wage increases generally shows moderate effects on consumer prices, although businesses employing large numbers of low-wage workers may need to adjust.

The Black Organizing Project, which helped organize the signature drive, claims the campaign is also about preventing longtime residents from being priced out of Oakland.

"We're fighting, not just for ourselves, but our family members, our neighbors, our comrades to be able to live and stay in Oakland," noted Keala Uchoa, the organization's communications manager.

Recent findings suggest that under the proposed schedule, large employers would reach a $30 hourly minimum wage by 2030, medium-sized employers by 2035 and small employers by 2037. The timing of the increases could depend on whether the council adopts the measure or sends it to voters, potentially in November 2028.

No minimum wage increase was approved at Thursday's committee meeting.

#150449. Tech Report: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1552 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that finding love is substantial business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business.
  • The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages.
  • As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that finding love is substantial business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app people to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

According to recent reports, so if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

In a recent development, perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user notes they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

Sources indicate that what do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

Industry observers note that the truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Recent findings suggest that with the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

An alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

Amie M. Gordon, Ph.D., is a social-personality psychologist who takes a dynamic, dyadic approach to investigating the affective, social-cognitive, and biological processes that shape interpersonal relationships. Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The Newly introduced York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. She blogs for Psychology Today in Between You and Me, and is right now completing a postdoctoral research fellowship at the University of California, San Francisco.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dr.Me and Waiting Room Press turn torn street posters into a 400-page book design, hand-ripping every cover of Accidental Collage.

Sources indicate that every copy of Accidental Collage arrives damaged on purpose. Created by Manchester studio Dr.Me and published by Waiting Room Press, the 400-page volume documents weathered billboard strata pulled from city walls. According to Itâs Nice That, Dr.Meâs Mark âEddyâ Edwards drew the cover idea from book artist Lydia Davies, who purposefully defiled the edges of her poetry books. That choice hits before the spine even opens. On the cover, bold sans-serif capitals stack vertically down the right edge, sliced diagonally by a physical paper tear: black letters sit on creased white stock above the rip, flipping to white ink over raw ochre pasteboard and red scraps underneath. It doesnât observe street decay from a polite distance. The book behaves like a city hoarding itself.

Inside, the book design drops white margins completely. Full-bleed photographs push straight to the trim edges, anchored only by tiny centered folios along the bottom border so nothing interrupts the torn paper layers. Thereâs no border competing for attention, so cross-gutter pairings drive the pace. On pages 74 and 75, two ripped portraits lock eyes across the fold â a face peeking through jagged olive-green stenciled stock opposite a monochrome eye buried under white shreds and a red slash. Turn to page 259 and red lips above torn yellow ribbons face giant blue halftone teeth bordered by an exposed CMYK color bar. Elsewhere, pages 312 and 313 pair a shredded magenta portrait and clipped white serif type against a violet sheet torn across the middle to reveal a mouth and ghosted lettering.

It has been revealed that edwards told Itâs Nice That the archive grew after lockdowns as a community began trading found dÃ©collages from Manhattan building hoardings, Parisian metro walls, and London Underground theatre posters. Interviews and essays by Sarah Boris, Nick Deakin, Braulio Amado, and experimental drummers Hisham Akira Bharoocha and Jeremy Gustin sit alongside the plates, linking ripped street bills to rhythm and print culture. On pages 354 and 355, a shredded gig poster dated 09.11.24 faces bold white ON A MISSION FOREVER lettering ripping open over yellow underlayers. Thatâs the discipline behind this book design: strip away gallery framing and let ruined commercial print hold the page on its own.

13 Sam's Club Bakery Items, Ranked Worst To Best

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2268 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery.
  • Industry observers note that to get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past.
  • Industry observers note that the double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery. The full-service department offers everything from sliced bread and rolls for everyday use to custom cakes for your most special occasions. Like the other items under the warehouse roof, the bakery stocks bulk quantities and super-sized versions of many of its best-loved bakes, giving your bank account a bit of a breather without requiring you to give up your appetite for the good stuff.

Industry observers note that to get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past. I scooped up a selection of breads, rolls, and sugary delights to put under the microscope — my taste buds — and see how they rank amongst one another. Simple items like plain bagels shared the table with deluxe creations like caramel pecan banana loaf, all purchased at my Phoenix, Arizona-area Sam's locations. Prices and products shown are likely to vary based on region and warehouse. Clearly, membership has its privileges, but they're not all equally worth your money or your attention.

Industry observers note that the double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf. It's crusty and tender, perfect for breaking off chunks and dipping into olive oil or cheese dip. But it does limit your uses to silver dollar-sized slices, making mini garlic toast or bruschetta the most likely purposes. Slicing it lengthwise in longer sections will extend your toasting potential, but it's still a lot of bread to blow through before it starts to get even crustier on the counter.

It has been revealed that unless you have a house load of diners to feed, you may be getting more bread than you need, in a size and shape that makes using leftovers a bit limited. So while the bread itself is a wonderful version of a bakery-style baguette, the drawbacks of having two super-skinny loaves to work through may be reason enough to make a more suitable choice than this grocery store French bread.

According to recent reports, there's no sense in raving over how good a plain bagel can be. They're plain for a reason: so they can hold all kinds of spreads and shmears and fillings without the taste of ramped-up bread getting in the way. But that doesn't mean every bakery gets the basic formula for plain bagels right. So having a bodacious bag of six overly large, unadorned bagels waiting at Sam's Club, among the fancier flavors, is a comfort to the purists of the bread-loving world. They do make an attractive haul at only $3.82 for six large pre-cut bagels, so there's that, at least.

In a recent development, I'm a fan of bagels, largely for the dense chewiness they offer, similar to a pretzel but with more potential for add-ons that don't fall off. I'd love to endorse these bagels more heartily, since they do their job perfectly well at a price that doesn't feel like you're being gouged. But in the end, they're just bagels, and Sam's has so many preferable baked goods waiting to be tossed in your cart.

It has been revealed that sam's Club is famous for its generous 12-inch pumpkin pies that appear at holiday time, priced at a seasonally considerate $5.98. But beyond the size and price, the warehouse bakery doesn't do much out of the ordinary with this bake. The crust is standard, the filling is customary, and the experience of digging into a slice is perfectly passable. In fact, if you're a dessert traditionalist, this will do nicely to replace anything you were planning on making yourself.

It has been revealed that but the fact that the company mass-produces its pumpkin pies every year means you know exactly what you're getting here. If you keep your expectations in check and top it with a drizzle of chocolate or caramel sauce, plus some king-sized dollops of whipped cream, you can make it through another serving this year. Just don't count on it being anything more than average, even under all the decorations. You might even fare a little better with the comparable-yet-superior Costco pumpkin pie this year instead.

According to recent reports, something about the recipe Sam's Club bakery uses for its yeast dinner rolls makes them better than the thaw-and-bake versions I've become accustomed to. The chewy crust and soft centers of these baked spheres make them far too easy to snack on, which could readily deplete your stock for actual meals. The oversized bag comes with 24 rolls, so maybe you'll have enough for both if you can keep your appetite for bread snacks under control.

Maybe the best thing about these rolls is the price. You can drop $3.98 and end up with more bread than you can shake a stick at — a true magic trick in an economy that seems intent on crushing shoppers just hoping to come home with the basics. It'll put your imagination to the test when you realize your leftovers are crying out for creativity — cream puffs, mini-sandwiches, and bread pudding are all possibilities. Even if you freeze what you don't use for meals down the line, you'll be glad you made the purchase.

Similar to the yeast dinner rolls, Sam's Club bakery's brioche slider rolls are three-bite beauties that come pre-sliced to be filled with your favorite accouterments. But whether you opt to use them as dinner rolls or just toast them up and spread a little peanut butter inside instead of making actual sliders, they'll be just as satisfying. They have a buttery, eggy flavor that mimics full-sized brioche buns; the only thing reduced here is the scale, and even that makes them a fun choice for kid-size sandwiches of all sorts.

In a recent development, for $6.98, you get a generous stash of 24 slider buns. That may seem like too many, but if you use them in place of sliced bread for school lunches and work them into weekend meals, you'll blow through a whole bag before you know it. And if they're among your DIY barbecue spread or holiday celebration as cold cut holders, your guests are sure to gush over how cute and delicious they are.

It has been revealed that tangy, chewy, and ready to eat right out of the bag, the sliced sourdough loaves from Sam's Club bakery are a fantastic alternative to the rectangular bagged loaves the warehouse sells in its commercial bread aisle. It's the sort of sturdy bread that holds up well as grilled cheese sandwiches, Reubens without rye, and French toast, though you'll need to cut the slices in half for easier handling. And you can certainly cut it into strips to add to your grazing board for get-togethers or brunch sessions. It's the every-bread, and it's only $3.96 a loaf.

I tried to think of some drawbacks for this accommodating bake, but came up short. Despite having a host of sugary bites on the list that knocked my socks off, I thought this sourdough was excellent. It's pushed aside my usual go-to seedy whole-grain loaves to become my preferred full-size bread and an every-visit purchase.

Recent findings suggest that cocktail croissants, as Sam's Club calls them, are the bakery's sensibly sized version of the French classic, given all the love and attention of their continental counterparts, even in a warehouse grocery department setting. There's flakiness galore, thanks to an all-butter recipe that also comes through in the rich flavor. A carton of 20 croissants priced at $5.98, yet made with the same quality as their boulangerie counterparts, could be the bargain of our lifetimes.

The size is perfect for snacking, much better than the larger, sandwich-friendly croissants that cry out for fillings. Sure, you can break a bigger croissant into smaller pieces to make noshing a little more restrained. But when you can complete one in a few bites and walk away? That's sensibly sized croissant business. And if you're a fan of French pastries but cringe at spending big money to enjoy them, this first-rate batch of happiness is your golden opportunity, no splurging necessary.

It has been revealed that now this savage bake looks like the Ferrari of Sam's Club offerings, even before you take it out of the box. Through the cellophane window on top, you can see a heart-stopping coating of crumble in the perfect shade of toasted brown. The split in the top reveals a peek of golden pound cake. The overall effect is that you've stumbled onto the most gourmet banana bread you've ever encountered — right across from the bulk fabric softener and double-paned window vendors.

According to recent reports, the chewy crust is just shy of decadence, feeling more like an old-fashioned homemade crumble top without the oats. The banana bread beneath is equal parts sweet loaf and pound cake, capturing the cozy vibe but with a stroke of elegance that elevates it. I would eat this in all forms: cold out of the freezer, room temperature straight out of the box, or warmed up with a scoop of ice cream on the side. There's no situation that this fantastic loaf can't handle.

Gourmet bakeries have nothing on the patisserie spirit of Sam's Club mini creme pies. These refrigerated bakes shrink the lush goodness of full-sized pies into a six-pack of petite pastries, two each of chocolate creme, peanut butter chocolate, and cherry cheese pie. The reduced scale doesn't diminish the delicious returns; there's bold flavor and silky texture that make even a single slice a luxurious moment.

In a recent development, though all of these pies are a real treat, there's a definite hierarchy to their enjoyability. The cherry cheese pie is a mellow bite that resurrects the vintage pie flavor from long-ago Sunday dinner desserts, while the chocolate creme reminds me of a dessert-style specialty. But the top spot belongs to the peanut butter chocolate pie, which calls to mind luxury cheesecakes made by maestros of the baking world. It's a sweet dream of a Sam's Club baked goodie, and at $10.98 for six, it's one that doesn't require reservations — of any kind.

According to recent reports, any Sam's Club shopper will tell you that the bakery muffins are a cake situation, not a muffin scenario. These super-sweet, super-sized bakes are too significant and too delicious to qualify as traditional muffins, and when the warehouse puts a holiday spin on the usual recipes, that dessert-ready razzmatazz doubles up. They're the domed bakery-style muffins too, so they look extra grand on your snacking spread.

Sources indicate that I've had the store's traditional chocolate, blueberry, and banana nut muffins enough to be inured to their charms by now. But slicing into these three upgraded flavors was a seasonal revelation I won't soon get over. The red velvet is the best of the bunch, tasting like a pricey chef-inspired creation, while the pumpkin spice takes a more measured approach than the usual fall-flavored treats. And the butter pecan is a study in subtlety, with just the right balance of sweet and earthy notes. These should be year-round items.

Another refrigerated item due to the meltable toppings and delicate frosting, the gourmet cupcake eight-pack at Sam's Club bakery is a fancier take on the workaday cupcakes that come in a set of 30, and all taste exactly the same. In this package, you get a variety of chocolate, strawberry, and Meyer lemon, all wearing the frills and finery you'd find in a much pricier cupcake at a specialty shop. The $12.97 price tag that splits into $1.62 per cake assures you that you can have nice things without having to cash in your IRA.

Industry observers note that even if you choose to crack open your piggy bank for these, you'll be getting more than your money's worth. The chocolate cupcake is exceptional, lush, and over-packed with fudgy goodness thanks to a generous heap of ganache frosting. The strawberry is well-balanced, with its own floral ganache whip, and the Meyer lemon, with a dollop of gelee in the center, is bright as sunshine, authentic-tasting. There's a moist crumb and silky frosting in every cake, too. They're a little too complex to pass off as a home bake, but these are top-tier bakes that make a perfect meal finisher at a dinner party or a lovely surprise for birthday revelers.

#150443. Industry News: Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition
